title: Explain It Aloud
text: Explain It Aloud A checkoff is oral : you'll be asked how can you tell? , why? , and what do you expect to happen? — often before you press anything. Practise answering out loud (or type your answer), then reveal the model answer. These are short on purpose: TAs want the right idea in a sentence or two, not an essay. 1. You're stopped on total += prices[i]; and total is 0 while prices[i] is 18. Has the 18 been added yet? How can you tell? Show model answer No. A breakpoint pauses before the highlighted line runs, so that line is about to execute, not finished. total still being 0 confirms it. 2. Why would you use a conditional breakpoint instead of a regular one? Show model answer When the line runs many times (like in a loop) but I only care about one situation. The condition is a C expression checked each time the line is reached; the debugger only pauses when it's true, but the other iterations still run normally. 3. How can you find out what a variable will be after the next statement, without running it? Show model answer Evaluate the arithmetic myself in the Debug Console — e.g. total + prices[i] . Evaluating an expression only reads values, so nothing in the running program changes. (An assignment like total = 0 would change it.) 4. In one sentence each: Step Over, Step Into, Step Out. Show model answer Step Over: run this line, including any function it calls, without entering the function. Step Into: if the line calls one of my functions, go inside and pause on its first line. Step Out: finish the current function and pause back in its caller. 5. What does the Call Stack show, and what happens when you click a lower frame? Show model answer It shows every function that has been called but hasn't returned yet, with the one executing now on top and main at the bottom. Clicking a lower frame runs nothing — it only changes which frame's variables I'm inspecting. The program's execution point stays where it was. 6. Talk me through how you'd find an unknown bug with the debugger. Show model answer A repeatable routine: 1. State expected vs. actual “It should have applied the surcharge; it didn't.” 2. Work backward from the symptom The surcharge depends on weight , so check weight first. 3. Breakpoint just before the suspect Not at the top of main — close to where the value goes wrong. 4. Predict, then step Say what you expect a line to do; Step Over or Into; compare. 5. Find the first divergence The first place actual ≠ expected is where the bug is (or feeds it). 6. Fix, save, recompile, re-run Then confirm the original symptom is gone. 7. What's the difference between launch.json and tasks.json ? Show model answer tasks.json defines how the program is built (the gcc -g ... command, using variables like \${file} ). launch.json defines how the debugger runs it (the executable path, gdb , program arguments, and a preLaunchTask that runs the build first). 8. Why does the “input redirected” configuration launch /bin/bash instead of the program itself? Show model answer The < redirection is a shell feature, not something the program understands. So the debugger starts Bash with -lc "program < file" ; Bash points stdin at the file, then runs the program under the debugger. To use a different input file I just edit the path after the < .

title: Common Mistakes on the Debugging Checkoff
text: Common Mistakes on the Debugging Checkoff Not obscure errors — the ones that look right. Read this tab right before your slot. 1. Showing up with the debugger not working. The handout says it in red: no extra time . Do the setup checklist on the first tab and make sure a test breakpoint really pauses — before your slot. 2. Reading the highlighted line as “already ran.” Breakpoints and every step stop before the highlighted line executes. Nearly every “is X already Y?” question in the sample depends on this. 3. Forgetting to restart the debugger between sections. The sample says “restart the program” several times. If you don't, you're still paused somewhere mid-run — your breakpoints won't hit where you expect, and your predictions will be about the wrong moment. Also remove or disable old breakpoints when told to (section 5 and section 9), or the program keeps stopping in places you no longer care about. 4. Typing = instead of == in a breakpoint condition or in the console. prices[i] = 40 doesn't test anything — it overwrites prices[i] with 40 and is always true. Comparisons use == , > , < . Assignments typed in the Debug Console change the running program, which is exactly what section 4d is asking about. 5. Using Step Into on a library call. There's no source for printf , scanf , or toupper , so Step Into just acts like Step Over. Step Into is for your own functions. 6. Editing the redirected configuration but launching the other one. If you pick Debug active file , nothing is redirected: the program sits there waiting for you to type the input (it looks frozen). Choose Debug with input redirected from the dropdown, and make sure the input file is in the same folder as the source (the path is built from \${fileDirname} ). Don't get < and > backwards either: > would erase your input file. 7. Not saving or recompiling after your fix. Save the file first. Then remember the two paths: the terminal runs whatever the last gcc produced (section 10a: re-run gcc to update it), while the debugger rebuilds with -g automatically via preLaunchTask . If the terminal still shows the old bug after you fixed it, you forgot to recompile. 8. Answering with the click, not the reason. You'll be asked “how can you tell?” and to predict before acting . Say the expectation first (“I expect to land on line 49 in process_order ”), then do it, then compare. A correct action with no explanation is worth less than one where you can say why. Related: the CL10 · Debugging lesson has the full launch.json / tasks.json reference and a worked bug hunt, and Checkoff 1 Prep covers the redirection commands ( < , > , >> ) this checkoff re-tests in section 10.

title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Assembling Computers cannot understand Python, Java, or C. They understand machine code : binary instructions — strings of 1s and 0s — that tell the processor what operations to perform. Everything else is a translation layer built to spare humans from writing that. How we got from bits to C Era What you wrote What made it possible Before the 1950s Machine code , entered by switches, punch cards, or paper tape nothing — you were the translator Early 1950s Assembly language — human-readable mnemonics like add x8, x9, x10 Assemblers , programs that translate assembly into machine code Late 1950s High-level languages that abstract away the hardware and focus on logic and algorithms Compilers Machines still cannot read assembly — only machine code. The assembler exists precisely to automate that conversion, and it is what let programmers write and debug far more efficiently. The three languages the slides name Year Language Why it mattered 1957 FORTRAN (FORmula TRANslation) First widely adopted high-level language; built by IBM for scientific and engineering calculations 1958 LISP (LISt Processor) Pioneered functional programming and symbolic processing 1959 COBOL (COmmon Business-Oriented Language) Business applications; emphasized readability and portability; became the enterprise/financial standard Low-level vs high-level Machine code Assembly (low-level) C (high-level) Looks like 0b0000000010100100... add x8, x9, x10 return num * num; Readable by the machine humans, with effort humans, easily Tied to a specific processor yes yes no C is a compiled high-level language. To execute it, the program is first translated into assembly by a compiler , then the assembler translates that assembly into machine code . Two translations, two different tools. Interpreted languages like Python are executed differently — no separate compile-then-run step producing a machine-code file. Multiple choice What does a compiler translate, and into what? Assembly language into machine code A high-level language into assembly language Machine code into a high-level language Source code directly into output on the screen Compiler: high-level → assembly . Option 0 is the assembler . Two distinct programs, run one after the other — gcc just hides the seam by doing both. Multiple choice Why do assemblers exist? Because machines cannot read machine code Because C is faster than assembly Because machines cannot read assembly language — something has to convert it to machine code Because assembly is a high-level language Machines read only machine code. Assembly is for humans; the assembler automates the conversion. Option 0 has it exactly backwards.

title: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program
text: Lesson 2 · Your First C Program #include <stdio.h> int main () { printf ( "Hello, world!\\n" ); return 0 ; } Line Why it is there #include <stdio.h> printf is a standard library function. C does not automatically include any standard library functions — to use printf you must explicitly include stdio.h . int main() All C programs begin executing at main . It returns an int — the program's exit status . return 0; A successful execution returns 0 . An abnormal execution returns a non-zero value. Note the direction of that convention: 0 means success , which is the opposite of the usual "0 is false" intuition. Non-zero is how a program reports which thing went wrong. The C Standard Library A collection of pre-written functions for common tasks: input/output, string manipulation, mathematical operations, memory management. The functions are grouped into header files . A header file contains the declarations of the functions, macros, and types you can use. Term Meaning Function declaration the function's name, return type, and parameters Function definition the body of the function The header gives you the declaration so the compiler knows how to call the function; the definition lives in the compiled library. Header file Purpose Example functions <stdio.h> Input/output printf, getchar, putchar, fopen <stdlib.h> General utilities malloc, free, exit, atoi, rand <string.h> String manipulation strlen, strcpy, strcat, strcmp <math.h> Mathematical operations sqrt, pow, sin, cos, tan, exp <time.h> Date and time time, clock, localtime, gmtime Multiple choice You call strlen but forget #include <string.h> . Why is that a problem? The function does not exist without the include C automatically includes it anyway, so it is fine C does not automatically include standard library functions — without the header the compiler has no declaration for strlen Header files are optional in C The function's definition exists in the library either way, but the compiler needs the declaration from the header to know its return type and parameters. The slides state it plainly: "C does not automatically include any standard library functions." Multiple choice What does the value returned by main represent? The number of lines the program printed The program's exit status — 0 for success, non-zero for abnormal The amount of memory used Nothing; it is ignored The exit status . This is how the shell (and tools like make ) find out whether your program succeeded.

title: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc
text: Lesson 2 · Compiling and Running with gcc Write your program. Save it with a .c extension — say hello.c . Open a terminal and cd to the directory where the program lives. Compile and assemble: gcc hello.c Run it: ./a.out gcc invokes the G NU C C ompiler. It converts your human-readable C code into a machine-readable executable file . Command Executable produced gcc hello.c a.out (the default) gcc hello.c -o hello hello gcc -o hello hello.c hello gcc hello.c -o hi hi The -o rule. The executable name must immediately follow -o . Everything else about the ordering is flexible — notice rows 2 and 3 produce the same result with -o hello on either side of the source file. What you cannot do is separate -o from its argument. Why ./ ? . means the current directory (straight from Lesson 1), so ./a.out says "run the a.out that is right here." The ./ is required because the current directory is not in your PATH — the list of directories the shell searches for commands. Type a bare a.out and the shell searches PATH , does not find it, and reports "command not found," even though the file is sitting right in front of you. This is a deliberate security decision: if . were on the PATH, dropping a malicious file named ls into a directory would hijack the real ls . If you named the executable hello , run it with ./hello . In-class problem — multiple select Which of these sets of commands compile, assemble, and execute the program in my_program.c ? Tick every one that works. A. gcc my_program.c then ./my_program.c B. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./a.out C. gcc my_program.c -o my_prog then ./my_prog D. gcc my_program.c then ./a.out E. gcc my_program.c -o my_program then ./my_program.c Check C and D. The single idea being tested: you run the executable, never the .c source file. A and E both try to execute my_program.c — that is source code, not a program. B renames the executable to my_program with -o , so a.out was never created; ./a.out fails. D uses the default name a.out and runs a.out . C names it my_prog and runs my_prog . Both are consistent.

title: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types
text: Lesson 2 · Variables and Types Property Meaning Scope Where in a program you can use a variable Lifetime When the variable exists in memory Type The range of values the variable can represent, and how the value will be interpreted That second half of "type" is the one worth underlining. A type does not only bound the values — it decides what the bits mean . The same byte is 65 or 'A' depending on how you read it, which is the entire subject of the next tab. C numeric types Type Usual size Values stored Declaration char 1 byte integers char x; short 2 bytes signed integers short x; int 4 bytes signed integers int x; long 4 or 8 bytes signed integers long x; long long 8 bytes signed integers long long x; float 4 bytes signed real numbers float x; double 8 bytes signed real numbers double x; 8 bits = 1 byte. So an int is 32 bits, and a char is 8. "Usual" is doing real work in that table. The exact number of bytes for each C type might vary from one architecture to the next — which is why long is listed as "4 or 8." Never hard-code a size you did not measure. Measuring with sizeof The sizeof operator takes the name of a type and evaluates to the number of bytes used to store it. printf ( "number of bytes in an int: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( int )); printf ( "number of bytes in a short: %lu\\n" , sizeof ( short )); sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so print it with %lu — not %d . This is a real compiler warning you will hit. Multiple choice Which placeholder should you use to print sizeof(int) ? %d %s %lu %c sizeof evaluates to an unsigned long , so %lu . Multiple choice How many bits are in a typical int ? 4 32 8 64 4 bytes × 8 bits per byte = 32 bits . The "4" in the table is bytes, not bits — read that column carefully.

title: Lesson 2 · printf
text: Lesson 2 · printf C's printf is very similar to Java's System.out.printf : the caller supplies a format string to print. The format string contains formatting specifiers — special characters that print tabs ( \\t ) or newlines ( \\n ), and placeholders for values. A placeholder is % followed by a type-specifier letter , and for each placeholder, printf expects an additional argument . Placeholders Placeholder Used for Example Output %d Signed integer printf("%d", 25); 25 %u Unsigned integer printf("%u", 25); 25 %f Floating-point number printf("%f", 3.14); 3.14 %c Single character printf("%c", 'A'); A %s String printf("%s", "Hello"); Hello %lu Unsigned long (e.g. sizeof ) printf("%lu", sizeof(int)); 4 Special characters (escape sequences) A special character has a specific meaning or function in the language rather than simply representing ordinary text. In C, escape sequences use a backslash ( \\ ) to represent them — which lets you include characters that are difficult to type or represent directly. Sequence Name Meaning Example \\n Newline Moves to the next line "Hello\\nWorld" \\t Tab Inserts a horizontal tab "Name:\\tJohn" \\\\ Backslash Prints a \\ "C:\\\\Users" \\" Double quote Prints a " inside a string "He said \\"Hello\\"" \\0 Null character Marks the end of a C string "Hello\\0" %% Percent sign Prints a % when using printf printf("50%%"); Two different escape characters doing two different jobs. \\ introduces a special character; % introduces a placeholder. That is why a literal percent sign is %% and not \\% — it is escaping within printf's own notation, not C's. Match each specifier %d — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %c — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %s — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\n — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign \\t — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign %% — choose — signed integer single character string newline tab a literal percent sign Check

title: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII
text: Lesson 2 · Characters and ASCII ASCII stands for American Standard Code for Information Interchange . It is a code that lets computers represent text using numbers. The C char type stores a numeric value — but it is most often used to hold the value of an ASCII character. Values worth memorizing Character ASCII value 'A' 65 'B' 66 'a' 97 '0' 48 space 32 '!' 33 Learn 65, 97, 48 and the rest follow: letters and digits run consecutively, and lowercase is exactly 32 above uppercase. With 8 bits An unsigned char holds the values [0, 2 8 −1] = [0, 255] . That is comfortably more than enough for the ASCII set. Bits are just bits. To give bits meaning you must assign them a representation , which defines how they correspond to meaningful information. Take the value 0b0100 0001 : • as a decimal integer it reads as 65 • as an ASCII character it reads as 'A' Nothing about the bits changed. Only the interpretation did. %c vs %d — the same value, two readings printf ( "%c\\n" , 'A' ); // A printf ( "%d\\n" , 'A' ); // 65 Give it a character and ask for a number: you get the ASCII code. printf ( "%c\\n" , 67 ); // C printf ( "%d\\n" , 87 ); // 87 Give it a number and ask for a character: you get the character with that ASCII encoding. The placeholder chooses the interpretation. The value being passed is a number either way. Character arithmetic Because a char is a number, you can do arithmetic with characters. printf ( "%d\\n" , 'a' - 'C' ); The ASCII value of 'C' is 67 and of 'a' is 97, so this prints 30 . The genuinely useful version of this trick is the constant 'a' - 'A' = 32 , the gap between lowercase and uppercase. Subtract it from a lowercase letter and you get the uppercase one — which is exactly how the in-class echo program works. Why we are learning this The slides make the point explicitly: ASCII is not specific to C. Computers ultimately represent all data using binary, including letters, digits, and symbols. Regardless of the language you use, characters must be represented numerically so the computer can store and process them. Learning ASCII is how you internalize the relationship between characters and their numeric representations — the same "bits are just bits" idea that runs through the entire course.

Uppercase 0b0100 0001 vs lowercase 0b0110 0001 : one bit apart.

title: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF
text: Lesson 2 · getchar , putchar , and EOF Function What it does getchar() Reads one character from the input (a keyboard or a file) and returns it as an integer putchar(c) Takes the character stored in c and prints it to the output Both live in <stdio.h> , so you need that include. #include <stdio.h> int main () { int my_char = getchar (); printf ( "The user entered: %c\\n" , my_char); } EOF, and why getchar returns an int EOF stands for End of File . It is a special value returned by getchar() when there is no more input to read. EOF is the reason getchar() returns an int instead of a char . EOF must be distinguishable from any valid character. In the ASCII character set all valid characters are encoded as integers from 0 to 255 ; if EOF were encoded as a char it could collide with a real character value. The slides give the concrete case: if EOF were represented as 255 on a system where char is unsigned, it would conflict with the ASCII value for the ÿ character. An int is wider than a char , so there is room for a value outside 0–255 that no real character can ever equal. You signal EOF manually with Ctrl + D on Linux/macOS, or Ctrl + Z on Windows. The echo loop, two ways This reads characters until EOF and prints each one — it copies input to output, one character at a time. Explicit int main () { int c = getchar (); while (c != EOF) { putchar (c); c = getchar (); } } Concise (the idiom) int main () { int c; while ((c = getchar ()) != EOF) { putchar (c); } } The right-hand version reads inside the condition: first c gets the next character, then the while checks whether that character is EOF. The inner parentheses around (c = getchar()) are required — without them, precedence would compare getchar() to EOF first and assign the resulting 0 or 1 to c . Multiple choice Why does getchar() return an int rather than a char ? Because int is faster on modern hardware Because characters can be larger than one byte So EOF can be a value distinguishable from every valid character (0–255) Because putchar requires an int EOF has to be a value that no real character can equal . A char has no spare values left; an int does. True / False In while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) , the inner parentheses are optional style. True False They are required . != binds tighter than = , so c = getchar() != EOF would compare first and then assign the comparison result (0 or 1) into c — the loop would run, but c would never hold a character.

title: CL13 · Fractions in Binary & Fixed Point
text: CL13 · Fractions in Binary & Fixed Point Binary works exactly like decimal, just with powers of 2. To the left of the binary point the places are 1, 2, 4, 8…; to the right they are ½, ¼, ⅛, 1/16… (that is 2 −1 , 2 −2 , 2 −3 , 2 −4 ). 2 3 2 2 2 1 2 0 . 2 −1 2 −2 2 −3 2 −4 8 4 2 1 . 0.5 0.25 0.125 0.0625 Decimal does the same thing: 234.56 = (2×100) + (3×10) + (4×1) + (5×0.1) + (6×0.01). Binary → decimal Add the place value under every 1. 101.101 = (1×4) + (0×2) + (1×1) + (1×0.5) + (0×0.25) + (1×0.125) = 5.625 01110.1011 = 14 + 0.5 + 0.125 + 0.0625 = 14.6875 Decimal → binary Convert the integer part as usual. For the fraction, build it from powers of ½: take the biggest one that fits, subtract, repeat. 12.75: 12 = 1100 0.75 = 0.5 + 0.25 = .11 → 1100.11 5/8 : 5/8 = 0.5 + 0.125 = .101 → 0.101 3.125: 3 = 11 0.125 = .001 → 11.001 Fixed point Fixed-point representation keeps the binary point at a fixed spot in the bit pattern (say, 4 bits before and 4 after). It is simple, but a given number of bits buys either range or fractional precision , never both. Floating point is the fix: let the point float . Check What is the place value of the third digit to the right of the binary point? 1/3 1/6 1/8 3/10 The places are ½, ¼, ⅛ : 2 −3 = 1/8. Check Convert 0b101.1 to decimal. Check 4 + 1 + ½ = 5.5. Check Convert 0b1100.011 to decimal. Check 8 + 4 + ¼ + ⅛ = 12.375. Check Write 3.75 as fixed-point binary (no prefix). Check 3 = 11 and 0.75 = ½ + ¼ = .11, so 11.11 . Check Write 6.625 as fixed-point binary (no prefix). Check 6 = 110 and 0.625 = ½ + ⅛ = .101, so 110.101 . Check Why is fixed point a poor way to cover both very large and very small numbers? It cannot store fractions Its binary point is fixed, so the bits spent on the fraction are taken away from the range (and vice versa) It always needs 64 bits Computers cannot add fixed-point numbers With a fixed split of bits you pick a range or fine precision. Floating point moves the point with an exponent.

title: CL13 · Scientific Notation, Normalized Form & the Implicit 1
text: CL13 · Scientific Notation, Normalized Form & the Implicit 1 Scientific notation writes a number as significand × base exponent : 9.2318 × 10 5 . It is normalized when the significand satisfies 1 ≤ |significand| < 10 . In binary the base is 2 and the normalized form requires 1 ≤ |significand| < 2 , so the digit left of the point is always 1 . 1.0101 × 2 6 ^^^^^^ ^ significand exponent (base 2; the point is the binary point) Convert: 1.0101 × 2 6 = 1010100 = 64 + 16 + 4 = 84 (move the point 6 places right). Normalize 10.5: 10.5 = 1010.1 ; move the point 3 places left → 1.0101 × 2 3 . The implicit 1 Because every nonzero normalized number looks like 1.xxxx × 2 e , the leading 1 carries no information. We do not store it . We store only the digits after the point (the significand bits , a.k.a. fraction or mantissa) and the exponent. That frees one bit for extra precision. Number Binary Normalized Stored significand bits Exponent 5 101 1.01 × 2 2 01 2 10.5 1010.1 1.0101 × 2 3 0101 3 0.375 0.011 1.1 × 2 −2 1 −2 7 111 1.11 × 2 2 11 2 Check Which of these is in normalized binary form? 0.10101 × 2 7 10.101 × 2 5 1.0101 × 2 6 101.01 × 2 4 Normalized means exactly one 1 to the left of the point: 1 ≤ significand < 2. Check Write 6 in normalized binary form: give the exponent. Check 6 = 110 = 1.1 × 2 2 . Check Write 6 in normalized binary form: give the significand bits stored (after the point). Check 1.1 → the stored bits are just 1 . Check Normalize 0.1875 (= 0.0011 in binary). What is the exponent? Check 0.0011 = 1.1 × 2 −3 . The point moves 3 places right, so the exponent is −3. Check What is 1.1 × 2 3 in decimal? Check 1.1 × 2 3 = 1100 = 12. Check Why does a floating-point format not store the leading 1? It would make the number negative Every nonzero normalized number starts with 1, so it is implied, and the saved bit buys one more bit of precision The hardware cannot store a 1 there It is stored in the sign bit The implicit 1 is free precision.

title: CL13 · Microfloat V1 (2 exponent bits, 2 significand bits)
text: CL13 · Microfloat V1 (2 exponent bits, 2 significand bits) Microfloat is a made-up 4-bit floating-point format for exploring design trade-offs. V1: 2 exponent bits then 2 significand bits , no sign bit, no bias. Value = 1. sig × 2 exp , where the exponent field is read as an ordinary unsigned number (0–3). Explorer: click bits to build a microfloat Every V1 value Bits (exp sig) Value form Decimal 00 00 1.00 × 2 0 1 00 01 1.01 × 2 0 1.25 00 10 1.10 × 2 0 1.5 00 11 1.11 × 2 0 1.75 01 00 1.00 × 2 1 2 01 01 1.01 × 2 1 2.5 01 10 1.10 × 2 1 3 01 11 1.11 × 2 1 3.5 10 00 1.00 × 2 2 4 10 01 1.01 × 2 2 5 10 10 1.10 × 2 2 6 10 11 1.11 × 2 2 7 11 00 1.00 × 2 3 8 11 01 1.01 × 2 3 10 11 10 1.10 × 2 3 12 11 11 1.11 × 2 3 14 Largest = 1.11 × 2 3 = 14. Smallest = 1. Nothing below 1, and the gaps widen (0.25 apart, then 0.5, 1, 2). Encoding — worked examples 3.5 = 11.1 = 1.11 × 2 1 exponent 1 = 01, significand 11 → 0111 7 = 111 = 1.11 × 2 2 exponent 2 = 10, significand 11 → 1011 1.25 = 1.01 × 2 0 exponent 0 = 00, significand 01 → 0001 Recipe: binary → normalize → drop the leading 1 → write exponent bits, then significand bits. If the exponent needs more than 2 bits, the value is out of range . If the significand needs more than 2 bits, it needs more precision than V1 has. Decoding — worked examples 0101: exponent 01 = 1, significand 01 → 1.01 × 2 1 = 10.1 = 2.5 1101: exponent 11 = 3, significand 01 → 1.01 × 2 3 = 1010 = 10 Representable? Four cases Value Normalized Fits? Encoding / reason 1.75 1.11 × 2 0 yes 0011 2.75 1.011 × 2 1 no needs 3 significand bits — not enough precision 5 1.01 × 2 2 yes 1001 12 1.1 × 2 3 yes 1110 16 1 × 2 4 no exponent 4 does not fit in 2 bits — not enough range Check Decode microfloat V1 1011 . Check Exponent 10 = 2, significand 11: 1.11 × 2 2 = 111 = 7. Check Decode microfloat V1 0110 . Check Exponent 01 = 1, significand 10: 1.1 × 2 1 = 11 = 3. Check Encode 6 in microfloat V1 (4 bits). Check 6 = 110 = 1.1 × 2 2 → exponent 10, significand 10 → 1010 . Check Encode 12 in microfloat V1 (4 bits). Check 12 = 1100 = 1.1 × 2 3 → exponent 11, significand 10 → 1110 . Check Encode 9 in microfloat V1, or write N/A if it cannot be represented. Check 9 = 1001 = 1.001 × 2 3 : three significand bits are needed but V1 has two (not enough precision), so N/A . Check Why can microfloat V1 not represent 4.5? There is not enough range There are not enough significand bits (4.5 = 1.001 × 2 2 needs three) The sign bit is missing 4.5 is not a binary fraction The exponent 2 fits easily; the significand 001 does not. That is a precision failure, not a range failure. Check Why can microfloat V1 not represent 16? Not enough precision Not enough range: 16 = 1.0 × 2 4 needs exponent 4, but 2 bits only reach 3 It is even The significand would be negative A range failure: the exponent is too large for its field.

title: CL13 · Design Trade-offs: Range vs Precision
text: CL13 · Design Trade-offs: Range vs Precision Four bits have to be shared between the exponent and the significand. More exponent bits → more range, less precision. More significand bits → more precision, less range. Both are limited by the total number of bits. Microfloat V2: 1 exponent bit, 3 significand bits Bits (exp sig) Value form Decimal 0 000 1.000 × 2 0 1 0 001 1.001 × 2 0 1.125 0 010 1.010 × 2 0 1.25 0 011 1.011 × 2 0 1.375 0 100 1.100 × 2 0 1.5 0 101 1.101 × 2 0 1.625 0 110 1.110 × 2 0 1.75 0 111 1.111 × 2 0 1.875 1 000 1.000 × 2 1 2 1 001 1.001 × 2 1 2.25 1 010 1.010 × 2 1 2.5 1 011 1.011 × 2 1 2.75 1 100 1.100 × 2 1 3 1 101 1.101 × 2 1 3.25 1 110 1.110 × 2 1 3.5 1 111 1.111 × 2 1 3.75 Fine steps (0.125) but the exponent is only 0 or 1, so the largest value is 3.75. Microfloat V3: 3 exponent bits, 1 significand bit Bits (exp sig) Value form Decimal 000 0 1.0 × 2 0 1 000 1 1.1 × 2 0 1.5 001 0 1.0 × 2 1 2 001 1 1.1 × 2 1 3 010 0 1.0 × 2 2 4 010 1 1.1 × 2 2 6 011 0 1.0 × 2 3 8 011 1 1.1 × 2 3 12 100 0 1.0 × 2 4 16 100 1 1.1 × 2 4 24 101 0 1.0 × 2 5 32 101 1 1.1 × 2 5 48 110 0 1.0 × 2 6 64 110 1 1.1 × 2 6 96 111 0 1.0 × 2 7 128 111 1 1.1 × 2 7 192 Range up to 192, but only two values per power of two (1 and 1.5 × 2 e ), so the gaps are huge: 96, 128, 192. Side by side Format Exp / Sig bits Smallest Largest Step near 1 V1 2 / 2 1 14 0.25 V2 1 / 3 1 3.75 0.125 V3 3 / 1 1 192 0.5 Why not? Reason about it in this order Write the number in binary and normalize it: 1. f × 2 e . Exponent too big (or, with no bias, negative)? → not enough range . Significand needs more bits than the format has? → not enough precision . Otherwise it fits: write exponent then significand bits. Check Moving one bit from the significand to the exponent generally… increases both range and precision increases range and decreases precision increases precision and decreases range changes neither Exponent bits set the range; significand bits set the precision. The total is fixed. Check What is the largest value microfloat V3 can represent? Check 1.1 × 2 7 = 192. Check What is the largest value microfloat V2 can represent? Check 1.111 × 2 1 = 11.11 = 3.75. Check Encode 12 in microfloat V3 (3 exponent bits, 1 significand bit). Check 12 = 1.1 × 2 3 → exponent 011, significand 1 → 0111 . Check Encode 1.125 in microfloat V2 (1 exponent bit, 3 significand bits). Check 1.125 = 1.001 × 2 0 → exponent 0, significand 001 → 0001 . Check In V3, why can 1.75 not be stored? Not enough range Not enough precision: 1.75 = 1.11 needs two significand bits and V3 has one The exponent is negative It is not positive V3 only has 1.0 and 1.5 at each exponent.

title: CL13 · Representing Small Values: the Bias (Microfloat V4)
text: CL13 · Representing Small Values: the Bias (Microfloat V4) V1–V3 can never store a value below 1, because the exponent field is unsigned. The fix is a bias : store exponent + bias , so the field can stand for negative exponents too. V4 keeps 2 exponent bits and 2 significand bits and uses bias 2 , so exponents run −2…1. Decoding: value = 1. sig × 2 exponent bits − bias . Encoding: exponent bits = exponent + bias . Encode 0.75 = 0.11 = 1.1 × 2 −1 field = −1 + 2 = 1 = 01, significand 10 → 0110 Encode 2.5 = 10.1 = 1.01 × 2 1 field = 1 + 2 = 3 = 11, significand 01 → 1101 Decode 0111: field 01 = 1, 1.11 × 2 1−2 = 0.111 = 0.875 Decode 1110: field 11 = 3, 1.10 × 2 3−2 = 11 = 3 Every V4 value Bits (exp sig) Value form Decimal 00 00 1.00 × 2 -2 0.25 00 01 1.01 × 2 -2 0.3125 00 10 1.10 × 2 -2 0.375 00 11 1.11 × 2 -2 0.4375 01 00 1.00 × 2 -1 0.5 01 01 1.01 × 2 -1 0.625 01 10 1.10 × 2 -1 0.75 01 11 1.11 × 2 -1 0.875 10 00 1.00 × 2 0 1 10 01 1.01 × 2 0 1.25 10 10 1.10 × 2 0 1.5 10 11 1.11 × 2 0 1.75 11 00 1.00 × 2 1 2 11 01 1.01 × 2 1 2.5 11 10 1.10 × 2 1 3 11 11 1.11 × 2 1 3.5 General bias: for an exponent field of n bits, bias = 2 n−1 − 1 . That gives almost equally many positive and negative exponents (one more negative). 2 bits → bias 1; 3 bits → bias 3. (V4 uses bias 2 just for this example.) Why bias and not two's complement for the exponent? Comparisons become easy: with a biased exponent larger numbers have larger bit patterns, so you can compare floats as unsigned integers. With two's complement, negative exponents (leading 1s) would look larger than positive ones. Check Decode microfloat V4 0111 (bias 2). Check Field 01 = 1, exponent 1 − 2 = −1: 1.11 × 2 −1 = 0.111 = 0.875. Check Decode microfloat V4 1110 (bias 2). Check Field 11 = 3, exponent 3 − 2 = 1: 1.10 × 2 1 = 11 = 3. Check Encode 0.5 in microfloat V4 (bias 2). Check 0.5 = 1.0 × 2 −1 → field −1 + 2 = 1 = 01, significand 00 → 0100 . Check Encode 3.5 in microfloat V4 (bias 2). Check 3.5 = 1.11 × 2 1 → field 3 = 11, significand 11 → 1111 . Check Can 0.125 be encoded in V4? Answer N/A, or the 4-bit encoding. Check 0.125 = 1.0 × 2 −3 , but the smallest exponent is −2: not enough range. N/A . Check What is the bias for an exponent field of 3 bits? Check 2 3−1 − 1 = 3. Check What is the main advantage of a biased exponent over a two's complement exponent? It uses fewer bits Floating-point numbers can be compared like unsigned integers It removes the sign bit It gives more significand bits Biased exponents grow with the value, so bigger numbers have bigger bit patterns.

title: CL14 · The Bias and the 8-bit Minifloat
text: CL14 · The Bias and the 8-bit Minifloat Bias. To represent negative exponents we store exponent + bias . For an exponent field of n bits, bias = 2 n−1 − 1 . With 3 exponent bits the bias is 3 , the field runs 0–7 and the true exponent runs −3…4. (Slight asymmetry: one more negative exponent than positive.) A biased exponent also lets you compare floats as unsigned integers; two's complement exponents would break that ordering. Minifloat layout (8 bits): bit: 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0 s e e e f f f f sign exponent significand (bias 3) (implicit leading 1) normalized value = (−1) s × 1.ffff × 2 eee − 3 0 101 1011 s=0, eee=5 → exponent 5−3 = 2, 1.1011 × 2 2 = 110.11 = 6.75 1 001 1000 s=1, eee=1 → exponent 1−3 = −2, −1.1 × 2 −2 = −0.011 = −0.375 Explorer Check What is the bias for a 3-bit exponent field? Check 2 3−1 − 1 = 3. Check What is the bias for a 2-bit exponent field? Check 2 2−1 − 1 = 1. Check Decode minifloat 0 100 0000 (decimal). Check Exponent field 4 − 3 = 1: 1.0 × 2 1 = 2. Check Decode minifloat 0 101 0110 (decimal). Check Exponent 5 − 3 = 2: 1.0110 × 2 2 = 101.10 = 5.5. Check Decode minifloat 1 011 1000 (decimal). Check Sign 1, exponent 3 − 3 = 0: −1.1 × 2 0 = −1.5. Check Why use a biased exponent instead of two's complement? It saves a bit Larger numbers get larger bit patterns, so floats compare like unsigned integers It makes the significand larger Two's complement cannot store negatives With two's complement, negative exponents have leading 1s and would look larger than positive ones.

title: CL14 · Encoding a Value in Minifloat
text: CL14 · Encoding a Value in Minifloat Procedure: (1) sign bit; (2) write |value| in binary and normalize to 1.f × 2 e ; (3) exponent field = e + 3; (4) store the fraction bits after the point (without the leading 1); (5) if the field is not in the valid range or the fraction does not fit, see special values and rounding in the next tabs. The four slide examples: 15 = 1111 = 1.111 × 2 3 field 3+3 = 6 = 110 → 0 110 1110 −4.25 = −100.01 = −1.0001 × 2 2 field 2+3 = 5 = 101 → 1 101 0001 −32 = −100000 = −1 × 2 5 field 5+3 = 8 = 1000 → too big for 3 bits: not enough range 12.25 = 1100.01 = 1.10001 × 2 3 needs 5 fraction bits: not enough precision (must round) Check Encode 6.75 in the minifloat. Answer like 0b0101_1011 . Check 6.75 = 110.11 = 1.1011 × 2 2 ; field 2 + 3 = 5 = 101: 0 101 1011 . Check Encode 1 in the minifloat. Check 1 = 1.0 × 2 0 ; field 0 + 3 = 3 = 011: 0 011 0000 . Check Encode −2.5 in the minifloat. Check 2.5 = 10.1 = 1.01 × 2 1 ; field 4 = 100; sign 1: 1 100 0100 . Check Encode 0.75 in the minifloat. Check 0.75 = 0.11 = 1.1 × 2 −1 ; field −1 + 3 = 2 = 010: 0 010 1000 . Check Encode −15.5 in the minifloat. Check 15.5 = 1111.1 = 1.1111 × 2 3 ; field 6 = 110; the largest finite magnitude: 1 110 1111 . Check The exponent field for a value with true exponent −2 is… 000 001 101 011 −2 + 3 = 1 = 001 .

title: CL14 · Special Values: Zero, Infinity and NaN
text: CL14 · Special Values: Zero, Infinity and NaN A few bit patterns are reserved for special cases. Normalized numbers use exponent fields 001 – 110 (1–6); the two extreme exponent fields are special. Value Exponent bits Significand bits Normalized number neither all zeros nor all ones anything Zero all zeros all zeros Infinity all ones all zeros NaN all ones nonzero Denormalized number all zeros nonzero +0 = 0 000 0000 −0 = 1 000 0000 +Inf = 0 111 0000 −Inf = 1 111 0000 NaN = x 111 (any nonzero significand), e.g. 0 111 0101 NaN (Not a Number) is the result of undefined or unrepresentable operations such as 0/0 , ∞/∞ , √−1 or log(−5). It propagates : if x is NaN then x + 5 is NaN, so an error is not silently lost. There are many NaN encodings so programs can tell different error sources apart. The largest finite value is therefore 0 110 1111 = 1.1111 × 2 3 = 15.5 , and the smallest positive normalized value is 0 001 0000 = 1.0 × 2 −2 = 0.25 . Check Decode 0 111 0000 (write +Inf, -Inf or NaN as appropriate). Check Exponent all ones with a zero significand is +∞. Check Decode 1 111 0000 . Check Sign 1, exponent all ones, significand zero: −∞. Check Decode 0 111 0101 . Check Exponent all ones with a nonzero significand is NaN. Check What is the largest finite minifloat value? Check 0 110 1111 = 1.1111 × 2 3 = 15.5. Check What happens to NaN in NaN + 5 ? 5 0 NaN ∞ NaN propagates through calculations so the error is not lost. Check Why does the format have many different NaN encodings? Hardware bugs So different error sources can be distinguished To store extra digits of pi They are all positive infinity Any nonzero significand with an all-ones exponent is a NaN, so a program can tag why the result is undefined. Check Select all correct statements. A. Exponent all ones and significand zero is infinity B. Exponent all zeros and significand zero is NaN C. Exponent all zeros and significand nonzero is denormalized D. Normalized numbers use exponent fields 1 through 6 Check All-zeros exponent with a zero significand is zero , not NaN.

title: CL14 · Rounding, Overflow and Underflow
text: CL14 · Rounding, Overflow and Underflow If a value cannot be represented exactly, the hardware stores the closest representable value . If it is in range but needs more fraction bits it is rounded ; if its magnitude is too large it overflows to ±infinity; if it is so close to zero that nothing smaller exists it underflows (to zero, or to a denormal). Round to nearest, ties to even: pick the nearest candidate; if the value is exactly halfway between two candidates, pick the one whose last significand bit is 0 (even). 12.25 = 1.10001 × 2 3 neighbours: 1.1000 × 2 3 = 12.0 and 1.1001 × 2 3 = 12.5 exactly halfway → ties-to-even → 12.0 (0 110 1000) 5.3125 = 1.010101 × 2 2 neighbours: 5.25 and 5.5; 5.3125 − 5.25 = 0.0625 vs 5.5 − 5.3125 = 0.1875 nearer to 5.25 → 5.25 (0 101 0101) 5.125 = 1.01001 × 2 2 neighbours: 5.0 (1.0100) and 5.25 (1.0101); exactly halfway → ties-to-even picks 1.0100 = 5.0 (0 101 0100) Overflow: −32 → −1 × 2 5 needs field 8 → stored as −Inf = 1 111 0000 Underflow: a value smaller than every denormal rounds to 0 Check What value is actually stored when you encode 12.25 in the minifloat? Check 12.25 is halfway between 12.0 and 12.5; ties-to-even gives 12.0. Check What value is stored for 5.3125? Check Closer to 5.25 (0.0625 away) than to 5.5 (0.1875 away). Check What value is stored for 5.125? Check An exact tie between 5.0 and 5.25; ties-to-even picks 5.0 (last bit 0). Check What value is stored for 9.1? Check Above 8 the spacing is 0.5 (9.0, 9.5). 9.1 is closer to 9.0. Check Encode 6.1875 (= 110.0011) in the minifloat. Check 6.1875 = 1.100011 × 2 2 . The extra bits 11 are over half a unit in the last place, so round up to 1.1001 = 6.25: 0 101 1001 . Check What does 100 become in the minifloat? (decimal; +Inf, -Inf or NaN as appropriate) Check 100 exceeds the largest finite value (15.5), so it overflows to +Inf. Check Which statement about 12.25 in the minifloat is true? It is stored exactly It is a tie between 12.0 and 12.5, so it is stored as 12.0 It overflows It becomes NaN Round to nearest, ties to even. Check Underflow is when… a value is too large to represent an operation is undefined a value is too close to zero to represent and becomes zero (or a denormal) the sign bit is wrong Overflow is too large; underflow is too small in magnitude.

title: CL14 · Denormalized Numbers
text: CL14 · Denormalized Numbers The gap problem. The smallest positive normalized minifloat is 0 001 0000 = 0.25, and the next is 0.265625 (a step of 1/64). But between 0 and 0.25 there is nothing : the implicit 1 that buys precision also leaves a big hole around zero. Denormalized numbers (exponent field all zeros , significand nonzero ) fill the hole by dropping the hidden 1 and using a fixed exponent of 1 − bias (= −2 for bias 3): value = (−1) s × 0.ffff × 2 1 − bias = (−1) s × 0.ffff × 2 −2 0 000 0001 = 0.0001 × 2 −2 = 2 −6 = 1/64 = 0.015625 (smallest positive denormal) 0 000 1111 = 0.1111 × 2 −2 = 15/64 = 0.234375 (largest denormal) The largest denormal (0.234375) is exactly one 1/64 step below the smallest normalized value (0.25), so the number line is continuous with evenly spaced values near zero. Pattern Kind Value 0 000 0000 zero 0 0 000 0001 denormalized 0.015625 0 000 1000 denormalized 0.125 0 000 1111 denormalized 0.234375 0 001 0000 normalized 0.25 0 001 0001 normalized 0.265625 Normalized or denormalized? Encoding steps Try normalized first. If the exponent field (e + bias) is ≤ 0 , the value is too small to be normalized: divide by 2 −2 (i.e. multiply by 4) and write the result as 0.ffff for a denormalized encoding. 1/32 = 1.0 × 2 −5 : field −5+3 = −2 ≤ 0 → denormalized. (1/32) × 4 = 1/8 = 0.0010 → 0 000 0010 (check: 0.0010 × 2 −2 = 1/8 × 1/4 = 1/32) −3/8 = −1.1 × 2 −2 : field −2+3 = 1 → normalized → 1 001 1000 Check Decode 0 000 0100 (decimal). Check Denormalized: 0.0100 × 2 −2 = 0.25 × 0.25 = 1/16 = 0.0625. Check Decode 0 000 1111 (decimal). Check 0.1111 × 2 −2 = 15/16 × 1/4 = 15/64 = 0.234375. Check What exponent do denormalized minifloat values use? Check Fixed: 1 − bias = 1 − 3 = −2. Check Encode 1/16 in the minifloat. Check 1/16 is below 0.25: denormalized. 0.0625 / 2 −2 = 0.25 = 0.0100 → 0 000 0100 . Check Encode −9/64 in the minifloat. Check 9/64 = 0.140625; ÷ 2 −2 = 0.5625 = 0.1001 → 1 000 1001 . Check Why do denormalized numbers drop the implicit 1? To add more range at the top To place values between zero and the smallest normalized number To make NaNs To save a bit Without the hidden 1 the significand can be smaller than 1, filling the gap near zero. Check The smallest positive normalized value is 0.25. What is the next smaller positive value? 0.234375 (the largest denormal) 0.125 0.1 0 Denormals run up to 15/64 = 0.234375, then 0.25 begins.

title: HW04 · Debugging: What the Homework Asks
text: HW04 · Debugging: What the Homework Asks HW04 is a practice-the-debugger homework: instead of finding bugs by reading source, you use the debugger to observe what the program does and let the evidence point at the bug. Every problem follows the same loop from CL10: Run the program normally and notice what is wrong (wrong output, failing test). Write down what you expected (a prediction table). Set a breakpoint (conditional if the loop is long) and start the debugger. Step (over / into / out), reading the Variables panel, the Watch panel or the Debug Console. The first line where reality differs from your prediction is the bug. Fix it, restart the debugger, rerun. title: HW04 · Problem 1: Breakpoints, Continue and the Debug Console
text: HW04 · Problem 1: Breakpoints, Continue and the Debug Console A breakpoint pauses the program before the marked line runs. Continue resumes until the next time a breakpoint is hit (in a loop, the next iteration). The Debug Console evaluates any C expression against the paused state, e.g. temps[i] > max (1 = true, 0 = false). Example program (not the homework's): highest temperature int temps[6] = {58, 61, 66, 63, 70, 62}; int max = temps[0]; for (int i = 1; i < 6; i++) { if (temps[i] > max) { // <-- breakpoint here max = temps[i - 1]; } } printf("%d", max); Run normally: it prints 63 , but the highest temperature is 70 . Set a breakpoint on the if . The debugger pauses each iteration: Pause # i temps[i] max 1st 1 61 58 after Continue 2 66 58 after Continue 3 63 61 after Continue 4 70 66 At the 2nd pause max is still 58 even though the first comparison (61 > 58) was true: the body assigned temps[i - 1] (= 58) instead of temps[i] (= 61). The first statement that gives max a wrong value is max = temps[i - 1]; . Fix: max = temps[i]; . Check What does the program above print when run normally? Check The final max is temps[3] = 63 because each assignment lags one element behind. Check When it first pauses at the breakpoint, what is max ? Check max starts as temps[0] = 58. Check After pressing Continue once, what is max ? Check The first iteration set max = temps[0] = 58 (the old value), so it is still 58. Check At the 2nd pause, what does temps[i] > max evaluate to in the Debug Console? Check 66 > 58 is true, so the console shows 1. Check Which statement first makes max incorrect? int max = temps[0]; if (temps[i] > max) max = temps[i - 1]; printf("%d", max); It stores the previous element rather than the current one. Check What does Continue do? Runs one line Resumes until the next breakpoint is hit (or the program ends) Restarts the program Steps into a function Continue resumes normal execution until a breakpoint pauses it again.

title: HW04 · Problem 2: Conditional Breakpoints
text: HW04 · Problem 2: Conditional Breakpoints A conditional breakpoint pauses only when its expression is true . In VS Code, right-click the breakpoint (or the gutter) and choose Edit Breakpoint → Expression . Use == (comparison), never = (assignment). Typical conditions: i==3 , weights[i]>25 , c=='x' . Example program: parcel shipping Rules: up to 8 lb costs $4; over 8 up to 20 lb costs $7; over 20 lb costs $11. int cost(int w) { int c = 4; if (w > 8) c = 7; if (w > 20) c = 7; // bug? return c; } int weights[5] = {3, 14, 9, 31, 22}; Running it shows costs 4, 7, 7, 7, 7. Package index 3 (31 lb) costs $7 but should be $11. Set a conditional breakpoint on int c = 4; with the condition w==31 (or in the caller, i==3 ) so you do not step through the earlier packages. Step Line just executed c pause (before int c = 4; ) garbage step 1 int c = 4; 4 step 2 if (w > 8) c = 7; 7 step 3 if (w > 20) c = 7; 7 ← should be 11 The last line assigns 7 again instead of 11. Fix: c = 11; . Check Write the condition (no spaces) that pauses only when i is 3. Check Use the equality operator == . Check Write the condition (no spaces) that pauses only when weights[i] is greater than 20. 20"> Check A relational expression on the array element. Check In the example, what is c after the second step ( if (w > 8) c = 7; ) for w = 31? Check w > 8 is true, so c becomes 7. Check In the example, what does cost(22) return (buggy code)? Check 22 > 8 sets 7; 22 > 20 sets 7 again. Check What should cost(31) return according to the rules? Check Over 20 lb costs $11. Check Why use a conditional breakpoint inside a loop? It runs the program faster It pauses only for the iteration you care about instead of every iteration It changes the loop condition It prevents crashes Otherwise you would press Continue through every earlier iteration. Check Which condition pauses only for index 2? i=2 i==2 i<2 2 = assigns (and would change i); == compares.

title: HW04 · Problem 3: Step Into, Step Over and Step Out
text: HW04 · Problem 3: Step Into, Step Over and Step Out Step Over : run the whole line (including any function it calls) and pause on the next line of the same function. Step Into : if the line calls a function, pause on that function's first line. Step Out : run the rest of the current function and pause back in the caller. Typical use: step over trusted functions, step into the suspect function, step out when you accidentally went into library code (e.g. strlen ). Example program: password strength Score = 1 per character + 1 per digit, +2 if the length is at least 8, +2 if there are at least 2 digits. int digits(const char *s) { // counts digit characters int c = 0; for (int i = 0; s[i]; i++) if (s[i] >= '0' && s[i] <= '9') c++; return c; } int strength(const char *pw) { int len = strlen(pw); int d = digits(pw); int s = len + d; if (len >= 8) s += 2; else if (d >= 2) s += 2; // bug? return s; } For "abc12345" : length 8, digits 5, base 13. Both bonuses apply, so the correct score is 17 ; the program returns 15 . Action (paused at int actual = strength(pw); ) Result Step Over actual is 15 (the call ran in one step) Step Into pauses on int len = strlen(pw); inside strength Step Into on strlen , then Step Out back in strength ; len is 8 Step Into digits , Step Out, Step Over d is 5 After int s = len + d; the debugger shows s = 13 . Both len >= 8 and d >= 2 are true, but the else if skips the second bonus. Fix: make the second test its own if . Check Using Step Over on int actual = strength(pw); , what value does actual get? Check The call executes completely and returns 15 (wrong; should be 17). Check After int s = len + d; , what is s ? Check 8 + 5. Check What should strength("abc12345") return by the rules? Check 8 + 5 + 2 (length) + 2 (digits) = 17. Check You are on int d = digits(pw); and want to watch inside digits . Which control? Step Over Step Into Step Out Continue Step Into pauses on the first line of the called function. Check You pressed Step Into on strlen(pw) by mistake. What returns you to strength ? Step Out Restart Step Over Delete the breakpoint Step Out finishes the current (library) function and pauses in the caller. Check Which is true of Step Over on a line that calls your own function? It pauses inside the function It skips the line The function runs to completion and you pause on the next line It restarts the program You see the result of the call but not the steps inside. Check Which fix repairs the scoring bug? Change >= to > in the length test Replace else if by a separate if Initialize s to 0 Remove the length bonus The two bonuses are independent; else made them mutually exclusive.

title: HW04 · Problem 4: Reading the Call Stack
text: HW04 · Problem 4: Reading the Call Stack When paused inside a function, the Call Stack panel lists the active calls: the function you are in at the top , its caller below, ending with main at the bottom. Clicking a frame shows that frame's local variables in the Variables panel. It only changes what you inspect: no instructions execute . Variables that have not been assigned yet show garbage. Example program: a checkout int tax(int amount, int pct) { int t = amount * pct / 100; // breakpoint after this line return t; } int total(int qty, int unit) { int sub = qty * unit; int t = tax(sub, 8); return sub + t; } int main(void) { int q = 5, u = 12; int bill = total(q, u); printf("%d", bill); } Pause in tax after t is set: Frame Variables tax (top) amount = 60, pct = 8, t = 4 total qty = 5, unit = 12, sub = 60 (t not yet assigned) main q = 5, u = 12, bill = not yet assigned The program prints 64 (60 + 4). Check In the tax frame, what is amount ? Check total computed sub = 5 × 12 = 60 and passed it as amount. Check In the tax frame, what is t ? Check 60 × 8 / 100 = 480 / 100 = 4 (integer division). Check Select the total frame. What is sub ? Check qty × unit = 5 × 12. Check Select the main frame. What is q ? Check main's local q. Check Selecting a different stack frame makes the program execute more instructions. True False False. You are only changing which frame's variables you look at; the program stays paused. Check Which frame is at the top of the call stack while paused in tax ? main total tax printf The innermost active call is at the top; callers are below it. Check Has bill in main received its final value when you are paused in tax ? Yes: 64 Yes: 60 No: total has not returned yet It is always 0 The assignment happens only after total returns.

title: HW04 · Problem 5: Modifying launch.json to Redirect Input
text: HW04 · Problem 5: Modifying launch.json to Redirect Input A program that reads stdin normally waits for you to type. To debug it with input from a file you use the second launch configuration, Debug with input redirected , which starts /bin/bash -lc "<program> < <file>" . VS Code first replaces its variables using the active file . Variable Meaning (active file /home/sam/hw/p5/avg.c ) Value \${file} full path of the file /home/sam/hw/p5/avg.c \${fileDirname} directory containing it /home/sam/hw/p5 \${fileBasenameNoExtension} file name without path or extension avg So "\${fileDirname}/\${fileBasenameNoExtension}" < "\${fileDirname}/temp.in" becomes "/home/sam/hw/p5/avg" < "/home/sam/hw/p5/temp.in" Run from a terminal the same way: ./avg < temp.in . To use another file, change the path in launch.json (e.g. \${fileDirname}/data/example.in ). Example program: it should print the average of the 4 numbers in temp.in ( 70 74 66 62 , average 68) but divides by (n + 1) : int total = 0, n = 4, x; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { scanf("%d", &x); total += x; // breakpoint here } printf("%d", total / (n + 1)); Debugging shows total climbing 70, 144, 210, 272 and n = 4 . After the loop, total / (n + 1) is 272 / 5 = 54 but the average is 272 / 4 = 68 . A breakpoint after the loop (removing the one in the loop, then Continue) shows the final total without stepping through every iteration. Check With active file /home/sam/hw/p5/avg.c , what is \${fileDirname} ? Check The directory part of the path. Check What is \${fileBasenameNoExtension} for that file? Check The name without the directory and without .c . Check In the example, what is total after the loop? Check 70 + 74 + 66 + 62. Check What does the buggy program print? Check 272 / (4 + 1) = 54 with integer division. Check What does the < in the launch arguments do? Compares two numbers Redirects the program's standard input from the file Pipes output to another program Redirects standard output to the file Input redirection: scanf / getchar read from the file. Check After editing launch.json you must… Recompile with -O3 Select the "Debug with input redirected" configuration in the debug dropdown Delete tasks.json Restart the computer Each configuration has a name; select the one you edited.

title: HW04 · Problem 6: Debugger Detective
text: HW04 · Problem 6: Debugger Detective The last problem leaves the tools to you : a program (here with bit flags) produces a wrong final state and you must find the first statement where the state becomes incorrect. Predict the value after each function, then break after each call or step into each function and compare. Example program: print/save/lock flags #define PRINT 1 #define SAVE 2 #define LOCK 8 int enable_save(int f) { return f | SAVE; } int unlock(int f) { return f ^ LOCK; } // bug? int main(void) { int flags = PRINT; // 1 flags = enable_save(flags); flags = unlock(flags); printf("%d", flags); } Expected: PRINT and SAVE on, LOCK off → 3 . The program prints 11 . After Expected Actual start 1 1 enable_save 3 3 unlock 3 11 The first mismatch is inside unlock : f ^ LOCK toggles LOCK, so a lock that was off is switched on (3 ^ 8 = 11). To clear a flag use f & ~LOCK (3 & ~8 = 3). Check What does the program print? Check 1 | 2 = 3, then 3 ^ 8 = 11. Check What is the value of flags after enable_save ? Check 1 | 2. Check What should return f ^ LOCK; be changed to (use f and LOCK , no spaces)? Check AND with the inverted mask clears the flag. Check Which function first makes the flag state incorrect? main enable_save unlock None After enable_save the state is right (3); after unlock it is wrong (11). Check Why did XOR not “clear” the lock? XOR cannot be used on integers XOR toggles: when the bit is already 0 it turns it on LOCK is not a power of two The mask must be 0 Clearing needs AND with the inverted mask; XOR flips whatever state the bit is in.

title: HW05 · Floating Point Representation: Overview
text: HW05 · Floating Point Representation: Overview HW05 has three question groups: Q1 fractional binary numbers (mixed numbers and binary place format), Q2 decoding and encoding in the 8-bit minifloat (1 sign, 3 exponent bits with bias 3, 4 significand bits), and Q3 a second design ( 1 sign, 2 exponent bits with bias 1, 4 significand bits ) where you classify each pattern or value as normalized, denormalized, not enough precision or not enough range, and give the stored value. Tool Rule Bias 2 n−1 − 1 for an n-bit exponent field (3 bits → 3, 2 bits → 1) Normalized value (−1) s × 1.f × 2 E − bias Denormalized (E = 0, f ≠ 0) (−1) s × 0.f × 2 1 − bias Zero E = 0, f = 0 Infinity / NaN E all ones, f = 0 / f ≠ 0 Rounding nearest representable value; exact ties go to the even one (last bit 0) Encoding checklist 1. sign bit 2. normalize |x| = 1.f × 2 e 3. field = e + bias 4. field ≥ all-ones? → infinity (not enough range) 5. field ≤ 0? → denormalized: x / 2 (1−bias) as 0.f 6. more fraction bits than fit? → round to nearest, ties to even (if rounding changes the value, the value is "not enough precision" but you still store the rounded one) Use the Floating Point II explorer to build bit patterns and see the formula applied. The Mastery checkpoints for HW5 (on the CL13 and CL14 units) test the same question types with different numbers. Explorer

title: HW05 · Q1: Fractional Binary Numbers
text: HW05 · Q1: Fractional Binary Numbers Two directions: binary → mixed number (add place values, leave the fraction in lowest terms: 1111.1111 = 15 15/16 ) and fraction/decimal → binary place format ( 5/8 = 0b0.101 ). Negatives keep the sign in front: -0b0.101 . 0b11.0101 = 2 + 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 = 3 5/16 7/8 = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 0b0.111 -3/8 = -(1/4 + 1/8) = -0b0.011 1 11/32 = 1 + 8/32 + 2/32 + 1/32 = 0b1.01011 9/32 = 8/32 + 1/32 = 0b0.01001 Tip: for a fraction with denominator 2 k , write the numerator in binary, pad it to k bits, and put the binary point in front: 9/32 → 9 = 01001 (5 bits) → 0.01001 . For 11/16: 11 = 1011 (4 bits) → 0.1011 . Check Write 0b101.11 as a mixed number (like 9 1/4 ). Check 4 + 1 + ½ + ¼ = 5 3/4. Check Write 0b1010.001 as a mixed number. Check 8 + 2 + 1/8 = 10 1/8. Check Write 0b110.1101 as a mixed number. Check 6 + ½ + ¼ + 1/16 = 6 13/16. Check Represent 11/16 in binary place format (e.g. 0b10.1011 ). Check 11 = 1011 over 16 → 0.1011. Check Represent −7/8 in binary place format. Check 7/8 = 0.111, so −0b0.111. Check Represent 5.625 in binary place format. Check 5 = 101; 0.625 = ½ + 1/8 = .101 → 101.101. Check Represent 1.34375 (1 11/32) in binary place format. Check 11/32 = 01011 over 32 → 1.01011. Check Represent 9/32 in binary place format. Check 9 = 01001 over 32 → 0.01001. Check Which decimal value is 0b0.101 ? 0.101 0.5 0.625 0.75 ½ + 1/8 = 0.625 = 5/8.

title: HW05 · Q2: The 8-bit Minifloat
text: HW05 · Q2: The 8-bit Minifloat Layout s eee ffff , bias 3. Decode by deciding the kind first (E all ones → ∞/NaN, E = 0 → zero/denormal, else normalized), then applying the matching formula. Encode with the checklist. Always give the sign with decoded answers when asked ( +0.015625 , -1.0625 , +Inf , NaN ). Pattern Kind Computation Value 1 011 0010 normalized −1.0010 × 2 0 −1.125 0 111 0000 infinity E all ones, f = 0 +Inf 0 111 0110 NaN E all ones, f ≠ 0 NaN 0 000 0010 denormalized 0.0010 × 2 −2 0.03125 0 110 1111 normalized (largest) 1.1111 × 2 3 15.5 Q2.1 What decimal number is encoded by 1 001 0100 ? (sign explicit; +Inf / -Inf / NaN as needed) Check Normalized: exponent 1 − 3 = -2; value -0.3125. Q2.2 What decimal number is encoded by 0 010 0110 ? (sign explicit; +Inf / -Inf / NaN as needed) Check Denormalized: 0.0011 × 2 −2 = 0.046875. Q2.4 What decimal number is encoded by 0 111 1001 ? (sign explicit; +Inf / -Inf / NaN as needed) Check Exponent all ones with a nonzero significand: NaN. Q2.5 What decimal number is encoded by 1 111 0000 ? (sign explicit; +Inf / -Inf / NaN as needed) Check Exponent all ones with a zero significand: infinity. Q2.6 What decimal number is encoded by 0 110 0000 ? (sign explicit; +Inf / -Inf / NaN as needed) Check Normalized: exponent 6 − 3 = 3; value 8. Q2.7 Represent 10.5 in the minifloat as 0bXXXX_XXXX . Check Encoding: 0 110 0101 . title: HW05 · Q3: Another Design (2 exponent bits, bias 1, 4 significand bits)
text: HW05 · Q3: Another Design (2 exponent bits, bias 1, 4 significand bits) Same rules, different widths: s ee ffff (7 bits), bias 1 . Exponent field 00 → zero/denormalized (fixed exponent 1 − 1 = 0 : value 0.ffff × 2 0 ); 01 and 10 → normalized (true exponents 0 and 1); 11 → ∞/NaN. For each value you must decide normalized / denormalized / not enough precision / not enough range and state the encoding stored. Landmark Pattern Value smallest positive denormal 0 00 0001 0.0625 largest denormal 0 00 1111 0.9375 smallest positive normalized 0 01 0000 1 largest finite 0 10 1111 3.875 +Infinity 0 11 0000 +Inf Largest finite = 1.1111 × 2 1 = 3.875. Anything beyond that overflows. Denormals have spacing 1/16 and run seamlessly into the normalized values at 1. decode 1 10 1010: E=10 (normalized), exponent 2−1 = 1, −1.1010 × 2 1 = −3.25 decode 0 00 0110: E=00, f≠0 → denormalized, 0.0110 × 2 0 = 0.375 encode −2.25: −10.01 = −1.001 × 2 1 , E = 1+1 = 2 = 10 → 1 10 0010 (exact, normalized) encode 0.625: 0.101 = 1.01 × 2 −1 , E = −1+1 = 0 → denormalized: 0.625 = 0.1010 × 2 0 → 0 00 1010 encode 2.15625 = 1.000101 × 2 1 : six fraction bits, only 4 fit → not enough precision ; tie between 2.125 and 2.1875 → ties-to-even → 0 10 0001 (2.125) encode −30: exponent 4 → E = 5 does not fit in 2 bits → not enough range → −Inf = 1 11 0000 Q3.1a 1 01 0100 : is it normalized or denormalized ? (then decimal in the next question) Check Exponent field is 01 or 10: normalized. Q3.2a 0 00 0100 : is it normalized or denormalized ? (then decimal in the next question) Check Exponent field 00 with a nonzero significand: denormalized. Q3.3a 0 10 0110 : is it normalized or denormalized ? (then decimal in the next question) Check Exponent field is 01 or 10: normalized. Q3.4a 0 01 1000 : is it normalized or denormalized ? (then decimal in the next question) Check Exponent field is 01 or 10: normalized. Q3.1b Decimal value of 1 01 0100 : Check Value -1.25. Q3.2b Decimal value of 0 00 0100 : Check Value 0.25. Q3.3b Decimal value of 0 10 0110 : Check Value 2.75. Q3.4b Decimal value of 0 01 1000 : Check Value 1.5. Q3.5 Encode 1.75 in the 7-bit design as 0bXXX_XXXX (round to nearest, ties to even; infinity if out of range). Check Classification: normalized . Stored: 0 01 1100 = 1.75. Q3.6 Encode -1.3125 in the 7-bit design as 0bXXX_XXXX (round to nearest, ties to even; infinity if out of range). Check Classification: normalized . Stored: 1 01 0101 = -1.3125. Q3.7 Encode 0.4375 in the 7-bit design as 0bXXX_XXXX (round to nearest, ties to even; infinity if out of range). Check Classification: denormalized . Stored: 0 00 0111 = 0.4375. title: CL15 · Denormalized Numbers: Exponent 1 − bias, Implicit 0
text: CL15 · Denormalized Numbers: Exponent 1 − bias, Implicit 0 Last lecture introduced denormals; this one explains why they line up . A normalized value is exponent = field − bias with an implicit 1 . The smallest normalized field is 001 , so its exponent is 1 − 3 = −2 . When the field is 000 the exponent is defined as 1 − bias (also −2), but the leading bit becomes an implicit 0 . Exponent field Form Example Smallest normalized 001 1.xxxx × 2 −2 0 001 0000 = 1.0 × 2 −2 = 16/64 All subnormals 000 0.xxxx × 2 −2 0 000 1111 = 0.1111 × 2 −2 = 15/64 Both use 2 −2 ; the only change is the implicit leading bit . That makes the hand-off smooth: the largest subnormal is 15/16 × 1/4 = 15/64 , the smallest normalized is 16/64 , exactly one 1/64 step apart. ... 13/64 14/64 15/64 (largest denormal) | 16/64 (smallest normalized) 17/64 18/64 ... Encode a small value: normalized or denormalized? Try normalized first. If exponent + bias ≤ 0 the value is too small: divide by 2 −2 and write the result as 0.ffff . 1/32 : 1.0 × 2 −5 → field −2 ≤ 0 → denormalized ; (1/32)×4 = 0.125 = 0.0010 → 0 000 0010 −3/8 : −1.1 × 2 −2 → field 1 → normalized → 1 001 1000 9/64 : 0.001001 → field ≤ 0 → denormalized ; (9/64)×4 = 0.5625 = 0.1001 → 0 000 1001 −3/4 : −1.1 × 2 −1 → field 2 → normalized → 1 010 1000 Check What exponent do minifloat denormals use? Check Fixed at 1 − bias = 1 − 3 = −2. Check The largest denormal is 0 000 1111. Give its value as a fraction over 64 (like 5/64). Check 0.1111 × 2 −2 = 15/16 × 1/4 = 15/64. Check Is 3/32 normalized or denormalized in the minifloat? (answer normalized or denormalized) Check 3/32 = 0.09375 = 1.5 × 2 −4 , so the exponent field would be −4 + 3 = −1 ≤ 0: it is denormalized (0.09375 × 4 = 0.375 = 0.0110). Check What differs between the smallest normalized number and the denormalized numbers? The exponent used The implicit leading bit (1 vs 0) The number of fraction bits The sign convention Both use 2 −2 ; normalized has implicit 1, denormalized implicit 0. Check What is the gap between the largest denormal and the smallest normalized value? 1/64 1/16 0.25 There is a hole 15/64 to 16/64 — the same spacing as inside the denormal range. Denorm Exponent Guide: three designs for exponent field 000 Minifloat with 3 exponent bits (bias 3) and 4 fraction bits. What should the all-zeros exponent field mean? Design Exponent field 000 means Smallest positive Result 1 · no denormals normal, exponent −3 1/8 big gap between 0 and 1/8 (abrupt underflow) 2 · denormals, exponent −3 (−bias) 0.f × 2 −3 1/128 reaches closest to 0, but a gap from 15/128 to 1/4 3 · denormals, exponent −2 (1 − bias) 0.f × 2 −2 1/64 no gap: 15/64 is directly followed by 16/64 Design 3 is the real rule. The trade-off: it cannot get as close to zero as Design 2, but the number line stays evenly spaced around the smallest normalized value. Check Which design has a gap between its largest denormal and its smallest normalized value? Design 1 only Design 2 (exponent −bias) Design 3 (exponent 1 − bias) All of them Design 2 jumps from 15/128 to 1/4. title: CL15 · IEEE-754: float and double
text: CL15 · IEEE-754: float and double IEEE-754 (1985) is the floating-point standard virtually all hardware uses. It is the minifloat design scaled up: single precision ( float , 32 bits) and double precision ( double , 64 bits). Single (float) Double (double) Total bits 32 64 Sign bits 1 1 Exponent bits 8 11 Bias 127 1023 Fraction (significand) bits 23 52 Range / precision smaller / less accurate larger / more accurate Storage / speed less space, faster more space, slower The special-value table is unchanged: exponent all ones → ±∞ (fraction 0) or NaN (fraction ≠ 0); exponent all zeros → ±0 or denormalized. The FPU (floating-point unit) is circuitry inside the processor that adds, subtracts, multiplies, divides and takes square roots directly in hardware using these rules, so the same calculation behaves the same on different machines (at the same precision). Explorer Decoding a float, step by step 0x44C00000 = 0100 0100 1100 0000 0000 0000 0000 0000 split 1 | 8 | 23: 0 | 10001001 | 10000000000000000000000 sign 0 (positive); exponent field 10001001 = 137; true exponent 137 − 127 = 10 fraction .1 → 1.1 2 × 2 10 = 1.5 × 1024 = 1536 Handy tool for checking your work: float.exposed (type a hex pattern or a number). Check Encode 1.5 as a single-precision float (8 hex digits). Check 1.5 = 1.1 × 2 0 : exponent field 127 = 0x7F, fraction .1 → 0x3FC00000 . Check Encode −2 as a single-precision float (8 hex digits). Check Sign 1; −1.0 × 2 1 : exponent field 128 → 0xC0000000 . Check How many exponent bits does a double have? Check 1 sign + 11 exponent + 52 fraction = 64. Check What is the bias of a float? Check 2 8−1 − 1. Check Which statement about double vs float is correct? Double has more range and precision but uses more space and is slower Double has less range but more precision Float is always more accurate They have the same precision More exponent bits give range; more fraction bits give precision.

title: CL15 · Precision Loss: Rounding Errors and Comparing Floats
text: CL15 · Precision Loss: Rounding Errors and Comparing Floats Most decimal fractions (0.1, 0.2, 0.3) have no finite binary expansion, so a computer stores the nearest representable value . Small errors appear and can accumulate. Do not compare floating-point values with == . double a = 0.1; double b = 0.2; printf("%.23f\\n", a); // 0.10000000000000000555112 printf("%.23f\\n", b); // 0.20000000000000001110223 printf("%.23f\\n", a + b); // 0.30000000000000004440892 The sum is 0.300000000000000044… — not the stored 0.3 (0.29999999999999998889777), so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false (prints 0). Use an epsilon instead An epsilon (ε) is a small threshold for “close enough”. float.h defines FLT_EPSILON (≈ 1.19×10 −7 ) and DBL_EPSILON (≈ 2.22×10 −16 ), the gap between 1.0 and the next representable number. #include <float.h> #include <math.h> int are_equal(double a, double b) { return fabs(a - b) < DBL_EPSILON; } Here fabs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) ≈ 5.55×10 −17 < 2.22×10 −16 , so are_equal returns 1. Check 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is true in C when all three are double . True False False. Rounding errors make the sum differ from the stored 0.3 in the last bits. Check What is the best way to test whether two doubles are “equal”? a == b fabs(a - b) < epsilon a - b == 0 a / b == 1 Compare the absolute difference against a small tolerance. Check Why is 0.1 not stored exactly? It has too many digits It has no finite binary expansion (0.0001100110011…) Computers cannot store decimals Doubles round all numbers to integers Its binary expansion repeats, so it is truncated/rounded. Check What does printf("%d", fabs(0.1 + 0.2 - 0.3) < DBL_EPSILON); print? Check The difference (≈ 5.55e-17) is below DBL_EPSILON, so the comparison is true (1).

title: CL15 · Exercise: When Adding a Number Has No Effect
text: CL15 · Exercise: When Adding a Number Has No Effect The in-class exercise: with x = 1.0 , make delta smaller and smaller until x + delta == x even though delta != 0 . float x = 1.0f; float delta = 0.1f; // try 0.1, 0.01, 0.001 ... printf("x + delta = %.23f\\n", x + delta); if (x + delta == x) printf("Adding delta had NO effect!\\n"); else printf("Adding delta changed x.\\n"); delta (float, x = 1.0f) x + delta == x ? 1e-6 no, x changed 1e-7 no, x changed 1e-8 yes (no effect) Q1.1: the smallest power of 10 with no effect for float is 1e-8 . Q1.2: both x and delta are representable; the problem is that x + delta is not — there are not enough fraction bits (23), so the result rounds back to x. delta (double, x = 1.0) x + delta == x ? 1e-15 no, x changed 1e-16 yes (no effect) Q2: for double the threshold is about 1e-16 . Q3: a double has 52 fraction bits vs 23 for a float, so representable doubles near 1.0 are far more closely spaced (gap ≈ 2.2×10 −16 vs 1.19×10 −7 ); a much smaller change produces a different representable value. Check For float x = 1.0f; does x + 1e-7f == x ? Answer 1 or 0. Check The float gap above 1.0 is about 1.19×10 −7 ; half of it is the rounding threshold, and 1e-7 is above it, so x changes. Check For float x = 1.0f; does x + 1e-8f == x ? Answer 1 or 0. Check 1e-8 is below half the gap, so the sum rounds back to 1.0. Check For double x = 1.0; does x + 1e-16 == x ? Answer 1 or 0. Check A double's gap above 1.0 is 2.2e-16; 1e-16 is below half of it. Check What does float f = 16777217.0f; printf("%.0f", f); print? Check A float has 24 significant bits; 2 24 + 1 needs 25, so it rounds to 16777216. Check Why can a double absorb a much smaller delta than a float before the addition stops having an effect? Doubles are always bigger numbers A double has 52 fraction bits vs 23, so representable values near 1.0 are much more closely spaced Doubles use two exponent fields float arithmetic is done in integers More fraction bits means a finer grid of representable numbers.

title: CL15 · Real-World Application: Floating Point in LLMs
text: CL15 · Real-World Application: Floating Point in LLMs A large language model is a program trained to predict what text comes next. It contains billions of parameters (weights) — learned numbers — and processes activations (temporary values) for every prompt and layer. All of them are floating-point numbers, so the number of bits per value decides memory use and speed. 7 billion parameters at… Bytes each Memory 32 bits (FP32) 4 7B × 4 = 28 GB 16 bits (FP16 / BF16) 2 7B × 2 = 14 GB 8 bits 1 7B × 1 = 7 GB Field FP32 FP16 BF16 Sign 1 1 1 Exponent 8 5 8 Fraction 23 10 7 Bias 127 15 127 Total 32 16 16 Character baseline more precision, less range more range, less precision Largest finite ≈ 3.4×10 38 65,504 ≈ 3.39×10 38 FP16 example: exponent field 10000 = 16 → actual exponent 16 − 15 = 1. BF16 (“brain float”) was designed for neural networks: it keeps FP32's 8 exponent bits (same bias 127, so about the same range) but only 7 fraction bits (much less precision). Why would an LLM want range? Values vary a lot in magnitude; with too few exponent bits you hit overflow (too large) or underflow (too small to represent normally). BF16's 8-bit exponent avoids that; FP16 overflows more easily but rounds less. Explorer Check Which 16-bit format has more range ? Check 8 × 2 bytes = 16 GB. Check The same LLM stored as BF16 needs how many GB? Check BF16 is also 16 bits: 16 GB. Check What is the FP16 pattern 0x4000 in decimal? (1 sign, 5 exponent with bias 15, 10 fraction) Check Exponent 16 − 15 = 1, fraction 0: 1.0 × 2 1 = 2. Check What is the largest finite FP16 value? Check 0 11110 1111111111 = 1.9990234 × 2 15 = 65504. Check Select all correct statements. A. FP16 is more likely to overflow than BF16 B. BF16 causes more rounding than FP16 C. FP16 needs half the memory of FP32 D. BF16 needs more memory than FP16 Check Both 16-bit formats use the same memory (half of FP32).

title: CL16 · Parts of Program Memory
text: CL16 · Parts of Program Memory A running program's memory is divided into regions. From the lowest address (0, reserved for the operating system) to the highest : Region Holds Behaviour Text program instructions (the machine code of main , max , …) fixed size Data global and static variables exists for the whole run Heap dynamically allocated memory grows as needed (later lectures) Stack function stack frames: parameters, return address, local variables grows toward lower addresses on each call, shrinks on return The stack is also called automatic memory : every call pushes a frame and every return pops it, without the programmer doing anything . Highest address +-----------------------+ | Stack (grows down) | ← function frames | ... | | Heap (grows up) | ← dynamic memory | Data | ← globals, statics | Text | ← instructions Lowest address 0 | Operating system | +-----------------------+ Scope and lifetime of a local variable. A local variable is visible only in the function body where it is declared, and it exists only while that function's stack frame is on the stack. That is why two functions can both have a local named val : their scopes do not overlap and each has its own slot in its own frame. When a function returns its frame is deallocated and its locals become inaccessible. Global variables live for the entire program, but they reduce modularity and make debugging harder, so they are discouraged. Check Where are the instructions of main stored? Stack Heap Text (code) segment Data segment Instructions live in the text segment. Check Which variable exists for the entire run of the program? A parameter of a function A local variable in a function A global variable A loop counter in main Globals live in the data segment. Check When change(10) is called, where is space for its parameter and locals allocated? The heap The stack (a new frame) The data segment Nowhere: they already exist Each call pushes a stack frame. Check What happens to a function's locals when it returns? They move to the heap They become globals Its stack frame is deallocated and they become inaccessible They stay accessible forever The frame is popped. Check In which direction does the stack grow? Toward higher addresses Toward lower addresses It does not grow Alternately up and down Frames are pushed at progressively lower addresses. Check Why can max and change both use a local named val ? C renames them internally Because their scopes do not overlap One shadows the other Because they are stored on the heap Each local is visible only inside its own function. Check Global variables are generally encouraged because they are easy to access from every function. True False False. They reduce modularity and make debugging harder.

title: CL16 · Memory Addresses and Address Size
text: CL16 · Memory Addresses and Address Size Memory is a long row of bytes . Each byte has a numbered address (the addresses are not stored anywhere — they are just positions). With n address bits you can name 2 n bytes, so naming N bytes needs log 2 (N) bits. Memory size Address bits 8 bytes log 2 (8) = 3 ( 0b000 … 0b111 ) 16 bytes log 2 (16) = 4 1 GB = 2 30 bytes 30 256 TB = 2 48 bytes 48 32-bit addresses can name 2 32 bytes = 4 GB . 64-bit addresses can name 2 64 bytes (16 exabytes). 32-bit machines dominated from the mid-1980s through the 1990s; the move to 64-bit began in the early 2000s and was largely complete by 2010 — this is why pointers are 8 bytes . Most 64-bit CPUs use only 48–52 of the 64 bits (2 48 bytes = 256 TB is plenty and leaves room to grow). Check How many address bits are needed for a 1 GB memory (1 GB = 2 30 bytes)? Check log 2 (2 30 ) = 30. Check How many address bits to address 32 bytes? Check 2 5 = 32. Check How many GB can a 32-bit address space name? Check 2 32 bytes / 2 30 = 4 GB. Check How many GB can a 35-bit address space name? Check 2 35−30 = 32 GB. Check Why are pointers 8 bytes on a modern machine? They store a double Modern machines use 64-bit addresses (8 bytes) Pointers always include the size of the variable The compiler pads them 64 bits = 8 bytes.
