title: === PAGE 1 === (part 1)
text: === PAGE 1 === Why Is the Denormalized Exponent -2? Our minifloat representation has: ● 1 sign bit ● 3 exponent bits ● 4 significand (fraction) bits For normalized numbers, the significand has an implied leading 1: 1.xxxx With a bias of 3, the exponent is: E = exponent field - 3 Exponent Bits Exponent 000 Special case 001 1 - 3 = -2 010 2 - 3 = -1 011 3 - 1 = 2 100 4 - 3 = 1 101 5 - 3 = 2 110 6 - 3 = 3 111 Special case The smallest exponent available to a normalized number is therefore -2. The smallest positive normalized number is: 1.0000 × 2^-2 = 1/4 What should we do with exponent field 000? Let's consider three possible designs. === PAGE 2 === Design 1: No Denormalized Numbers One option would be to use 000 as another normalized exponent. Since we are using a bias of 3: 000 -> exponent -3 Numbers with exponent field 000 would therefore have the form: 1.xxxx × 2^-3 The smallest positive number would be: 1.0000 × 2^-3 = 1/8 The spacing between numbers with this exponent is: 0.0001 × 2^-3 = 1/128 So the first positive values are: 16/128, 17/128, 18/128, ... Evaluating the Tradeoffs: Advantage: ● We gain another exponent for normalized numbers. Disadvantage: ● There are NO representable nonzero values between 0 and 1/8. ● There is a large gap around zero. ● Very small values can suddenly become zero. This behavior is called "abrupt underflow. " === PAGE 3 === Design 2: Denormalized Exponent = -3 Instead, suppose we reserve exponent field 000 for denormalized numbers. A denormalized number does NOT have the implied leading 1. Instead of: 1.xxxx we use: 0.xxxx At first, it might seem like we should give these numbers an exponent of -3: 0.xxxx × 2^-3 After all, if 000 were interpreted normally with a bias of 3, it would mean -3. If we did this, the smallest positive denormal would be: 0.0001 × 2^-3 = 1/16 × 1/8 = 1/128 The largest denormal would be: 0.1111 × 2^-3 = 15/16 × 1/8 = 15/128 So the positive denormalized values would be: 1/128, 2/128, 3/128, ... , 15/128 But remember that the smallest normalized value is still: 1.0000 × 2^-2 = 1/4 That creates a large gap where are no representable values between: 15/128 and 32/128 === PAGE 4 === So although we gained very small numbers near zero, we created a large gap between the denormalized and normalized numbers. Evaluating the Tradeoffs: Advantage: ● We can represent very tiny values. ● The smallest positive value is 1/128. Disadvantage: ● There is a large gap between the denormalized and normalized ranges. ● The spacing suddenly changes when we move from denormalized to normalized numbers. === PAGE 5 === Design 3: Denormalized Exponent = -2 Now suppose we give denormalized numbers an exponent of -2. A denormalized number has the form: 0.xxxx × 2^-2 The smallest positive denormal is: 0.0001 × 2^-2 Since: 0.0001 = 1/16 we get: 1/16 × 1/4 = 1/64 The next denormal is: 0.0010 × 2^-2 = 2/64 Then: 0.0011 × 2^-2 = 3/64 And so on. The largest denormal is: 0.1111 × 2^-2 = 15/64 So the positive denormalized values are: 1/64, 2/64, 3/64, ... , 15/64 Now look at the smallest normalized value: 1.0000 × 2^-2 = 1/4 = 16/64 === PAGE 6 === Here values around the transition from denormalized to normalized values: 13/64 14/64 15/64 (largest denormal) 16/64 (smallest normalized) 17/64 18/64 ... There is NO GAP! The spacing stays exactly the same as we cross from denormalized numbers to normalized numbers: 14/64 -> 15/64 -> 16/64 -> 17/64 Evaluating the Tradeoffs: Advantage ● Smooth transition between denormalized and normalized values ● No abrupt underflow Disadvantage ● Cannot represent numbers as close to 0 compared with Design 2

title: Denorm Exponent Guide: own notes (part 1)
text: Denorm Exponent Guide: own notes Minifloat: 3 exponent bits, bias 3, 4 fraction bits. Question: what does exponent field 000 mean? Design 1: no denormals; field 000 is a normal exponent of -3. Smallest positive 1/8; large gap from 0 to 1/8. Design 2: denormals with exponent -bias = -3 (0.f x 2^-3). Smallest positive 1/128; gap between 15/128 and the smallest normalized 1/4. Design 3: denormals with exponent 1 - bias = -2 (0.f x 2^-2). Smallest positive 1/64; 15/64 is directly followed by 16/64: no gap. Design 3 is the standard rule. Trade-off: it does not reach as close to zero as Design 2.

title: RD00 reading notes - Dive into Systems 17.1.2 (Unix command line and file system) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD00 reading notes - Dive into Systems 17.1.2 (Unix command line and file system) - study notes written for this guide Current working directory: the directory you are operating in. Commands act relative to it: a file created without a path lands in the cwd. Absolute path: starts at the root /. Example: cd /home/sam/classes/CS31. Relative path: starts from the cwd. Example: cd classes/CS31. Special names: . is the current directory, .. is the parent, ~ alone is your home directory, ~sarita is user sarita's home directory. pwd prints the cwd. cd path changes it; cd with no argument returns to the home directory; cd .. moves to the parent. ls lists the cwd, ls -a also shows hidden entries including . and .. (names starting with a dot are hidden). mkdir makes a directory. touch makes an empty file. echo "text" >> file appends a line to a file. cat file prints a file. wc file counts lines, words, bytes. cp source destination copies a file; cp -r copies a directory and its contents recursively. mv source destination moves or renames a file or directory. Both take two arguments. rm removes a file permanently (no recycle bin). rm -i prompts first, -r removes directories recursively, -f forces without prompting. rmdir removes only empty directories (a safety feature). rm -rf in the wrong place is catastrophic: run pwd and ls first to confirm where you are. Some administrators alias rm to rm -i. File names are case sensitive (basics and Basics are different files). Spaces in names must be escaped or quoted, so Unix users use underscores: hello_there. Example trees: /home/sam has classes/CS31, letters, projects; /home/sarita has unix_notes/basics.

title: RD01 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.1 (getting started in C), 16.2 (input/output), 16.3 (conditionals and loops), 16.5 (arrays and strings) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD01 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.1 (getting started in C), 16.2 (input/output), 16.3 (conditionals and loops), 16.5 (arrays and strings) - study notes written for this guide 16.1 A C program is a set of functions with a required main. main returns an int (0 = success). Source files end in .c. Libraries are brought in with #include at the top of the file (for example stdio.h, math.h). C is procedural and has no classes; Java is object oriented and runs on a JVM, while C is compiled to a binary the OS runs directly. Compile: gcc file.c makes a.out; gcc -o name file.c names the output; run with ./name. -Wall adds warnings, -g adds debug info, -lm links the math library. If compilation fails the executable is not rebuilt, but an older one may still exist. Variables are declared before use: int x; char letter; float winpct; double pi; unsigned int y; int i, j, k;. Sizes: char 1, short 2, int 4, long 4 or 8, long long 8, float 4, double 8. sizeof gives the byte size (print with %lu). 'h' is a char (ASCII 104); "h" is a string literal. Integer division truncates (11 / 2 is 5, 11 / 2.0 is 5.5); % needs integers. x++ uses the value then increments; ++x increments first. Mixed int/float operations convert the int to float. printf does not add a newline; write \n yourself. 16.2 printf takes a format string plus one argument per placeholder. %d decimal int, %g or %f float/double, %s string, %c character (shows the ASCII character for a numeric value). Escapes: \n newline, \t tab. scanf reads values the user types and stores them at the memory addresses you give with &: scanf("%d", &num1). It skips whitespace between numeric values, is picky about format, and is not robust to bad input (it can loop forever; Ctrl-C ends it). stdio.h must be included. 16.3 if / else if / else work as in Java. C has no boolean type: 0 is false, any nonzero value is true. Relational operators == != < <= > >=; logical ! && ||. && and || short-circuit: evaluation stops as soon as the result is known. Use parentheses around complex conditions for readability. Loops: while tests first; do-while runs the body at least once; for (init; test; step) evaluates init once, then test, body, step repeatedly. while and for are equally powerful. C has no enhanced for loop. 16.5 Arrays: int nums[10]; int small[] = {1, 3, 5}; capacity is fixed at declaration; valid indices are 0 to capacity-1. C does no bounds checking at compile time or run time: reading or writing past the end is undefined behavior. Passing an array to a function passes its base address, so changes to elements persist in the caller; scalar parameters are copied. Functions usually take a size parameter because the array alone does not tell the function its capacity. void print_array(int arr[], int size). Strings are char arrays ending in the null character '\0'; "hi" needs at least 3 chars. string.h: strlen (length without the null), strcpy (copies up to and including the null; destination must be large enough, otherwise undefined behavior and a security risk). printf %s prints characters until it reaches '\0'.

title: RD02 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.5 (strings), 17.12 (I/O redirection), 17.13 (pipes) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD02 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.5 (strings), 17.12 (I/O redirection), 17.13 (pipes) - study notes written for this guide Strings (16.5): C has no string type; a string is an array of char ending with the null character '\0'. To store "hi" you need capacity 3 (h, i, \0); "hello" needs 6. printf("%s") prints characters until it reaches '\0'. strlen returns the number of characters before the null (not the array capacity). If the array is not null-terminated, library functions run past the end (undefined behavior). strcpy copies up to and including the null and assumes the destination is big enough: unsafe if it is not, and the programmer is responsible for valid strings. Java hides these details; C does not. I/O redirection (17.12): every process starts with three open streams: stdin (file descriptor 0, keyboard), stdout (1, terminal), stderr (2, terminal). A file descriptor is a positive integer referring to an open file; Unix treats devices like terminals as files too. Operators handled by the shell: < redirects stdin; > (same as 1>) redirects stdout and overwrites; >> appends stdout; 2> redirects stderr; &> redirects both stdout and stderr to one file (shorthand for 1> file 2>&1). Examples: wc < quote; cat quote > another; cat blah 2> error_out; echo "Again:" >> another; cat blah quote &> err_out; grep teach < another 1> grep_out 2> grep_error. Redirections are processed left to right, so 2>&1 must come after the stdout target to follow it. Pipes (17.13): cmd1 | cmd2 sends cmd1's stdout to cmd2's stdin with no intermediate file. Pipes chain: cat quote | grep th | wc. ls | wc counts lines/words/chars of ls output; ls | xargs wc runs wc on every file listed by ls.

title: RD03 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.4 (functions in C) and the array/strings background in 16.5 - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD03 reading notes - Dive into Systems 16.4 (functions in C) and the array/strings background in 16.5 - study notes written for this guide C is imperative and procedural: programs are organized as functions, starting at main (Java organizes into classes and objects; a Java program with one class, no data members and only public static methods looks most like a C program). A function definition is: return type, name, parameter list, body. A prototype (declaration) gives only the name, return type and parameter list. All functions must be declared before they are called (so the compiler knows the type information), which is why prototypes often sit above main. A function that returns nothing has return type void. A call looks like function_name(argument_list); arguments are expressions. Arguments are passed by value: each parameter receives a copy of the argument's value, so changing a parameter inside the function is not visible to the caller (in the max example, x = y changes only max's own x). The execution stack tracks active functions; each call creates a stack frame (activation record) holding the function's parameters and locals; it is pushed on call and popped on return. Only variables in the active frame are in scope. Functions break code into manageable pieces and reduce duplication; document each with what it does, each parameter, and what it returns. Arrays and functions (16.5): pass the array name (its base address); the function can change elements of the caller's array, but scalar parameters like size are copies. Functions usually take a size parameter because the array does not tell the function its capacity.

title: RD05 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.1-4.3 (number bases, binary, hexadecimal) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD05 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.1-4.3 (number bases, binary, hexadecimal) - study notes written for this guide Unsigned means zero or positive only. Decimal is base 10: each digit is multiplied by a power of 10 by position (8425 = 8x10^3 + 4x10^2 + 2x10^1 + 5x10^0), and adding 1 to the digit 9 needs another digit because a digit cannot exceed base-1. Binary is base 2: each digit (bit) is 0 or 1 and a position is worth a power of 2. Add 1 to a bit that is already 1 and it resets to 0 with a carry into the next bit. Labeling bits d0, d1, d2 ..., d0 is the rightmost (least significant). The prefix 0b marks binary; no prefix means decimal. Binary suits hardware because a bit maps to two reliable electrical states. Decimal does not align with powers of two, so it is a poor way to reason about fixed-size binary data such as 16-bit addresses. Hexadecimal is base 16: digits 0-9 then A-F for 10-15. Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so hex is a compact, human-readable notation for binary (this is why memory addresses are printed in hex even though they are stored as bits). Adding 1 to F gives 0 with a carry (0xF + 1 = 0x10). Prefix 0x. Conversions: binary to decimal by summing powers of two; decimal to binary by subtracting the largest power of two that fits; binary to hex by grouping four bits from the right; hex to binary by expanding each digit to four bits.

title: RD06 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.3.2-4.3.3 (two's complement and bit extension) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD06 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.3.2-4.3.3 (two's complement and bit extension) - study notes written for this guide Two's complement represents signed integers: the most significant bit contributes a large NEGATIVE weight (-2^(n-1)) to the sum, so an MSB of 1 means a negative number. Arithmetic wraps around naturally between negative numbers and zero (so addition uses the same hardware as unsigned addition, with no special cases and only one zero), which is why it is superior to sign-magnitude and one's complement. To negate a two's complement number: flip every bit and add one. C declares int as a signed two's complement integer. printf with %d interprets the bits as signed and %u as unsigned, so the same variable can print -100 and 4294967196: the bit pattern is the same, the interpretation differs. Bit extension: arithmetic needs operands of the same width, so a narrower value is extended before use (for example adding a 32-bit int and a 16-bit short). Sign extension repeats the most significant (sign) bit into the new high bits and preserves the value and sign of a two's complement number. Zero extension fills with zeros and is used for unsigned values; zero-extending a negative two's complement number changes its value.

title: RD07 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.6 (bitwise operators and shifts) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD07 reading notes - Dive into Systems 4.6 (bitwise operators and shifts) - study notes written for this guide Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integers; logical operators work on truth values. AND (&) gives 1 only where both bits are 1; OR (|) where at least one bit is 1; XOR (^) where exactly one bit is 1; NOT (~) flips every bit. Example: 0b011010 & 0b110110 = 0b010010; | = 0b111110; ^ = 0b101100; ~0b011010 flips all bits. Shifts move bits by a number of places. Left shift fills the right with zeros and usually grows the value (multiplies by 2^k), but bits shifted past the end are lost, which can make it smaller (0b00101101 << 2 = 0b10110100 in 8 bits). Right shift discards bits that fall off the right. Whether zeros or ones enter on the left depends on whether the number is signed or unsigned: a logical right shift fills with zeros, an arithmetic right shift copies the leftmost (sign) bit.

title: RD08 reading notes - Bitwise operators review (DiS 4.6, based on the previous lecture, 2.4 Bitwise Operators) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD08 reading notes - Bitwise operators review (DiS 4.6, based on the previous lecture, 2.4 Bitwise Operators) - study notes written for this guide Identities for any integer n: n | 0b000...0 = n; n | 0b111...1 = all ones; n | ~n = all ones; n & 0b111...1 = n; n & n = n; n & ~n = all zeros; n ^ n = all zeros; n ^ 0 = n. Shifts: x << k multiplies by 2^k (if no bits overflow); x >> k divides by 2^k. A logical right shift (unsigned) fills the left with zeros; an arithmetic right shift (signed) preserves the sign bit. In C an unsigned right shift is logical and a signed right shift is implementation-defined (usually arithmetic). With int8_t x = -5 and an arithmetic shift, x >> 1 is -3. Masks select, set, clear or toggle specific bits. Test bit i: num & (1 << i). Set bit i: num | (1 << i). Toggle: num ^ (1 << i). Clear: num & ~(1 << i).

title: RD10 reading notes - Dive into Systems 17.14 (dot files and .bashrc) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD10 reading notes - Dive into Systems 17.14 (dot files and .bashrc) - study notes written for this guide Dot files are configuration files whose names begin with a period. They are hidden by default (ls -a shows them) and customize how programs behave when they start: .bashrc configures the Bash shell (environment variables, aliases), .vimrc configures the vim editor (colors, encoding), .xsession configures the X Windows session. .bashrc is loaded when Bash starts. Changes to it do not affect an already-running shell; run source ~/.bashrc (or start a new shell) to apply them. Environment variables control how features work. PATH lists, in order, the directories the shell searches for programs when a command is typed. env prints all environment variables, echo $PATH shows one, and which ls shows which executable will run. To extend PATH in .bashrc: PATH=$PATH:/home/sarita/mybin (appends to the end of the existing value). Aliases are shortcuts for commands, defined in .bashrc: alias rm="rm -i" (confirm before deleting) and alias gt31="cd ~/classes/CS31" (jump to a directory).

text: [Slide 27] Binary in Normalized Form 27 1.0101 x 26 Significand Exponent Binary Point Base In normalized form, 1 <= |significand| < 2 This means the value to the left of the binary point is always 1. We can increase the precision by not storing this 1! [Slide 28] Implicit 1 • In normalized binary floating point, every (nonzero) number has a leading 1 before the binary point. • Since that leading one is always there, we don’t need to store it • Hence the name “Implicit 1” • By not storing it, we free up one extra bit for the significand • This extra bit increase precision • The range is unaffected by this • (Since the range is determined by the exponent bits) 28 [Slide 29] Example: Decimal to Microfloat V1 29 Exponent Bits Significand Bits 7 [Slide 30] Example: Decimal to Microfloat V1 30 1 0 1 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits 1.112 x 22 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> 7 0b111 [Slide 31] Example: Decimal to Microfloat V1 31 Exponent Bits Significand Bits 1.25 [Slide 32] Example: Decimal to Microfloat V1 32 0 0 0 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits 1.012 x 22 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> 1.25 0b1.01 [Slide 33] Example: Microfloat V1 to Decimal 33 0 1 0 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits [Slide 34] Example: Microfloat V1 to Decimal 34 0 1 0 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits 1.01 x 21 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> 2.5 [Slide 35] Example: Microfloat V1 to Decimal 35 1 1 0 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits

title: RD12 reading slides - Minifloat (sign, 3 exponent bits with bias 3, 4 significand bits) (part 1)
text: RD12 reading slides - Minifloat (sign, 3 exponent bits with bias 3, 4 significand bits) - text extracted from the slides for search [Slide 1] Minifloat COMP211 Connor McMahon [Slide 2] Minifloat 2 Exponent Bits Significand Bits Sign Bit Sign Bit (1 bit): • 0: Positive number • 1: Negative number Exponent (3 bits): • Represents the exponent using a fixed bias of 3 Significand (4 bits): • Represents the fractional part • Assumes an implicit leading 1 for normalized numbers [Slide 3] Bias • Why do we use a bias instead of 2’s complement? • Simplifies Comparison Operations • With a biased exponent, larger numbers have higher bit values, and smaller numbers have lower bit values, making it easy to compare them as unsigned integers. • If two’s complement were used, negative exponents (which have leading 1s) would be greater in unsigned comparison, breaking the ordering. 3 Bias = 2n-1-1 [Slide 4] Minifloat 4 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits Sign Bit (-1)S x 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> – <bias> Bias = 3 [Slide 5] Minifloat 5 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 1 Exponent Bits Significand Bits Sign Bit (-1)S x 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> – <bias> (-1)0 x 1.1011 x 25 – 3 Bias = 3 110.11 = 6.75 [Slide 6] Minifloat 6 1 0 0 1 1 0 0 0 Exponent Bits Significand Bits Sign Bit (-1)S x 1.<significand bits> x 2<exponent bits> – <bias> Bias = 3

title: RD13 reading notes - Floating point review: minifloat normalized vs denormalized (follow-up to RD11/RD12) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD13 reading notes - Floating point review: minifloat normalized vs denormalized (follow-up to RD11/RD12) - study notes written for this guide For each value decide whether it is normalized or denormalized in the 8-bit minifloat (1 sign, 3 exponent bits with bias 3, 4 significand bits) and give the encoding. Try normalized first: write the value as 1.f x 2^e and compute the exponent field e + 3. If the field is 1 to 6 the value is normalized. If it is less than or equal to 0 the value is too small to be normalized, so it is denormalized: divide by 2^-2 (the fixed denormalized exponent 1 - bias) and write the result as 0.ffff with the exponent field 000. Examples: 1/32 is denormalized (0b0000_0010); -3/8 is normalized (0b1001_1000); 9/64 is denormalized (0b0000_1001); -3/4 is normalized (0b1010_1000).

title: RD14 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.1 (parts of program memory) and 2.2 (pointers) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD14 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.1 (parts of program memory) and 2.2 (pointers) - study notes written for this guide Program memory is divided into parts: the code (text) segment holds the function instructions (main, max, change ...); the data segment holds global variables, which exist for the entire run; the heap holds dynamically allocated memory; the stack holds a stack frame for each active function call (parameters, local variables, return address). Space is allocated on the stack when a function is called and its frame is deallocated when it returns, so its locals become inaccessible. A local variable's scope is the function body in which it is declared, which is why two functions can each have a local named val. Global variables are generally discouraged because they reduce modularity and make debugging harder. A pointer variable stores a memory address, not a primitive value. int *ptr; declares ptr as a pointer to an integer. The address-of operator & obtains a variable's address; the dereference operator * accesses the value stored at the address a pointer refers to. A valid initialization is int x; int *ptr = &x;. Assigning NULL to a pointer means it does not point to a valid memory location.

title: RD15 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.3 (pointers and functions) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD15 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.3 (pointers and functions) - study notes written for this guide Pass-by-pointer lets a function modify a caller's variable: the parameter is a pointer, and the value copied into it is the address of the caller's variable. Dereferencing the pointer parameter (*p = ...) changes the caller's variable, because the pointer stores the address of the caller's variable. A prototype such as void f(int *x); allows modification of an int passed by the caller, called as f(&x). Assigning to the pointer parameter itself (p = NULL or input = &y) changes only the local copy. Pass-by-value cannot modify the caller's variable because the parameter is copied into a new memory location. The pointer argument typically points into the stack frame of the calling function (for example main).

title: RD16 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.4 (dynamic memory allocation) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD16 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.4 (dynamic memory allocation) - study notes written for this guide Programs use dynamic memory allocation to get memory whose size is only known at run time. Dynamically allocated memory lives on the heap. A local pointer variable (int *p; inside main) is stored on the stack, and the heap memory it points to is anonymous: it is not bound to a variable name. malloc(sizeof(int)) returns the base address of the allocated heap memory on success and NULL on failure, so the return value should be checked before dereferencing (dereferencing NULL can crash). The best way to allocate an array of 20 ints is arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * 20); arr then contains the base address of a contiguous block in the heap. d_array[i] works on a pointer because indexing is defined as offset plus dereference from the base address (d_array[i] is *(d_array + i)); *d_array = 8 stores 8 into element 0. After free(p), setting p = NULL helps catch accidental use-after-free (a crash on NULL dereference instead of silent corruption). free does not need the size because malloc stores metadata (such as the size) in a header before the block. When a dynamically allocated array is passed to a function, the base address (the pointer value) is passed, which is why functions taking arrays often also take a size parameter: so they know how many elements they can safely access.

title: RD17 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.5 (arrays in C) - study notes written for this guide (part 1)
text: RD17 reading notes - Dive into Systems 2.5 (arrays in C) - study notes written for this guide Statically declared local arrays are stored on the stack. When an array is passed to a function the base address of the array is passed (not a copy), so modifying the array parameter changes the caller's array. Space for 50 ints is malloc(sizeof(int) * 50); malloc's return value is checked because it may return NULL. After free(p_array), setting p_array = NULL prevents dangling-pointer use. Array elements are stored contiguously (no gaps between elements): with a 4-byte int the address difference between iarray[2] and iarray[3] is 4. Constants rather than numeric literals are used for array sizes for readability and maintainability. A 2D array with 50 rows and 100 columns is int a[50][100]; a statically allocated 2D array is stored in row-major order. The column dimension must be specified in a 2D array function parameter so the compiler can compute element offsets. Method 1 of dynamic 2D allocation is a single malloc of rows*cols elements (all elements contiguous, an int * accessed as arr[i*M + j]; arr[i][j] cannot be used). Method 2 is an array of row pointers (an int ** whose elements, the rows, are separately allocated; only elements within a row are contiguous; arr[i] is an int *). Methods 1 and 2 differ in layout and type, so they cannot share one function parameter type.

title: Mastery: Unix basics: file system, paths & core commands
text: Terminal vs shell vs CLI, the file system tree, absolute and relative paths, and the everyday commands (pwd, cd, ls, mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm, rmdir, echo, cat). The foundation for every later shell question. Three different things: the CLI is the text-based style of interaction, the terminal is the window that shows text and forwards your keystrokes, and the shell (bash here) is the program that actually interprets and runs your commands. Terminals came from teletypes typing to a computer; CRT screens replaced the paper, but the name stuck. Terminals stayed because they are scriptable, remote-friendly and powerful . The file system is a tree . The root / is on top; directories are branches that hold files and other directories; files are the leaves. Every item has a unique absolute path from the root. A relative path starts from the current working directory ( pwd shows it). . is here, .. is the parent, ~ is your home, ~name is that user’s home. Plain cd goes home. cp src dst copies (source stays); mv src dst moves or renames (source is gone). Both take exactly two arguments, and neither changes your working directory. Deletion is permanent. rm has no recycle bin; rmdir only removes empty directories (a safety net); rm -r recurses and -f silences prompts. Run pwd and ls before any rm -rf . Common trap: Thinking a command moved you. cp , mv , mkdir and touch never change the working directory; only cd does. Common trap: Confusing . and .. , or forgetting that a path with no leading / is relative to where you are . Common trap: mv a b when b is an existing directory puts a inside b ; it does not rename or merge. Common trap: cp on a directory needs -r . rm on a directory needs -r too (or use rmdir if empty). Common trap: Unix names are case sensitive , and spaces in names need escaping or quotes, which is why convention is hello_there .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Terminal vs shell vs CLI in one line each? — Terminal: the app/window that shows text and sends your keystrokes. Shell: the program that interprets and runs the commands (bash). CLI: the text-based style of interaction.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Why does the word “terminal” still exist? — Early teletype terminals were replaced by CRT screens, but the name stuck even though the technology changed.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Why do programmers still use the terminal? — It is scriptable, works well remotely, and is extremely powerful. Servers often have no GUI at all.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What does the shell prompt mean? — The shell saying “I’m ready for a command.” The loop is: prompt, you type, Enter, text output, prompt again.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What is the root directory, on Mac/Linux and on Windows? — / on Mac/Linux; a drive letter like C:\ on Windows. It is the top of the file-system tree.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Directories vs files in the tree? — Directories are branches (they contain files and other directories). Files are the leaves and hold data.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What do pwd , cd , ls do? — pwd: print the current working directory. cd: change it (no argument = home). ls: list the cwd, or the directory you name.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What do . , .. , ~ and ~sarita mean? — Current directory, parent directory, your home directory, and sarita’s home directory.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: How do you see hidden files, and what makes a file hidden? — ls -a . A name beginning with a dot ( .git , .vscode , .bashrc ) is hidden; it also shows . and .. .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: cp vs mv ? — cp duplicates (the original stays); mv relocates or renames (the original is gone). Both take source then destination. Neither changes your cwd.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: How do you copy a whole directory? — cp -r source_dir dest_dir . Without -r cp refuses a directory.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: rm vs rmdir vs rm -r vs rm -rf ? — rm deletes a file permanently (no recycle bin). rmdir deletes only an empty directory. rm -r deletes a directory and everything inside. -f suppresses all prompting.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What should you do before running rm -rf ? — Run pwd and ls to confirm you are in the right directory and see what you are about to destroy. ( rm -i prompts first, and some admins alias rm to it.)

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Which command shows a file’s contents, appends text to one, and counts it? — cat file shows it. echo "text" >> file appends. wc file counts lines, words and bytes.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Naming rules worth remembering? — Names are case sensitive ( basics ≠ Basics ). Spaces need escaping or quotes, so convention avoids them: hello_there .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You open Terminal.app on a Mac and type ls . Which component actually interprets and runs that command? — Terminal → shell → your command. The shell is the interpreter.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: CRT screens replaced paper teletypes. Why is the window you type into still called a “terminal”? — Teletype and console terminals connected to computers; CRTs kept the word.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: In the file-system tree, which items can contain other items ? — Directories are branches; files are the leaves.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You want to rename report.txt to report_final.txt without keeping the old name. Which command does that? — mv with source then destination both moves and renames.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Select all true statements about removing things in Unix. — rmdir’s refusal is a safety net, and rm -rf is the deliberate escape hatch. Check where you are first.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: A directory contains a file named basics . Which statement is true? — basics and Basics are two separate names.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You start in /home/carla . After cd comp211/labs , then cd ../notes , then cd ../.. , what does pwd print? — comp211/labs → .../comp211/labs ; ../notes goes up to comp211 and down into notes; ../.. goes up two levels: notes → comp211 → carla.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You are in /home/carla . What do these print? (Names separated by spaces.) — ls with a path lists that directory without moving you there.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You start in /home/carla . After this sequence, fill in the results. cd comp211 mkdir build touch build/a.o cd build mkdir ../out cp a.o ../out mv a.o b.o cd .. — The last cd .. leaves you in comp211. build now holds the renamed b.o; out holds the earlier copy a.o; comp211 now has build and out alongside labs and notes.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: From /home/carla/comp211 you run cp notes/lec1.note ../comp301 and then mv notes/lec2.note ../comp301 . Fill in the results. — cp left lec1.note in notes and added a copy to comp301. mv took lec2.note out of notes. Neither command moved you.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: In an empty directory you run touch .secret visible . What do the two listings print? (Names in order, separated by spaces.) — A name starting with a dot is hidden from plain ls . ls -a shows everything, including . and .. .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You run mkdir d; touch d/f . Does rmdir d work now? After rm d/f , does rmdir d work? (Answer “works” or “fails”.) — rmdir only removes empty directories. That refusal protects content you forgot was inside.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: How many lines does basics contain at the end? touch basics echo "ls: list directory contents" >> basics echo "cd: change directory" >> basics cat basics | grep -c . — touch makes an empty file; each >> appends one line. cat shows both lines and grep -c . counts the non-empty ones.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: A cleanup script is meant to empty the build folder. One day it deleted the whole project instead. Which line is the root cause? — Never run a destructive command after an unchecked cd . Use cd dir && rm -rf ./* so the delete only runs if the cd succeeded, and check pwd first.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: cp unix_notes notes_copy fails with a complaint about omitting a directory. Which part of the command is the problem? — cp -r unix_notes notes_copy copies the directory and its whole contents.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You are in /work/src . The tree has /work/src/main.c , /work/docs/notes.md and /work/tmp/ . Fill the blanks using paths relative to where you are. cp __0__ /work/tmp mv main.c __1__ ls __2__ — From src, the docs directory is a sibling: go up with .. then down into docs. Renaming is mv old new .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Arrange the commands so that main.c ends up inside proj/src , starting from an empty directory. Two commands do not belong. — proj must exist before you cd into it, and src before you put a file in it. cd main.c fails (main.c is a file) and rmdir would delete what you are building.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: The tree is /lab/x/y/data.txt , /lab/x/notes.txt and /lab/z/out.log . Write the relative path that names the target from each starting directory. — Go up with .. to the lowest common directory ( /lab ), then down. From y: up to x, up to lab, down into z. From z: up to lab, down x, y. From x: up to lab, down z.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Your home is /home/carla and you start in /home/carla/comp211/labs . Fill in pwd after each command in sequence. cd cd ~/comp301 cd ../comp211/notes cd ../../.. — cd with no argument goes home. ~ expands to the home directory. ../comp211/notes goes up from comp301 to carla, then down. Three .. from notes climb notes → comp211 → carla → home.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: In an empty directory you run mkdir a b , touch a/f , then mv a b . What do these list? — Because b already exists as a directory, mv a b moves a into it (making b/a ); it does not rename or merge.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You are in /home/jake/comp211/labs/lab00 , which holds file1.c and file2.c . You want both files moved up into labs , then lab00 removed. Select all command sequences that work. — You must first empty lab00 (mv, not cp), then leave it, then remove it. rmdir needs it empty; rm -r works either way.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: The tree is /home/sam/classes/COMP211/notes.txt , /home/sam/letters/draft.txt , /home/sam/projects/demo.c , and you are in /home/sam/classes/COMP211 . Write commands for each task, then redo the first two using absolute paths and say when you would prefer each style. (1) show the contents of demo.c ; (2) copy notes.txt into letters ; (3) remove letters only if it is empty; (4) create a new directory archive in projects . — (1) cat ../../projects/demo.c · abs: cat /home/sam/projects/demo.c (2) cp notes.txt ../../letters · abs: cp /home/sam/classes/COMP211/notes.txt /home/sam/letters (3) rmdir ../../letters (rmdir refuses non-empty directories, so it is the safe choice; letters still holds draft.txt so this would fail) (4) mkdir ../../projects/archive Relative paths are shorter and work well when you are already nearby; absolute paths are unambiguous and safer in scripts or when you are not sure where you are.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Teach it. Explain the difference between a terminal, a shell and a CLI, and describe what happens, step by step, between typing ls and seeing the output. — The terminal is just the window. When you press Enter, it hands your line to the shell, which parses it and runs ls . The output text is passed back and the terminal displays it. CLI describes this whole text-command style.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Explain absolute vs relative paths, what . , .. and ~ mean, and what “current working directory” has to do with all of it. — Everything is interpreted relative to the cwd unless the path starts with / . .. climbs one level; ~ jumps to home. That is why the same relative path can name different files depending on where you are.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Explain how rm and rmdir differ, why Unix deletion deserves care, and the habits that keep you from destroying the wrong files. — Because nothing goes to a trash, a mistake is permanent. rmdir’s restriction is deliberate friction. When you do need rm -rf, confirm where you are and what is there first, or use -i.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What does the current working directory represent? — Relative paths and default file operations are interpreted from the cwd.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You run touch notes.txt without giving a path. Where is the file created? — With no path, a name means “in the current directory.”

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Which command appends a line of text to a file called log ? — >> appends; > overwrites.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Which command prints the contents of a file in the terminal? — cat concatenates and displays file contents.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Which directory is the parent of /home/pat/music/rock ? — The parent is the path with the last component removed.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What happens when you run cd with no arguments ? — cd alone returns home, the same as cd ~ .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Your cwd is /home/pat . Which directory does cd music/rock move you into? — A relative path is appended to the cwd.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What does ~lee refer to? — ~name names the home directory of user name .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What is the key difference between cp and mv ? — After cp there are two files; after mv there is still one.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: In cp report.txt backup.txt , which item is the source ? — Syntax: cp source destination .

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What does the -r option do in cp -r photos photos_backup ? — Without -r , cp refuses to copy a directory.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What restriction does rmdir have by default? — The refusal protects content you may have forgotten about.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What does rm -i do? — The interactive flag asks for confirmation, which is why some systems alias rm to rm -i.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Why should you run pwd and ls before rm -rf ? — rm -rf has no undo, so check the location and contents first.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: The tree is /exam/a/c/e.md , /exam/a/f.md , /exam/b/d/g.md , /exam/b/h.md , and your cwd is /exam/a/c . Give each answer. — From c, one .. reaches a (where f.md lives). Two .. reach /exam, then down b/d/g.md. The parent of c is /exam/a.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Same tree, but now your cwd is /exam/b . Give the relative path to each target. — Climb with .. only when the target is outside the current subtree. g.md is already below b, so no climbing is needed.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: The tree is /home/ana/classes/COMP211/notes.txt , /home/ana/letters/draft.txt , /home/ana/projects/demo.c . Your cwd is /home/ana/classes/COMP211 . Fill in each command’s path using relative paths. cat __0__ cp notes.txt __1__ ls __2__ — From COMP211, two .. reach /home/ana , then down into projects or letters.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: You are in /home/jake/comp211/labs/lab00 , holding file1.c and file2.c . You want both moved up into labs and then lab00 removed. Select all sequences that work. — Empty the directory with mv, step out of it, then remove it. rm -r also works.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What is machine code ? — Machine code is the only language the CPU runs; everything else is translated into it.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: What is the relationship between assembly language and machine code? — One assembly instruction maps to one machine instruction.

title: Mastery: Unix file system
text: Which command compiles demo.c into an executable named demo ? — The name right after -o is the output file.

title: Mastery: CL02 · Intro to C (+ RD01)
text: From machine code to the C compiler, your first program, gcc, types and printf, characters as numbers, reading input with getchar, plus the reading’s conditionals, loops, arrays and strings. Machine code is binary the CPU runs. Assembly is a human-readable form of it, translated by an assembler . High-level languages (C, Java, Python) are translated further down: C goes compiler → assembly → assembler → machine code before running. Python is interpreted instead. Every C program starts at main , which returns an int exit status: 0 = success , non-zero = something went wrong. Library functions need their header: #include <stdio.h> for printf . C includes nothing automatically. gcc hello.c builds a.out ; -o name picks the name (the name must immediately follow -o ). Run it with ./a.out : the ./ is needed because the current directory is not on your PATH. Compile errors mean no new executable is made, but an old one may still be there . A type gives a variable its size and its interpretation. Typical sizes: char 1, short 2, int 4, long 4 or 8, long long 8, float 4, double 8. sizeof yields an unsigned long, printed with %lu . Characters are numbers. 'A' is 65, 'a' is 97, '0' is 48. %c prints a value as a character and %d prints the same bits as an integer. 'h' is a char; "h" is a string. getchar() returns an int so EOF can never collide with a real character. The idiom is while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) . In C, 0 is false and any nonzero value is true ; && and || short-circuit. Common trap: if (x = 5) assigns instead of comparing: it is always true. Common trap: 11 / 2 is 5 , not 5.5. Integer division truncates; 11 / 2.0 is 5.5. Common trap: x++ uses the old value then increments; ++x increments first. Common trap: The letter test c >= 'A' && c <= 'z' also accepts [ \ ] ^ _ ` , which sit between ‘Z’ and ‘a’. Common trap: Using the wrong placeholder ( %d for a double) prints garbage. Forgetting \n leaves the prompt on the same line.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What is machine code, and what is assembly? — Machine code: binary instructions the CPU executes directly. Assembly: a human-readable form of those instructions (e.g. add x8, x9, x10 ), turned into machine code by an assembler.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Compiler vs assembler? — A compiler translates high-level code (C) into assembly. An assembler translates assembly into machine code. gcc runs both.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Compiled vs interpreted language? — Compiled (C): translated to machine code before running. Interpreted (Python): executed by another program without a separate machine-code file.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Why do C programs need #include <stdio.h> ? — C does not include library functions automatically. The header supplies the declarations (name, return type, parameters) for printf, getchar, etc.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does main return, and what do the values mean? — An int exit status: 0 for success, non-zero for an abnormal run.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: gcc basics? — gcc hello.c → a.out . -o name sets the output name (name right after -o). Run with ./name .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Why ./a.out and not a.out ? — The current directory is not in your PATH, so the shell would not find it; ./ names it explicitly.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: A compile error occurred. Why might an old version still run? — A failed compile does not create or overwrite the executable, so one from an earlier successful build may still exist.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Usual sizes of char, short, int, long, long long, float, double? — 1, 2, 4, 4 or 8, 8, 4, 8 bytes. Use sizeof to check; print with %lu .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Escape sequences to know? — \n newline · \t tab · \\ backslash · \" quote · \0 null · %% prints a percent sign (in printf).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Placeholders to know? — %d int · %u unsigned · %f / %g float/double · %c char · %s string · %lu unsigned long.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: ‘h’ vs "h"? — 'h' is a single char (ASCII 104). "h" is a string literal: the char h plus a null terminator.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: ASCII anchors? — A = 65, B = 66, a = 97, '0' = 48, space = 32, ! = 33. Lowercase is 32 above uppercase. 'a' - 'C' = 30.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Why does getchar return an int? — So EOF (a special value) can never be confused with a real character code (0 to 255).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: How do you signal EOF from the keyboard? — Ctrl+D on Linux/macOS (Ctrl+Z on Windows).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Truth values in C? — No boolean type: 0 is false, any nonzero value is true. Relational operators give 1 or 0.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Short-circuit evaluation? — a && b skips b if a is false; a || b skips b if a is true.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: x++ vs ++x ? — x++ uses the old value, then increments. ++x increments first, then uses the new value.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: while vs do-while vs for ? — while tests first (may run 0 times). do-while runs the body first (at least once). for = init once; test; body; step; repeat.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Array facts in C? — Fixed size set at declaration, indices 0 to size-1, no bounds checking (undefined behavior). A function that changes an array parameter changes the caller’s array, so pass the size too.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What are the three rules for matching printf arguments? — One argument per placeholder, in the same order, and each argument’s type must suit its placeholder.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Which placeholder for an int , a double , a char , a string, a sizeof ? — %d , %f , %c , %s , %zu (or %lu ).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does %f print by default? — Six digits after the decimal point: printf("%f", 3.14) prints 3.140000 .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does %.2f do? Is it rounded or cut? — Prints exactly 2 digits after the point, rounded to nearest and zero-padded: 5.678 → 5.68, 2.5 → 2.50.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: %5d vs %-5d vs %05d for 42? — 42 (padded left) · 42 (padded right) · 00042 (zero padded).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: How do you print a literal percent sign? — %% . A single % starts a placeholder.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: printf("%c", 66) and printf("%d", 'A') ? — B and 65 . A char is a small number; the placeholder picks the view.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Which placeholder does qty * price need, with int qty , double price ? — %f (e.g. %.2f ): int times double is a double.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What happens with printf("%d", 4.5) ? — The double’s bits are read as an int: garbage. Use %f or cast with (int) .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Method to build a format string from a target? — Cut the target into pieces; mark the variable parts; pick placeholders by type; assemble in order with arguments in the same order; check counts and types.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does an assembler do? — Assembly is human-readable; the assembler converts it into the binary the CPU runs.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: “C is a compiled language.” What does that say about how a C program is run? — C is translated ahead of time into a binary the machine runs directly.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: In int main() { … return 0; } , what does returning 0 communicate? — 0 means success; non-zero reports that something went wrong.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What is the key difference between 'h' and "h" in C? — Single quotes: one character (ASCII 104). Double quotes: a null-terminated string.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: You want to call sqrt . Which header declares it? — math.h holds sqrt, pow, sin, cos and friends (you may also need -lm when linking).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Which statement about booleans in C is true? — if (5) and if (-1) are both true; if (0) is false.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Select all true statements about C types and sizes. — sizeof is an unsigned long, hence %lu ; sizes shown are typical and architecture-dependent.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? (three values separated by spaces) printf("%d %c %d", 'A', 'A' + 2, 'a' - 'C'); — %d of 'A' is 65. 'A' + 2 is 67, which %c prints as 'C'. 'a' (97) minus 'C' (67) is 30.

", 11 / 2.0); printf("%d
", 11 % 2); — Two ints use integer division, which truncates (5). One double operand makes it real division (5.5). % gives the integer remainder (1).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? (three values separated by spaces) int x = 9; int y = x++ + 2; int z = ++x * 2; printf("%d %d %d", x, y, z); — x++ + 2 uses 9 (y = 11) and then x becomes 10. ++x makes x 11 first, so z = 11 × 2 = 22. Final x is 11.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: This loop prints one number per line. Fill in the lines in order. int num = 10, val = 1; while (val < num) { printf("%d\n", val); val = val * 2; } — val doubles each time: 1, 2, 4, 8. The next value, 16, fails val < 10 , so the loop ends before printing it.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Fill in what each loop prints (digits run together). int n = 5; do { printf("%d", n); n++; } while (n < 5); printf("\n"); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { printf("%d", i * i); } — A do-while runs its body once before testing, so it prints 5 even though n < 5 is false. The for loop prints 0, 1, 4, 9.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Fill in y after each if statement runs (cumulative). int x = 0, y = 0; if (x != 0 && (y = 5)) { } // after A if (x == 0 || (y = 7)) { } // after B if (x == 0 && (y = 9)) { } // after C — In A, x != 0 is false so && never evaluates the assignment. In B, x == 0 is true so || never evaluates it either. In C, both sides must be checked, so y = 9 runs.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: scanf reads numbers and stores them at the addresses given with & . ( sscanf does the same from a string.) What does this print? int a, b; sscanf("30 67", "%d %d", &a, &b); printf("%d + %d = %d", a, b, a + b); — scanf-family functions skip whitespace between numbers. Each value is stored through its address ( &a , &b ).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? (the letter, then its number) char c = 'a'; c += 3; printf("%c %d", c, c); — 'a' is 97; adding 3 gives 100, which is the ASCII code of 'd'. %c and %d show the same value two ways.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: This is supposed to print “five” only when x is 5, but it prints it even though x starts as 3. Find the root cause. — Use == to compare. A single = inside a condition is a classic C bug.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: This prints a strange number instead of 3.14. Which line is wrong? — Each placeholder must match its argument’s type: %d int, %f / %g float or double.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The program should say “letter” only for letters, but it also says “letter” for _ and [ . Why? — Test the two ranges separately: (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') , or use isalpha from <ctype.h> .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Complete the test for “is a letter.” if ((c >= 'A' && c = 'a' && c <= __1__)) { printf("letter\n"); } — Uppercase runs ‘A’ to ‘Z’ (65 to 90); lowercase ‘a’ to ‘z’ (97 to 122). Splitting into two ranges excludes the symbols in between.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Arrange a complete program that copies stdin to stdout one character at a time. Two lines do not belong. — c must be an int so EOF is distinguishable, and putchar(c) prints one character. printf(c) would treat the value as a format string.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: You edit hello.c but make a typo. gcc hello.c -o hello reports an error, yet ./hello still runs and prints the old output. Why? — Always confirm the compile succeeded (no errors) before trusting what you run.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The source is hello.c . Select all commands that create an executable named hi . — The name must come right after -o ; its position relative to the source file does not matter.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: A Caesar shift moves a lowercase letter forward by 3 and wraps from z back to a. Fill in the results. char c = 'x'; int shift = 3; char r = 'a' + (c - 'a' + shift) % 26; printf("%c %d", r, r); — 'x' is 23 letters after 'a'. 23 + 3 = 26, and % 26 wraps it to 0, so the result is 'a' + 0 = 97.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? char s[] = "a1b22c3"; int sum = 0; for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) { if (s[i] >= '0' && s[i] <= '9') { sum += s[i] - '0'; } } printf("%d", sum); — The digit characters are 1, 2, 2, 3. s[i] - '0' converts each to its numeric value, giving 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8. The loop stops at the null terminator.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Fill in main’s values after the call. void fill(int a[], int n, int v) { for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) a[i] = v + i; n = 0; } int main(void) { int arr[4] = {9, 9, 9, 9}; int n = 3; fill(arr, n, 10); } — The function changes the caller’s array through the array parameter (only the first n = 3 elements). arr[3] is untouched. n = 0 changed only the callee’s copy.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? (format: text|number) char s[6] = "cat"; s[3] = 's'; printf("%s|%zu", s, strlen(s)); — The partial initializer fills s[3] and s[4] with nulls. Overwriting s[3] with 's' leaves s[4] as the null terminator, so the string is now "cats" with length 4.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Write a complete C program that reads all of stdin and prints, on one line, the number of letters and the number of digits it saw (for example letters=5 digits=2 ). Do not use ctype.h . — #include <stdio.h> int main() { int c, letters = 0, digits = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if ((c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') || (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z')) { letters++; } else if (c >= '0' && c <= '9') { digits++; } } printf("letters=%d digits=%d\n", letters, digits); return 0; }

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Write int is_vowel(int c) that returns 1 if c is a vowel (a, e, i, o, u in either case) and 0 otherwise. Then explain what short-circuit evaluation does for your condition. — int is_vowel(int c) { if (c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z') { c = c + ('a' - 'A'); // normalize to lowercase } return c == 'a' || c == 'e' || c == 'i' || c == 'o' || c == 'u'; } With || , evaluation stops at the first true comparison, so a vowel ‘a’ never checks the remaining four. Comparisons produce 1 or 0, which is exactly the return value wanted.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Teach it. Explain what happens between writing hello.c and seeing its output: the translation steps, what gcc produces, how -o works, why you type ./ , and what can go wrong when the compile fails. — gcc runs the compiler and assembler to make an executable file. Nothing executes until you run it by path ( ./name ). If the build fails, the old file can fool you into thinking your change had no effect.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Explain why printf("%c", 67) prints C while printf("%d", 'C') prints 67 , and why getchar() returns an int . — Bits get meaning only through a representation. ASCII maps numbers to characters; printf’s placeholder picks which lens. getchar returns int so “no more input” is a value that cannot be mistaken for real data.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: You know Java. Explain the main differences you must keep in mind writing C: how code runs, structure, output, booleans, and arrays. — C trades Java’s safety nets for direct control. Nothing is imported automatically, nothing checks array bounds, and booleans are plain integers. You manage sizes, formats and headers yourself.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Which placeholder prints a double such as 3.14 ? — %f handles float and double.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: How many arguments must follow the format string in printf("%d + %d = %d", ...) ? — One argument per placeholder.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does printf("%f", 3.14) print by default? — Add a precision ( %.2f ) to control the digits.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: How do you make printf print a literal percent sign? — In a format string %% prints one % .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: printf("%d", 'A') prints which output? — A char is a small number; %d shows the number.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does the 5 in %5d mean? — 42 prints as three spaces then 42.

Leading = before the digits, trailing = after. printf("%5d", 42); printf("%-5d", 42); printf("%8.2f", 3.14159); — %5d makes a 5-column field: 42 uses 2, so 3 spaces on the left. title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? char food[] = "pizza"; int slices = 3; printf("I ate %d slices of %s.", slices, food); — The first placeholder ( %d ) takes slices , the second ( %s ) takes food .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print? (three items separated by spaces) char w[] = "hello"; printf("%s %c %c", w, w[0], w[4]); — %s prints the whole string. w[0] and w[4] are single characters printed with %c .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Count the spaces for the string "hi" . printf("%10s", "hi"); printf("%-10s", "hi"); — The field is 10 columns and “hi” uses 2, so 8 spaces: before it by default, after it with the minus flag.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: This is meant to print Total: 4.5 but prints a strange number. Which line is the root cause? — The placeholder must match the argument’s type: double needs %f .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

text: The program prints a nonsense number for the count of items. Which line is the root cause? — int → %d . Using %f with an int reads the wrong bits.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Variables: char item[] = "mug"; double price = 6.5; Fill in the two placeholders so it prints mug costs $6.50 . printf("%__0__ costs $%__1__", item, price); — A string is %s . Two decimals with a double is %.2f .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Fill in the width so that the number 42 is printed in a field of 5 columns , padded on the left (3 spaces then 42). printf("%__0__d|", 42); — %5d right-aligns in 5 columns, so there are 3 leading spaces.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Variables: char name[] = "Sam"; int assignments = 8; double average = 91.67; Which format string prints Sam completed 8 assignments with an average of 91.7. ? — String, int, then a double with one decimal, in argument order.

text: Fill in the output of each call. (Remember: the type of an expression decides what it prints as.) int qty = 4; double price = 2.5; printf("%d x $%.2f = $%.2f\n", qty, price, qty * price); printf("%c %d %c\n", 'a' + 1, 'a' + 1, 'A' + 25); — qty * price is a double (10.0) so %.2f shows 10.00. 'a' + 1 is 98: %c shows b and %d shows 98. 'A' + 25 is 90, which is Z.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: This loop prints three lines. Fill them in. for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) { printf("%d^2 = %d\n", i, i * i); } — Each pass uses the loop variable twice: once as itself and once squared.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Which call is wrong (undefined or garbage) for int n = 7; double d = 7.0; char c = 'x'; char s[] = "ok"; ? — A double needs %f. Reading a double with %d is the classic placeholder mismatch.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

The literal percent sign is written %% , and the newline is typed as \n .

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Teach it. Explain how printf turns a format string and arguments into output: what a placeholder is, how arguments are matched, how to choose the right placeholder, how %.2f and %5d change the output, and what goes wrong when types or counts do not match. — printf walks the format string, copying plain text and swapping each placeholder for the next argument formatted as that placeholder says. If the types, order or count are wrong, it reads the wrong bits and prints garbage.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What is printed? int items = 6; double each = 2.5; printf("I sold %d items at $%.2f each.", items, each); — %d takes items (6) and %.2f takes each with two decimals (2.50).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Variables: char pet[] = "cat"; int age = 4; . You want printf to produce My cat is 4 years old. Which format string is correct? — A string uses %s , an int uses %d , in the order of the arguments.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: You want printf to produce these two lines exactly: Menu: "Soup" costs 5% Thanks! Which format string is correct? — Escape the quotes ( \" ), write %% for a literal percent sign, and use \n for the line break.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: How many characters are in the string "a\tb\n" ? ( strlen counts each escape sequence as one character.) — The characters are: a, tab, b, newline. Each escape sequence is a single character.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: On this machine char is 1 byte, short is 2 bytes and float is 4 bytes. What is the exact output? printf("%zu %zu %zu", sizeof(char), sizeof(short), sizeof(float)); — sizeof reports each type’s size in bytes, printed with the %zu placeholder.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Assume int is 4 bytes and double is 8 bytes. Fill in what each sizeof evaluates to. double d = 1.5; int arr[5]; printf("%zu\n%zu\n", sizeof(d), sizeof(arr)); — A double takes 8 bytes. An array of 5 ints takes 5 × 4 = 20 bytes (sizeof sees the whole array when it is declared in the same scope).

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: Assume char is 1 byte, int is 4 bytes and double is 8 bytes, with char g = 'A'; int n = 95; double avg = 92.5; . Which statement is true? — sizeof depends only on the type: char 1, int 4, double 8.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: What does this print if the user types Hi! and presses Enter? int c; while ((c = getchar()) != '\n') { putchar(c); putchar(c); } — Every character is printed twice, in order.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The input is eleven followed by EOF. What does this print? int c; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == 'e') putchar('#'); else putchar(c); } — Each ‘e’ becomes ‘#’ and every other character is copied: # l # v # n.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C

Three lines but only two newlines, because the last line is not terminated.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The input is aBc 9 then EOF. What does this print? int c; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c >= 'a' && c <= 'z') c = c - ('a' - 'A'); putchar(c); } — Lowercase letters shift down by 32 into uppercase. ‘B’, the space and ‘9’ are unchanged.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: in_word is a state variable. The input is one two three , a newline, four , then EOF. What is the final count ? int c, in_word = 0, count = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == ' ' || c == '\n') { in_word = 0; } else if (in_word == 0) { in_word = 1; count++; } } — A word is counted at the moment the state flips from “outside” to “inside.” Extra spaces do not create extra words: one, two, three, four.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The input is the three lines below (the middle line is empty ), each ending in a newline, then EOF. What does it print? ab cd int c, state = 0, count = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == '\n') state = 0; else if (state == 0) { state = 1; count++; } } printf("%d", count); — The state turns on at the first character of a line. The empty line never has a first character, so only “ab” and “cd” count.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The input is "a" b "c d" "e then EOF (the last quote is never closed). What does this print? int c, state = 0, count = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == '"') { if (state == 0) state = 1; else { state = 0; count++; } } } printf("%d", count); — A quoted string is counted when its closing quote arrives. "a" and "c d" close; the final “e has no closing quote, so it is never counted.

title: Mastery: CL02 Intro to C
text: The input is x"abc"y"de" then EOF. What does this print? (It counts the characters that are inside quotes.) int c, inside = 0, count = 0; while ((c = getchar()) != EOF) { if (c == '"') inside = !inside; else if (inside) count++; } printf("%d", count); — The quote characters toggle the state and are not counted. Inside the quotes are abc (3) and de (2).

title: Mastery: CL03 · Arrays, I/O redirection, pipes & strings (+ RD02)
text: Counting with arrays and #define, the three standard streams, redirecting them with >> 2>, connecting programs with pipes, and how C strings really work. A C array is a block of memory that does not store its size : you track it yourself, often with a #define . #define NAME value is text substitution by the preprocessor before compiling: no memory, no type, cannot change. It removes “magic numbers.” The build has four stages: preprocessor ( #include , #define ) → compiler (C to assembly) → assembler (to machine code) → linker (combines with libraries into the executable). Every process starts with three streams: stdin = 0 , stdout = 1 , stderr = 2 , all attached to the terminal. A file descriptor is a non-negative integer naming an open file. The shell rewires the streams before the program runs: < file (stdin), > file (overwrite stdout), >> file (append), 2> file (stderr). The program is unaware: getchar still reads stdin. putchar and printf always write to stdout . To write to stderr use fputc(c, stderr) or fprintf(stderr, ...) . stderr exists so errors can go somewhere different from normal output. A pipe a | b connects a’s stdout to b’s stdin with no temporary file. Stderr is not piped. wc -l / -w / -c count lines, words, bytes. A string is a char array ending in '\0' . strlen counts characters before the null; sizeof is the array’s total size. A {'h','i'} array with no null is not a string. Common trap: ndigit[c]++ uses the character code (48..57) as an index: out of bounds. You need c - '0' . And 'c' - '0' is the letter c (99), not your variable. Common trap: Using > twice destroys the first run’s output; >> appends. Common trap: printf errors do not go to stderr, so 2> err.txt stays empty. Common trap: Redirection order matters: > out.txt 2>&1 sends both to the file, but 2>&1 > out.txt sends stderr to the terminal . Common trap: #define MAX 3+1 then MAX*2 is 3+1*2 = 5, not 8: it is only text.
