title: Mastery: CL04 · Function stack frames & memory diagrams (+ RD03)
text: What a call does to memory, how to draw it the way the course expects, what is copied versus shared, and what the reading adds about functions, prototypes and pass-by-value. The stack manages function calls. Each call gets a stack frame (an activation record) holding the return address (RA) , the arguments and the local variables . Caller makes the call; callee is the function called. The stack pointer (sp) marks the current top of the stack. In the course’s diagrams the stack grows downward, toward lower addresses : a new frame is drawn below the caller’s, and sp moves down with it. On return, the callee places its return value in the caller’s frame (labelled RV(callee) ), its frame is deallocated (put an X through it) and sp moves back up . The old bytes may still be there physically, but the memory is no longer valid and gets reused by the next call. Draw sizes in bytes: RA (8) , an int8_t is 1, int32_t 4, a pointer 8. main ’s RA is just “return to the OS” (shown as 0). Return addresses are line numbers in the diagrams. Pass by value: scalar arguments are copies ; changing them never changes the caller. Arrays are not copied: the callee gets an 8-byte pointer ( pointer to stack , drawn with an arrow) to the caller’s array, so element changes are visible. #define names are replaced by the preprocessor, so they take no space in any frame. Functions must be declared before use : put a prototype (name, return type, parameters) above main . Common trap: Drawing a callee’s frame above the caller, or letting a deallocated frame stay un-X’d. Common trap: Forgetting the RV(...) slot: the return value goes in the caller’s frame, not the callee’s. Common trap: Copying a whole array into the callee’s frame. Only an 8-byte pointer goes in. Common trap: Giving a #define constant its own box in the diagram. Common trap: Thinking local variables survive the call: they die with their frame, which is why returning a pointer to a local is a bug and why unbounded recursion overflows the stack.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is the stack and what is a stack frame? — The stack is the area of memory managing function calls. A stack frame is one function’s workspace: return address, arguments and local variables.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Caller vs callee? — The caller makes the call; the callee is the function being called. Every call has one of each.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is the stack pointer (sp)? — It holds the address of the current top of the stack. It moves to make room on a call and moves back on a return.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Which direction does the stack grow in the course diagrams? — Toward lower addresses: a new frame is drawn below the caller’s frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does the return address (RA) record? — Where in the caller execution continues after the callee returns. ( main ’s RA is the OS, drawn as 0.)

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Where does the return value go and how is it labelled? — Into the caller’s frame, labelled RV(callee) .

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What do you do to the diagram when a function returns? — Put an X through its frame and move sp back up. Its data may remain but is invalid and will be reused.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why do local variables disappear when a function returns? — They live in the callee’s frame, which is deallocated on return.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: How is an array parameter represented in a frame? — As an 8-byte pointer to stack with an arrow to the original array in the caller’s frame. Nothing is copied.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Pass by value vs pass by pointer? — By value: the callee gets a copy, so changes are invisible to the caller. By pointer: the callee gets an address and can change the original.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Sizes to draw: RA, int8_t, int16_t, int32_t, int64_t, pointer? — 8, 1, 2, 4, 8, 8 bytes.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Does #define SIZE 5 get a box in a stack frame? — No. The preprocessor replaces it with 5 in the code, so it is not stored in any frame.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is a function prototype and why put it above main? — It declares a function’s name, return type and parameter list so it can be called before its full definition appears.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why must functions be declared before they are called? — The compiler must know a function’s type information (return type and parameters) before the call.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What goes wrong with deep or endless recursion? — Each call pushes another frame; the stack runs out of space (a stack overflow).

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What is a process? — A running instance of a program (active), with its own memory, CPU state and resources. A program on its own is passive code.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Main calls foo . In the course’s memory diagrams, where is foo’s frame drawn and which way does the stack grow? — New frames are drawn below the caller and sp moves down.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What happens to the stack pointer when a new function’s frame is created? — sp always points at the top (the newest frame).

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does the return address (RA) in a frame represent? — The CPU needs it to resume the caller at the right line.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Main calls add , which returns a value main needs. What label marks that location in main’s frame? — The return value is placed in the caller’s frame as RV(callee) .

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Why do we put an X through a stack frame after its function returns? — Deallocated means invalid, not zeroed.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Select all things that may be stored in a function’s stack frame. — Arguments, locals and the return address.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: What does a function prototype specify? — It lets main call functions defined later in the file.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: How does the reading characterize C compared to Java? — A C program is a collection of functions starting at main.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Using the course sizes (RA is 8 bytes), how many bytes does each frame take? int8_t add(int8_t a, int8_t b) { int8_t result = a + b; return result; } /* main: */ int8_t x = 5, y = -10; int8_t result = 2 * add(x, y); // main also holds RV(add) (1 byte) — add: RA 8 + a 1 + b 1 + result 1 = 11. main: RA 8 + x 1 + y 1 + result 1 + RV(add) 1 = 12.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in each variable as the program runs. void C(int z) { int c = z + 1; } void B(int y) { int b = y * 2; C(b); } void A() { int a = 10; B(a); } int main() { A(); } — a (10) is copied into y; b = 20 is copied into z; c = z + 1 = 21. At C’s deepest point four frames exist: main, A, B, C.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in the values. ( square returns before addOne is called.) int square(int x) { int result = x * x; return result; } int addOne(int x) { int result = x + 1; return result; } int calculate() { int answer = addOne(square(5)); return answer; } — The inner call finishes first: square(5) = 25 is placed in RV(square), its frame is X’d, and only then is addOne(25) called. addOne’s frame may reuse the memory square’s frame used.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in the values after the call returns. int32_t example(int32_t a[3], int32_t b[3], int32_t size, int32_t c) { for (int64_t i = 0; i < size; i++) { a[i] = b[i] + i; b[i] = a[i] - c; c++; } return c; } /* main: */ int32_t x[3] = {10, 20, 30}; int32_t y[3] = {40, 50, 60}; int32_t demo = x[0] + y[0]; int32_t ret_val = example(x, y, 3, demo); — Both arrays are shared (changed in main), while c is a copy that counts 50, 51, 52, 53 and is returned. demo, passed by value, stays 50.

title: Mastery: CL04 Stack frames
text: Fill in main’s values after the call. #define ARR_SIZE 5 int32_t example(int32_t arr[ARR_SIZE], int32_t size, int32_t sum) { sum = 0; for (int16_t i = 0; i < size; i++) { sum += arr[i]; arr[i]++; } return arr[0]; } /* main: */ int32_t a[ARR_SIZE] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}; int32_t sum = 7; int32_t ret_val = example(a, ARR_SIZE, sum); — Every element is incremented through the pointer (arrays are shared). title: Mastery: CL05 · $PATH, globbing, regex, find & grep
text: How the shell finds a command, how globs expand before a command runs, how regular expressions match text, and how find and grep use them. A command containing a slash ( ./hello , ../bin/hello , /usr/bin/hello ) is a path : run exactly that file. A command with no slash ( hello , ls ) makes the shell search $PATH . $PATH is a colon-separated list of directories searched left to right; first match wins . To make your own program win, prepend its directory: export PATH="/home/me/project:$PATH" . The current directory is deliberately not on PATH: otherwise a malicious file named ls in a downloaded folder could run instead of the real one. ./ says “yes, I mean this one.” Globbing is filename expansion by the shell, before the command runs : * any characters, ? exactly one, [abc] / [a-z] one from a set or range. cat *.txt becomes cat dog.txt notes.txt ; cat never sees the star. Regex is a pattern a program uses to match text: classes [abc] , quantifiers * + ? {n} {n,} {n,m} , anchors ^ $ , and \ to escape ( . means any one character, \. a literal dot). Glob vs regex: any sequence is * vs .* ; any one char ? vs . ; literal dot . vs \. . find -name takes a glob (quote it); grep takes a regex (use -E for {n,m} , + , ? ). Common trap: Typing hello for a program in the current directory. No slash means a PATH search, which does not look in . . Common trap: Appending to PATH when you needed to prepend: a directory at the end loses to any earlier match. Common trap: An unquoted glob in find -name *.c : the shell expands it first, so find receives file names instead of a pattern. Write -name "*.c" . Common trap: grep "_[0-9]{2}$" without -E treats the braces literally and matches nothing. Common trap: Un-anchored regexes match inside longer text: ID-[0-9]{3} matches abcID-123xyz ; ^ID-[0-9]{3}$ does not.

title: Mastery: CL06 · Number representation: bases, binary & hex
text: Positional notation in base 10, 2 and 16; converting by hand in every direction; bit positions, bytes and words; how many values n bits can hold. Every positional system works the same way: each digit is multiplied by base position and the products are added. 507 in decimal is 5×10² + 0×10¹ + 7×10⁰; 0b1011 is 1×2³ + 0×2² + 1×2¹ + 1×2⁰ = 11. Bits are numbered from the right starting at 0 . In an n-bit number the leftmost bit is bit n−1 (the most significant bit, MSB ) and the rightmost is bit 0 (the least significant bit, LSB ). Decimal → binary : repeatedly subtract the largest power of 2 that fits and put a 1 in that position (114 = 64 + 32 + 16 + 2 = 0b111_0010 ). Know 0 through 15 in binary by heart, and the powers 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. Hex uses digits 0–9 then A–F (A=10 … F=15). One hex digit is exactly 4 bits , so hex ↔ binary is a digit-by-digit lookup with no arithmetic: 0xA7 = 1010 0111 . Group binary in fours from the right ( 0b10_1010_0011 ). When going binary → hex pad the leftmost group with leading zeros mentally; when going hex → binary keep every leading zero. n bits hold 2 n distinct patterns. Unsigned that is 0 to 2 n −1. A byte is 8 bits (two hex digits); a word here is 32 bits (4 bytes). Common trap: Numbering bits from the left. In 0b1000_0001 the 1s are bits 7 and 0. Common trap: Reading a prefix-less number as base 10 when it has 0b or 0x in front (and the reverse). Common trap: Forgetting leading zeros in hex → binary: 0x3C9 is 0011_1100_1001 , 12 bits, not 10. Common trap: Saying n bits hold 2n values. It is 2 n , and the largest unsigned value is one less than that. Common trap: Grouping binary from the left instead of the right when converting to hex.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How do you read a positional number in base b? — Multiply each digit by b position (position 0 on the right) and add. 0b1011 = 8+0+2+1 = 11.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Which bit is bit 0, and which is the MSB? — Bit 0 is the rightmost (LSB, worth 1). The MSB is the leftmost bit, bit n−1 of an n-bit number.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How do you write a binary number in C or by hand? — 0b prefix ( 0b1001 ) or a subscript 2. Group in fours from the right, with spaces by hand and underscores when typed: 0b1010_1111_0101 .

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Decimal → binary method? — Find the largest power of 2 ≤ the number, put a 1 there, subtract, repeat until the remainder is 0. Unused positions are 0.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Binary → decimal method? — Add the powers of 2 under every 1 bit. 0b10010 = 16 + 2 = 18.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What digits does hex use? — 0–9 then A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15. Prefix 0x .

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How many bits is one hex digit? — Exactly 4 (a “nibble”). That is why hex is the compact form of binary.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Binary → hex? — Group bits in fours from the right , pad the left group with zeros, and translate each group: 1101 0101 → D5.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Hex → binary? — Replace each hex digit by its 4 bits and keep leading zeros: 0x3C9 → 0011 1100 1001.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Hex → decimal? — Multiply digits by powers of 16: 0x2A = 2×16 + 10 = 42; 0x7C = 7×16 + 12 = 124.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How many bits in a byte? A word? — A byte is 8 bits (2 hex digits). In this course a word is 32 bits = 4 bytes.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How many values can n bits represent? — 2 n patterns. 7 bits → 128; 8 bits → 256; 16 bits → 65,536.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Unsigned range of n bits? — 0 to 2 n − 1. 8 bits: 0–255; 4 bits: 0–15.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Why do we use hex for addresses and masks? — It is shorter and readable for humans yet maps digit-by-digit onto the bits the hardware stores. Decimal does not align with powers of two.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What does the prefix on a number tell you? — 0b = binary, 0x = hex, no prefix = decimal. Always check before converting.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What does the 0x prefix tell you about 0x1A ? — 0x marks hex; 0b marks binary; no prefix means decimal.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: In 0b1100 , which statement is true? — Bits are named n−1 down to 0 from left to right, so the rightmost is bit 0.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What is the value of the hex digit C ? — A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14, F=15.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Which bit is the most significant bit of 0b0100_1101 ? — The MSB is the leftmost position, bit n−1, whether or not it is a 1.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What happens when you add 1 to the hex digit F ? — Like 9 + 1 in decimal: the digit resets to 0 and a carry goes left. 0xF + 1 = 0x10.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Select all statements about bits, bytes and bases that are true. — n bits give 2 n patterns, not n².

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: For 0b1010_0110 give the value of each (as 0 or 1): bit 0, bit 1, bit 4, bit 7. — Count from the right starting at 0: positions 7..0 hold 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 0.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: How many distinct values can each hold, and what is the largest unsigned value? — 2 6 = 64 patterns, the largest is 63 = 0b111111; 2 12 − 1 = 4095.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: A student converts 0b101101 to decimal and gets 52 instead of 45. Which line has the root cause? — The leftmost bit is the MSB (position 5, worth 32), not position 0. Numbering bits left-to-right reverses every weight.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert 0b1_0011_1010 to hex. The student writes 0x13A as 0x1A3 . Find the faulty step. — Hex digits stay in the same order as the bit groups: 1, 3, A → 0x13A.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Arrange the steps to convert 45 to binary. One step does not belong. — Subtract powers of two from largest to smallest until the remainder is zero; unused places are zeros.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Which value is the largest? — 0b1111_0000 = 240, 0xEF = 239, 0xF1 = 241, and decimal 238. Convert them all to one base before comparing.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: A byte is written 0xB4 . Give its bits, its decimal value, and how many of its bits are 1. — B=1011, 4=0100 → 1011 0100 = 128+32+16+4 = 180, with four 1s.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What does this print? int a = 0x2A; int b = 0b101010; printf("%d %d %d", a, b, a == b); — Both are 42: 0x2A = 2×16 + 10 and 0b101010 = 32 + 8 + 2. Equal values compare true (1).

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: What does this print? (uppercase hex digits, no prefix) printf("%X %d", 200, 0xFF + 1); — 200 = 12×16 + 8 = C8, and 0xFF is 255, so 255 + 1 = 256 (as an int; no wrap).

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert 77 to binary and hex, then explain in one or two sentences why every hex digit is exactly four bits. — 77 = 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 0b100_1101 = 0x4D (0100 1101). Four bits give 2^4 = 16 patterns, exactly the 16 hex digits 0-F, so each digit ↔ one 4-bit group with no arithmetic.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Teach it. Explain how to convert a decimal number to binary and a binary number to hex, and why we number bits from the right. — Binary is positional with weights 1, 2, 4, 8… Subtract powers of two to build the pattern; group fours from the right to get hex. The rightmost bit has weight 2^0, so it is bit 0.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each unsigned binary number to decimal. — Sum the powers of 2 under each 1: 4+2; 16+4+2+1; 64+32+4+2.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each decimal number to unsigned binary using the fewest bits. — 21 = 16+4+1; 58 = 32+16+8+2; 75 = 64+8+2+1.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each hex number to decimal. — 3×16+11; 9×16+1; 5×16+13.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each decimal number to hex using the fewest digits. — 96 = 6×16; 175 = 10×16 + 15; 254 = 15×16 + 14.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each binary number to hex. — Group fours from the right and pad: 1110 0011; 0001 0101 1100; 0010 0110.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Convert each hex number to binary. Keep leading zeros (a multiple of 4 bits). — Each hex digit is its own 4-bit group.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Give each count. — A hex digit is 4 bits, a byte 8; three words = 3×4 bytes; 2 9 = 512.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: For 0b1011_0010_0110_1001 give the value of each (use 0/1 or an 8-bit pattern). — Bits are numbered from the right: ...1001 means bit 0 = 1, bit 1 = 0, bit 2 = 0, bit 3 = 1. The low byte is the right 8 bits, the high byte the left 8.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: In a 6-bit number, which bit is the most significant ? — The MSB is bit n−1 = bit 5.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Why are memory addresses usually printed in hex? — The 4-bits-per-digit alignment makes hex readable for humans working with binary data.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: For 5-bit two’s complement , give the most negative and the most positive value (decimal), and the largest unsigned value. — [−2 4 , 2 4 −1] = [−16, 15]; unsigned 2 5 −1 = 31.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Which pattern has the largest value when read as two’s complement ? — 0b0111_1110 is 126; the others are 1 or negative.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Which of the same patterns has the largest value when read as unsigned ? — Unsigned just adds powers of two; 1111_0000 = 240 is largest.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Interpret the 6-bit pattern 0b100110 in each representation (decimal). — Sign-magnitude: −(00110) = −6. Unsigned 32+4+2 = 38. One’s: flip → 011001 = 25 → −25. Two’s: 38 − 64 = −26.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Interpret the 6-bit pattern 0b111000 in each representation (decimal). — Sign-magnitude: −(11000) = −24. Unsigned 32+16+8 = 56. One’s: flip → 000111 = 7 → −7. Two’s: 56 − 64 = −8.

title: Mastery: CL06 Number rep
text: Interpret the 6-bit pattern 0b010011 in each representation (decimal). — When the MSB is 0 every representation agrees: 16+2+1 = 19.

title: Mastery: CL07 · Signed integers & binary arithmetic
text: Reading the same bits as unsigned, one’s complement or two’s complement; ranges; adding in binary with carries; unsigned vs signed overflow; subtraction by negating; sign and zero extension. Bits have no meaning until you pick a representation. 0b1010 is 10 unsigned, −5 in one’s complement and −6 in two’s complement. One’s complement is a teaching step (never used today); two’s complement is what C uses for int ; unsigned is for values that are never negative. Two’s complement: the MSB has weight −2 n−1 ; the rest are normal. To negate: flip every bit, then add 1 . MSB = 1 means negative. To interpret a negative pattern: negate it and read the magnitude. Ranges for n bits: unsigned 0 to 2 n −1; two’s complement −2 n−1 to 2 n−1 −1. There is one more negative than positive (3 bits: −4 to 3). One’s complement and sign-magnitude waste a pattern on −0. Adding in binary is column by column, right to left: each column has a carry-in and produces a sum bit and a carry-out. 1+1 = 10 (sum 0, carry 1); 1+1+1 = 11. Overflow means the true answer does not fit the bit width, so the stored result is wrong (it wraps). Unsigned: overflow iff the carry-out of the top column is 1. Two’s complement: overflow iff the two operands have the same sign and the result has a different sign (equivalently carry-in to the MSB ≠ carry-out of the MSB). Adding a positive and a negative can never overflow. Subtraction a − b = a + (−b): negate b (flip, add 1) and add. Widening: sign-extend two’s complement (copy the MSB into the new bits), zero-extend unsigned (fill with 0s). C does the right one from the variable’s type. Common trap: Applying the carry-out rule to signed overflow. 0111 + 0001 has no carry-out but overflows as signed (7 + 1 ≠ −8). Common trap: Using the sign rule on unsigned numbers: 1111 + 0001 is 15 + 1 = 16 → overflow, even though no sign changed. Common trap: Negating by only flipping the bits (that is one’s complement). Add 1 afterwards. Common trap: Zero-extending a negative two’s complement number: 4-bit 1011 (−5) becomes 11 instead of −5. Common trap: Thinking -x is always positive for negative x. In n bits, negating the most negative value gives itself. Common trap: Forgetting that the bit pattern does not change when printed with %d vs %u ; only the interpretation does.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Which representations did we learn for integers? — Unsigned, (sign-magnitude), one’s complement and two’s complement. Only unsigned and two’s complement are used in practice.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Where is each representation used? — Two’s complement: signed integers (C int ). Unsigned: values that are never negative (larger positive range). One’s complement: never; taught as a stepping stone.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Range of n-bit unsigned? Two’s complement? — Unsigned [0, 2 n −1]. Two’s complement [−2 n−1 , 2 n−1 −1]. 8 bits: 0–255 and −128–127.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Why does two’s complement have one more negative than positive? — 2 n patterns split evenly into 2 n−1 with MSB 0 and 2 n−1 with MSB 1. Zero uses one of the non-negative patterns.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: How do you negate a two’s complement number? — Flip every bit, then add 1. Doing it twice returns the original.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: How do you read a negative two’s complement pattern? — MSB is 1, so negate it (flip, add 1) and read the magnitude; or subtract 2 n from the unsigned value.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: One’s complement value of a pattern? — If the MSB is 1, flip all bits and read the magnitude as negative. 1111 is −0 and 1010 is −5.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Columns in binary addition? — Per column: bit + bit + carry-in → sum bit and carry-out. 0+0=0, 0+1=1, 1+1=10, 1+1+1=11.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Unsigned overflow rule? — Overflow iff the carry-out of the most significant column is 1.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Two’s complement overflow rule? — Overflow iff both operands have the same sign and the result’s sign differs (equivalently carry-in to MSB ≠ carry-out of MSB).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Can a positive plus a negative overflow? — Never: the true sum lies between the two operands, so it fits.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What happens to the stored result on overflow? — It wraps around (like an odometer): the answer is the true sum modulo 2 n , which is wrong for the intended value.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: How is subtraction done in hardware? — a − b = a + (−b): negate b with flip-and-add-1, then add. No separate subtractor needed.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Sign extension? — Widen a two’s complement number by copying the MSB into every new high bit. The value is unchanged: 1011 → 1111_1011 (−5).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Zero extension? — Widen an unsigned number by filling new high bits with 0. Used for unsigned types.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What if you zero-extend a negative two’s complement number? — The value changes: it becomes a positive number. 4-bit 1011 (−5) zero-extended to 8 bits is 0000_1011 = 11.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Same variable printed with %d and %u? — The same bits are read two ways: int x = -100; prints −100 with %d and 4294967196 with %u (32 bits).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: When does C extend a value? — When mixing widths, e.g. adding an int16_t and an int32_t : the narrower is sign-extended (signed) or zero-extended (unsigned) first.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Why is two’s complement preferred over sign-magnitude or one’s complement? — Adding two’s complement numbers is the same circuit as unsigned addition, and there is a single representation of zero.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What is the range of 5-bit two’s complement ? — [−2 4 , 2 4 −1] = [−16, 15].

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: In 4-bit unsigned addition, how do you know the result overflowed? — A carry out of the top column has nowhere to go; the stored result is off by 2 n .

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: In two’s complement addition, which situation always means overflow? — Same-sign operands with a result of the opposite sign is the signed overflow rule.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What is the standard way to negate a two’s complement number? — Invert, then +1. For example 0101 → 1010 → 1011 (5 → −5).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: You widen the unsigned 8-bit value 0b1111_0000 to 16 bits. Which is right? — Unsigned values extend with zeros so the value stays 240.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: An int holds −100 and is printed with %d and then %u . Why do the outputs differ? — Bits are bits: 0xFFFFFF9C is −100 as signed and 4294967196 as unsigned.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Select all true statements about overflow. — Carry-out is the unsigned test; the signed test compares signs. They can disagree.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Interpret the 6-bit pattern 0b101100 in each representation (decimal). — Unsigned: 32+8+4 = 44. Sign-magnitude: sign bit 1, magnitude 01100 = 12 → −12. One’s: flip → 010011 = 19 → −19. Two’s: 44 − 64 = −20.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Interpret the 6-bit pattern 0b110111 in each representation (decimal). — Unsigned 32+16+4+2+1 = 55. Sign-magnitude: −(10111) = −23. One’s: flip → 001000 = 8 → −8. Two’s: 55 − 64 = −9.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Give the smallest and largest value for each type. — Unsigned max is 2 7 −1; two’s complement is −2 6 to 2 6 −1; 10 bits: −2 9 .

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Add the 5-bit unsigned numbers 0b10110 + 0b01101 . Give the stored result and the overflow answer. — 22 + 13 = 35, which needs 6 bits. The stored 5 bits are 00011 (35 − 32 = 3) and there is a carry out of the top column.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Add the 6-bit two’s complement numbers 0b110100 + 0b001011 . Give the stored result, its decimal value and the overflow answer. — 110100 = −12 and 001011 = 11. The sum −1 fits, so the stored 111111 is correct. Opposite signs can never overflow.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Add the 5-bit two’s complement numbers 0b10100 + 0b10011 . Give the stored result and the overflow answer. — 10100 = −12 and 10011 = −13. The true sum −25 is below −16, so it wraps to 00111 (+7): two negatives gave a positive.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Compute in 5-bit two’s complement by negating and adding. Give the stored result. — a − b = a + (−b). 13 − 5 = 8 = 01000. 4 − 10 = −6 = 11010. 14 − (−1) = 15 = 01111 (it just fits).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Extend each to 8 bits as stated. — Sign extension copies the MSB: 1011 → 1111_1011 (−5) and 010110 → 0001_0110 (22). Zero extension fills with 0: 0000_1011 = 11.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: A function claims to detect signed 4-bit overflow when adding a and b, but reports no overflow for 7 + 1 ( 0111 + 0001 = 1000 ). Find the faulty line. — Carry-out is the unsigned test. 7 + 1 has no carry out but wraps to −8; the signed test is “same-sign operands, different-sign result”.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: The student negates the 4-bit number 0101 (5) and wants −5, but gets 1010 which is −6. Which step is wrong? — Two’s complement negation is flip and add 1: 1010 + 1 = 1011 = −5.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: The code widens a signed 8-bit value but the result is wrong for negative numbers. Which line is the root cause? — (uint8_t)(-3) is 253; widening that to 16 bits gives 253, not −3. Convert directly: int16_t wide = small; sign-extends.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Arrange the steps to add two 4-bit unsigned numbers and test for overflow. One step does not belong. — Unsigned overflow is detected by the carry out of the top column, not by looking at the MSB of the result.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What does this print? uint8_t x = 200; uint8_t y = 100; uint8_t s = x + y; int8_t t = s; printf("%d %d", s, t); — 200 + 100 = 300, which is 300 − 256 = 44 in 8 bits. 44 reads the same signed (MSB 0).

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What does this print? int8_t a = 100; int8_t b = 60; int8_t c = a + b; printf("%d", c); — 100 + 60 = 160, which does not fit in int8_t (max 127). The stored bits 1010_0000 read as 160 − 256 = −96.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What does this print? int8_t a = -3; printf("%d %u", a, (uint8_t)a); — -3 is 1111_1101. Cast to uint8_t the bits are read as 253. The bits never change, only the interpretation.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: What does this print? int a = -1; unsigned int b = 1; printf("%d", a < b); — In a comparison the signed operand is converted to unsigned, so -1 becomes 4294967295, which is not less than 1. Mixing signed and unsigned is a classic bug.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: In 4-bit arithmetic, compute 0b0110 + 0b0101 as unsigned and as two’s complement. Say whether each overflows and why the answers differ. — Sum is 1011. Unsigned: 6 + 5 = 11 fits in 0..15, no carry out, no overflow. Two’s complement: 6 + 5 = 11 is above 7, and two positives gave a result with MSB 1 (-5), so it overflows. The same bits and same addition, but the representations have different ranges.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Teach it. Explain how two’s complement represents negative numbers, how to negate one, and how to detect overflow when adding. — Two’s complement gives the top bit a negative weight. Flip-and-add-1 negates. Adding uses the unsigned circuit; overflow is detected from the signs rather than the carry-out.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Sign-extend the two’s complement number 0b0101 to 8 bits. — Copy the MSB (0) into every new high bit.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Sign-extend the two’s complement number 0b1010 to 8 bits. — Copy the MSB (1) into every new high bit.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Sign-extend the two’s complement number 0b1_0011 to 8 bits. — Copy the MSB (1) into every new high bit.

title: Mastery: CL07 Signed & arithmetic
text: Sign-extend the two’s complement number 0b01_1010 to 8 bits. — Copy the MSB (0) into every new high bit.

title: Mastery: CL08 · Bitwise operators, shifts & masks
text: AND, OR, XOR and NOT on every bit position; the identities that make them useful; left, logical-right and arithmetic-right shifts; masks to get, set, clear and toggle bits. Bitwise operators work on each bit position independently ; logical operators ( && || ! ) work on whole truth values. & gives 1 only where both bits are 1; | where at least one is 1; ^ where the bits differ ; ~ flips every bit. Identities (n any integer, 0…0 all zeros, 1…1 all ones): n | 0 = n , n | 1…1 = 1…1 , n | ~n = 1…1 , n & 1…1 = n , n & 0 = 0 , n & ~n = 0 , n ^ 0 = n , n ^ n = 0 , n ^ ~n = 1…1 . XOR with 1 flips a bit; XOR with 0 keeps it. Left shift n << k fills the right with 0s: multiplies by 2 k as long as no 1s are shifted off the top. Right shift divides by 2 k : logical (unsigned) fills the left with 0s; arithmetic (signed, usually) copies the MSB and rounds toward negative infinity: −5 >> 1 is −3. A mask is a pattern chosen so that one operator does a precise job: get with & ( num & (1 << i) is nonzero iff bit i is 1), set with | , clear with & ~mask , toggle with ^ . A mask selects the bits you care about and ignores the rest: data & 0b00001111 keeps the low nibble and zeroes the high one. The 1s of the mask are the bits you keep (AND) or touch (OR, XOR). ~ flips bits; it is not mathematical negation. ~5 is −6 for a signed int (bitwise NOT equals −x−1), while -5 flips and adds 1. Common trap: & vs && : 5 & 2 is 0 but 5 && 2 is 1. Common trap: Precedence: num & 1 << i == 0 parses as num & ((1 << i) == 0) . Parenthesize every mask expression. Common trap: Using OR to clear or AND to set: set needs | , clear needs & ~mask . Common trap: Expecting >> on a negative signed value to fill with zeros. It copies the sign bit. Common trap: Believing a left shift always multiplies by 2 k . Bits shifted off the top are lost ( 0b1100_1101 << 2 in 8 bits is 52). Common trap: Writing if (player) when you only care about one status bit: it fires for any set bit. Mask first.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: Bitwise vs logical operators? — Bitwise ( & | ^ ~ ) act on every bit position of integers; logical ( && || ! ) act on whole truth values and give 0 or 1.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: When is a bit 1 in a & b? a | b? a ^ b? — AND: both bits 1. OR: at least one bit is 1. XOR: exactly one bit is 1 (the bits differ).

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: What does ~ do? — Flips every bit. ~0b0110_1010 = 0b1001_0101. It is not negation; for signed ints ~x = −x − 1.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: What does x ^ y recover? — XOR undoes itself: (x ^ y) ^ y = x. So to get the number that XORs 0101 into 1111, compute 0101 ^ 1111 = 1010.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: Logical right shift? — For unsigned: fills the left with 0s. Equals integer division by 2 k (truncating). 0b1010 >> 1 = 0b0101.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: Arithmetic right shift? — For signed: fills the left with copies of the MSB. Divides by 2 k rounding toward −∞. −5 >> 1 = −3, −5 >> 3 = −1.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: Which right shift does C use? — Unsigned types: logical. Signed types: implementation-defined but usually arithmetic.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise
text: What is a mask? — A bit pattern used to select (get), set, clear or toggle specific bits of a number.

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL08 Bitwise

title: Mastery: CL09 · Applications of bitwise operators
text: Turning the CL08 mask toolkit into functions (clear_bit, update_bit), using shifts for arithmetic, packing several small values into one integer, and pulling colour channels out of a hex colour. Build the mask, then apply the operator. The one-bit mask for position i is 1 << i . Get: num & mask . Set: num | mask . Toggle: num ^ mask . Clear: num & ~mask (the inverted mask has a 0 only at position i). update_bit(num, i, x) sets bit i to x (0 or 1) in two steps: clear the bit first, then OR in x << i . The clear step is what makes writing a 0 work, because OR alone can only turn bits on. Shifts as arithmetic: x << k is x * 2^k . To multiply by a constant, split it into powers of two: 20 = 16 + 4, so (n << 4) + (n << 2) . Always parenthesize each shift : + binds tighter than << , so n << 4 + n << 2 means n << (4 + n) << 2 . Bit-packing stores several small values in one integer: shift each value into its field, then OR the fields together. packed = (high << 4) | low . Unpacking reverses it: high = packed >> 4 and low = packed & 0x0F . Colours are packed the same way: 8 bits per channel, so a 24-bit colour 0xRRGGBB has red in bits 23–16, green in 15–8, blue in 7–0. Extract a channel by shifting it down, then masking with 0xFF : red = (c >> 16) & 0xFF , green = (c >> 8) & 0xFF , blue = c & 0xFF . One hex digit is 4 bits, so channel shifts are multiples of 8, not of 2 or 4. Additive colour: red, green and blue light add toward white (0xFFFFFF); no light is black (0x000000). Adding a fourth alpha channel (transparency) gives 32-bit RGBA: 0xRRGGBBAA . Common trap: Clearing with OR or setting with AND. Set needs | ; clear needs & ~mask . Common trap: Forgetting that update_bit must clear before OR-ing: num | (x << i) cannot write a 0. Common trap: Shifting by hexit counts instead of bit counts: green in 0xRRGGBB sits at bit 8, not bit 4 (a hexit is 4 bits, a channel is 2 hexits = 8 bits). Common trap: Extracting a middle channel with a shift but no mask: c >> 8 still carries the red bits above green. Common trap: Writing n << 4 + n << 2 without parentheses. Common trap: Packing a value that is wider than its field: (high << 4) | low is only correct if low fits in 4 bits (mask it with & 0x0F if unsure).

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: What are the four mask operations and their operators? — Get: & . Set: | . Clear: & ~mask . Toggle: ^ . The mask for position i is 1 << i .

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: How do you multiply by 4 with shifts? By 20? — By 4: x << 2 . By 20 = 16 + 4: (x << 4) + (x << 2) . Split the constant into powers of two.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Why parenthesize shifts when combining with +? — + has higher precedence than << , so n << 4 + n << 2 parses as (n << (4 + n)) << 2 .

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Where are shifts used in practice? — Embedded systems, game engines and performance-critical code, where shifts are cheaper than multiply/divide, plus bit-packing for compression and encoding.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: What is bit-packing? — Storing several small values (flags, short integers) in one larger integer using shifts and OR.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Pack two nibbles into a uint8_t. — uint8_t packed = (high_nibble << 4) | low_nibble; High nibble in bits 7–4, low nibble in bits 3–0.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Additive vs subtractive colour? — Additive (light: R, G, B) gets lighter as you add, all colours = white, none = black. Subtractive (pigment) gets darker, all colours = black, none = white. Screens use additive.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: How is a colour like 0x7BAFD4 laid out? — Three bytes: red 0x7B, green 0xAF, blue 0xD4. 8 bits per channel, 0 = off, 0xFF = full intensity.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Extract the three channels of a 24-bit colour. — red = (c >> 16) & 0xFF; green = (c >> 8) & 0xFF; blue = c & 0xFF;

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Why mask after shifting? — The shift moves the channel to the bottom but the channels above it come along. The mask 0xFF keeps only the bottom byte.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: What is the alpha channel? — A fourth byte for transparency. RGBA packs four 8-bit channels into 32 bits, e.g. 0xA53C72FF .

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Bits per hex digit vs bits per channel? — A hex digit is 4 bits; a colour channel is 8 bits (two hex digits). Channel shift amounts are multiples of 8.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Which expression clears bit i of num without changing any other bit (the CL09 clear_bit function)? — The inverted mask has a 0 only at position i, so AND zeroes that bit and keeps the rest.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Why does update_bit clear the bit before OR-ing in x << i ? — If the old bit is 1 and x is 0, num | 0 leaves the 1 in place. Clearing makes the position a known 0 first.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: Which expression is equivalent to n * 8 (no overflow)? — 2 3 = 8, so shift left by 3.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications
text: In 0xRRGGBB , which expression extracts green ? — Green is one byte (8 bits) up. Shift it to the bottom, then mask the byte.

title: Mastery: CL09 Applications

title: Mastery: CL10 · Debugging with the VS Code debugger
text: Breakpoints, stepping, watch expressions, why output and input are buffered, how launch.json and tasks.json start the debugger (including input redirection), and the predict-then-compare habit that finds bugs. A debugger runs your program under control. A breakpoint (click the gutter left of a line number; a red dot appears) pauses execution before that line runs. Then you step and watch the state change. Compile with -g so the debugger can map machine code back to source lines. Step over runs the current line completely, treating any function it calls as one step. Step into pauses inside the called function so you can walk through it line by line. Use step over for functions you trust ( getchar , putchar ), step into for your own function you suspect. The Variables panel shows locals as plain numbers: an int my_char holding 'a' shows 97. A watch expression evaluates anything you type each time you stop, e.g. (char)my_char shows the letter, and x in hex when you want to read bit patterns. Buffering. Input from stdin waits in a buffer until the user presses Enter (or the buffer fills), so getchar() blocks while you step over it until you type in the terminal. Output from printf is held in a buffer and flushed on a newline , when the buffer is full , when the program ends , or on fflush(stdout) . While stepping, call fflush(stdout) or you will not see output when you expect it. How VS Code launches the debugger. It reads .vscode/launch.json (hidden folder: names starting with . are hidden). The preLaunchTask: "build" runs tasks.json first, which calls gcc -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic ${file} -o ${fileDirname}/${fileBasenameNoExtension} . For /home/student/project/main.c that builds /home/student/project/main . Then cppdbg (the C/C++ extension) drives GDB ( "MIMode": "gdb" ), which is the actual debugger. Debug with input redirected launches /bin/bash -lc "program < test" instead of the program itself: -c means run this command then exit, -l makes it a login shell, and < is ordinary input redirection from the file test in the source directory. Change the file name or path in launch.json to read a different input. Process: (1) run the tests, find the failing one; (2) write down what you expect at each step; (3) breakpoint at the start of the failing test; (4) step and compare against your prediction; the first mismatch is the bug. If the file does not compile the debugger will not start; if you edit and do not restart you debug the old executable. Common trap: Expecting the breakpoint line to have run already. Execution stops before the marked line. Common trap: Stepping over getchar() and thinking the debugger froze: it is waiting for you to type input and press Enter. Common trap: Missing output while stepping because printf without a newline (or fflush ) stays in the output buffer. Common trap: Reading the Variables panel as characters: a char / int shows its numeric code, so add a watch like (char)c . Common trap: Editing source and not restarting the debug session: you are debugging the old build. A compile error means no debugger at all. Common trap: Stepping into library functions you do not need to inspect ( getchar , putchar ) instead of stepping over. Common trap: Confusing bit counts and hexit counts when predicting values: show the watch in hex and compare digit by digit.

title: Mastery: CL11 · Shell config: variables, $PATH, .bashrc
text: The prompt (PS1), shell vs environment variables, export, child shells, changing $PATH temporarily and permanently, .bashrc, aliases, source, and how Python virtual environments work by editing $PATH. The prompt is the shell saying “ready”. In instructions, the leading $ is the prompt: do not type it . Its content is controlled by the variable PS1 ( echo $PS1 to see it). A shell variable is a named value in this shell only ( COURSE="COMP 211" , no spaces around = ). An environment variable is one that is exported ( export EDITOR=vim ) and so is inherited by child processes . A child shell (started with bash , left with exit ) sees exported variables but not plain shell variables. Read a variable with $VAR or ${VAR} (the braces mark where the name ends); without the $ you get the literal text. printenv / env list the environment, unset VAR removes one. Common ones: PATH , HOME , USER , SHELL , OLDPWD (used by cd - ), PS1 . Modify PATH by building on the old value: export PATH="/home/student/bin:$PATH" puts your directory first (higher priority); export PATH="$PATH:/home/student/bin" puts it last . export PATH="/home/student/bin" replaces everything and ls , cat , grep stop being found. which cmd shows which executable PATH will find. Changes are temporary : they last only for the current shell session. To make them apply to every new interactive Bash shell , put the commands in ~/.bashrc (a hidden file in your home directory; ls -a ~ shows it). It contains ordinary Bash commands that run at startup: prompt, aliases, exports, PATH changes. Editing .bashrc does not change shells that are already running. Open a new shell or run source ~/.bashrc to execute the file in the current shell . An alias is a shortcut: alias ll='ls -al' ; alias rm="rm -i" makes plain rm ask for confirmation. Python virtual environments ( python3 -m venv .venv , then source .venv/bin/activate ) work by prepending the environment’s bin directory to PATH , so python and pip resolve to the project’s copies before the system ones. which python shows the change. source is required because the script must modify the current shell. Common trap: Typing the $ prompt as part of the command. Common trap: Spaces around = : EDITOR = vim tries to run a program called EDITOR. Common trap: Setting a variable but forgetting export , then wondering why a child shell or program cannot see it. Common trap: Overwriting PATH ( export PATH="/my/bin" ) instead of extending it, which breaks basic commands. Common trap: Editing .bashrc and expecting the current terminal to change. Run source ~/.bashrc . Common trap: Running the activate script as ./.venv/bin/activate . That runs in a child process and changes nothing; use source . Common trap: Mixing up the order: a directory appended to the end loses to an earlier directory holding a command of the same name.

title: Mastery: CL12 · Quiz 1 applied review
text: The kinds of problems the Quiz 1 review used: pack/unpack a colour with bitwise operators, trace a program that passes an array and reason about sizes, work out size vs length of C strings, and write glob and find commands. Four problem families show up together on the review. (1) Bitwise on packed data: extract, modify and re-insert a field. (2) A program with several functions: draw the stack, then predict output including sizeof . (3) Character arrays: size, length and the terminating NUL. (4) Shell globs and find . Field edit recipe: extract (c >> shift) & 0xFF ; compute the new value (clamp if needed); clear the field with c & ~(0xFF << shift) ; insert with | (new << shift) . Clamp before inserting or an overflow would spill into the neighbouring channel. Stack-diagram traces: a frame holds the return address (RA), parameters and locals, each with its own size from the type ( int64_t 8, int32_t 4, int8_t 1; an array parameter is a pointer, 8 bytes). Scalars are passed by value (the callee changes a copy); an array parameter is a pointer to the caller’s array , so element writes are visible to the caller. sizeof on an array variable in the function that declares it is the total bytes (elements × element size). sizeof(x) follows the declared type, not the current value. C strings: sizeof counts every byte of the array (including the NUL and any unused space); strlen counts characters before the first NUL . An explicit \0 in the middle ends the string for printf("%s") and strlen but not for sizeof . char s[] = "211" has size 4 and length 3; escapes like \n and \" are one character each. Glob recipes: starts with → temp* ; contains a digit → *[0-9]* ; begins with a or b and ends .txt → [ab]*.txt ; ends with a digit → data*[0-9] . Recursive search needs find . -name "*.log" (quote the glob). Common trap: Adding two channels without clamping first, so the sum carries into the next channel. Common trap: Forgetting to clear the old field before OR-ing the new value in. Common trap: Saying an array parameter is “copied” into the callee. Only the pointer is copied; the elements are shared. Common trap: Reporting the element size as the array size: sizeof(int32_t a[5]) is 20, not 4 or 5. Common trap: Using sizeof where strlen is needed (and the reverse) for strings with extra space or an embedded \0 . Common trap: An unquoted glob in find -name *.log : the shell expands it first. Common trap: Glob * vs regex .* ; [ab] is one character, not the word “ab”.

title: Mastery: CL13 · Floating point: fractions, implicit 1 & microfloat
text: Binary place values to the right of the point, normalized binary form, why the leading 1 is not stored, and how a handful of exponent and significand bits trade range against precision (microfloat V1 to V4). Fractions in binary are place values below the point. Positions to the right are 2 −1 = ½, 2 −2 = ¼, 2 −3 = ⅛, 2 −4 = 1/16 …. So 101.101 = 4 + 1 + ½ + ⅛ = 5.625 , and 01110.1011 = 14 + ½ + ⅛ + 1/16 = 14.6875 . To convert decimal → binary, take the integer part as usual and build the fraction from powers of ½ (0.75 = ½ + ¼ = 0.11 ). Fixed point keeps the point in a fixed position, so a given number of bits buys either range or fractional precision but never both. Floating point stores the pieces of scientific notation instead: a significand (digits) and an exponent that moves the point. In normalized binary form 1 ≤ |significand| < 2 , so a number looks like 1.0101 × 2 6 . Example: 10.5 = 1010.1 = 1.0101 × 2 3 . Because a normalized nonzero number always starts with 1. , that leading 1 is implicit : it is not stored . Only the digits after the point (the significand bits , also called the fraction or mantissa) and the exponent are stored. The saved bit buys one more bit of precision. Microfloat V1 is a 4-bit teaching format: 2 exponent bits then 2 significand bits, value = 1. significand × 2 exponent with the exponent read as an unsigned number (0–3). So 0111 = 1.11 × 2 1 = 3.5 and 1011 = 1.11 × 2 2 = 7. It cannot represent anything below 1 or above 14. Design trade-off. A fixed number of bits is split between exponent and significand. More exponent bits → larger range, but fewer significand bits → less precision ; more significand bits do the opposite. V2 (1 exponent bit, 3 significand bits) has fine precision over a tiny range (1 to 3.75); V3 (3 exponent bits, 1 significand bit) reaches 1.5 × 2 7 = 192 but with huge gaps. A value that does not fit fails for one of two reasons: not enough range (exponent too big) or not enough precision (needs more significand bits). Microfloat V4 adds a bias so the exponent field can mean negative exponents: value = 1. significand × 2 exponent bits − bias with bias 2 (exponents −2…1). So 0110 = 1.1 × 2 1−2 = 0.75 and to encode 2.5 = 1.01 × 2 1 you store exponent 1 + 2 = 3 → 1101 . Common trap: Counting the places to the right of the point as 2 1 , 2 2 …. They are 2 −1 , 2 −2 …. Common trap: Storing the leading 1. In a normalized format it is implicit; the stored significand bits are only the digits after the point. Common trap: Forgetting that normalizing moves the point: 5 = 101 = 1.01 × 2 2 , so the stored significand is 01 and the exponent is 2. Common trap: Saying “not enough range” when the real problem is precision (4.5 = 1.001 × 2 2 needs 3 significand bits, so V1 fails on precision ), or the reverse (16 needs exponent 4, so V1 fails on range ). Common trap: Forgetting the bias when decoding a biased format: subtract the bias from the stored exponent bits (and add it when encoding). Common trap: Assuming more bits always helps both. Moving a bit from the significand to the exponent trades precision for range.

title: Mastery: CL14 · Floating point: bias, minifloat, special values & rounding
text: The 8-bit minifloat (1 sign, 3 exponent, 4 significand bits, bias 3): decoding and encoding, why a bias, zero/infinity/NaN, round-to-nearest ties-to-even, overflow and underflow, and denormalized numbers that fill the gap around zero. Bias. An exponent field with n bits stores exponent + bias where bias = 2 n−1 − 1 (3 bits → bias 3, field range 0–7, true exponents −3…4; 2 bits → bias 1). A biased exponent keeps bigger numbers looking bigger when compared as unsigned integers; two’s complement exponents would put negative exponents (leading 1s) above positive ones and break the ordering. Minifloat layout: s eee ffff = 1 sign bit, 3 exponent bits, 4 significand bits (bits 7 | 6–4 | 3–0). A normalized value is (−1) s × 1.ffff × 2 eee − 3 . Example: 0 101 1011 = 1.1011 × 2 5−3 = 110.11 = 6.75. Example: 1 001 1000 = −1.1 × 2 1−3 = −0.375. Special patterns. Exponent bits all ones + significand zero = ±infinity ; all ones + significand nonzero = NaN (undefined results such as 0/0 or ∞/∞; it propagates: NaN + 5 = NaN; many encodings so different errors can be told apart). Exponent all zeros + significand zero = ±zero ; all zeros + significand nonzero = denormalized . So normalized numbers use exponent fields 1 through 6, giving a largest finite value of 0 110 1111 = 1.1111 × 2 3 = 15.5. Not representable? If the exponent is too large the value overflows to ±infinity (−32 → 1 111 0000 ; “not enough range”). If it is in range but needs more significand bits it is rounded to the closest representable value; ties go to the one whose last bit is even ( round to nearest, ties to even ): 12.25 sits exactly between 12.0 (1.1000) and 12.5 (1.1001), so it becomes 12.0 ; 5.3125 is nearer 5.25 than 5.5, so it becomes 5.25 . A value so small it rounds to zero is underflow . Denormalized numbers fix the gap at zero. The smallest normalized value is 0 001 0000 = 1.0 × 2 1−3 = 0.25 and the next is 0.265625, but without help nothing exists between 0 and 0.25. Denormals (exponent field all zeros) drop the hidden 1 and use a fixed exponent 1 − bias = −2: value = (−1) s × 0.ffff × 2 −2 . Smallest positive: 0 000 0001 = 2 −6 = 1/64; largest: 0 000 1111 = 15/64. They run smoothly into the normalized values. Encode procedure: sign → normalize 1.f × 2 e → exponent field = e + bias. If field ≥ 7: infinity (range). If field ≤ 0: try denormalized (value / 2 −2 as 0.ffff). If more than 4 fraction bits are needed: round to nearest, ties to even (and the rounding can carry into the exponent). Common trap: Forgetting to subtract the bias when decoding (or add it when encoding). 0 101 … has true exponent 5 − 3 = 2. Common trap: Treating exponent field 111 as an ordinary exponent. All ones means infinity or NaN. Common trap: Decoding a denormal with the hidden 1 and exponent −3. Denormals use 0.ffff × 2 −2 . Common trap: Rounding ties up instead of to even, or truncating instead of rounding to nearest. Common trap: Confusing overflow (too large → ±∞) with underflow (too small → 0 or a denormal) and with imprecision (rounding). Common trap: Mixing the sign into the exponent. The sign bit is separate: negating a minifloat flips only bit 7.

text: Encode each of these numbers as an 8-bit minifloat (they need rounding or the denormalized form). — 6.1875 = 110.0011 = 1.100011 × 2 2 has six fraction bits; the dropped bits 11 are more than half of the last place, so round up to 1.1001 (6.25): 0 101 1001. 1/16 is below 0.25, so it is denormalized: 0.0100 × 2 −2 = 0 000 0100. −17/64 = −1.0001 × 2 −2 is the second-smallest normalized magnitude: 1 001 0001. 3.0625 = 1.10001 × 2 1 is exactly halfway between 3.0 and 3.125, so ties-to-even gives 3.0: 0 100 1000.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: What decimal value is actually stored for each when encoded in the 8-bit minifloat? — Round to the nearest representable value: 9.1 → 9.0 (1.0010 × 2 3 ; spacing 0.5 up there is 9.0 or 9.5, nearest 9.0). 0.1 is denormalized with spacing 1/64: nearest is 6/64 = 0.09375. 16 exceeds 15.5 and overflows to +Inf.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Which statement about the minifloat value 0 111 0000 is correct? — Exponent all ones and fraction all zeros is +∞.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Why is −32 encoded as negative infinity in the minifloat? — −32 = −1 × 2 5 needs exponent field 8, which does not fit in 3 bits.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Another design: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits (bias 1) , 4 significand bits (7 bits total), same special-value rules. For each pattern answer normalized or denormalized , then give the decimal value. — 1 10 1010 = −1.1010 × 2 2−1 = −3.25. 0 00 0110 is denormalized: 0.0110 × 2 1−1 = 0.375. 0 01 0000 = 1.0 × 2 0 = 1. 0 10 0001 = 1.0001 × 2 1 = 2.125.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Can -2.25 be encoded in the 7-bit design (2 exponent bits, bias 1, 4 significand bits)? Answer normalized , denormalized , precision or range for how it fits; then give the stored 7-bit encoding (round to nearest, ties to even) and the decimal value stored. — Normalize: −2.25 = −1.001 × 2 1 ; exponent field 1 + 1 = 2 = 10; fraction 0010.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Same design. Can 0.625 be encoded? Answer how it fits, give the stored encoding and the stored value. — 0.625 = 1.01 × 2 −1 : the field would be −1 + 1 = 0, so it uses the denormalized form 0.1010 × 2 0 .

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Same design. Can 3.125 be encoded? Answer how it fits, give the stored encoding and the stored value. — 3.125 = 11.001 = 1.1001 × 2 1 : field 2, fraction 1001, exact.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Same design. Can 2.15625 (2 5/32) be encoded? Answer how it fits, give the stored encoding after rounding and the stored value. — 2.15625 = 10.00101 = 1.000101 × 2 1 needs six fraction bits, so it is not exactly representable (precision). The neighbours 2.125 and 2.1875 are 1/32 and 1/32 away; 2.15625 is exactly halfway so ties-to-even gives 2.125.

title: Mastery: CL14 Minifloat
text: Same design. Can -30 be encoded? Answer how it fits, give the stored encoding and the stored value. — −30 = −1.1110 × 2 4 needs exponent field 5, but the largest normalized field is 2 (field 3 is reserved). It overflows to −∞ = 1 11 0000.

title: Mastery: Checkoff 1 · CLI practical
text: The Checkoff 1 skills as quick-fire commands: orient, create vs append, compile with -o, the three redirection operators, pipes vs redirects, building and verifying a directory tree, hidden files, relative vs absolute cp/mv, and safe cleanup. A checkoff rewards typing the right command from a spec , live, with a TA watching and asking “how can you tell?”. Practise with fill-in commands, not just recognising options. Averages ~15 minutes in a 30 minute slot; set up your container beforehand; a redo caps at 80/100. Orient first: pwd before anything else. git clone URL creates a directory named after the repo, then cd into it. Create vs append: > creates or overwrites ; >> appends . One missing character silently destroys data. Compile: gcc file.c -o name (or gcc -o name file.c ): the executable name must come right after -o . Without -o you get a.out . Three streams, three operators: < file stdin, > file stdout, 2> file stderr (no space between 2 and >). They compose in any order. End typed input with Ctrl+D (EOF). Pipe vs redirect: a pipe | joins two running programs ; a redirect < / > joins a program and a file . A file can not be on the left of a pipe: ./a < numbers.txt | ./b , not numbers.txt | ./b . Trees and paths: mkdir -p a/b/c builds nested directories in one go, touch creates empty files, tree dir verifies. ls hides names starting with . ; ls -a shows them. cp -r is needed for directories. .. climbs one level, . is here. rm -rf is irreversible: cd .. out first and check pwd . Common trap: Using > where >> was meant. Common trap: 2 > errors.txt with a space (that passes “2” as an argument). Common trap: Putting a file on the left of a pipe. Common trap: Forgetting -p for nested mkdir , or -r for cp on a directory. Common trap: Running rm -rf from inside the directory you are deleting, or one level off. Common trap: Not running pwd first and working in the wrong place.

title: Mastery: Checkoff 2 · Debugging practical
text: The ten sections of the debugging checkoff as quick questions: run the program, regular and conditional breakpoints, the Debug Console, step over/into/out, the call stack, finding the bug, and input redirection with launch.json. Format: one-on-one with a TA, practical, ~30 minutes. Get the debugger working before you walk in; setup time comes out of your slot. The TA asks you to predict before you act and to explain how you can tell. Skills (official list): compile and name the executable ( gcc -o ); run with typed stdin; redirect a file to stdin ( < ); write to a file ( > vs >> ); what launch.json and tasks.json do; Ctrl+C (SIGINT) and Ctrl+D (EOF); breakpoints and conditional breakpoints; step over/into/out/continue; watch expressions; print/evaluate in the Debug Console; the call stack; find a logic bug and explain the fix. Sample sections: run the program → regular breakpoint → conditional breakpoint → Debug Console → step over/into/out → call stack (other frames' variables) → find the bug → input redirection with launch.json . Breakpoint pauses BEFORE the line. Watch = you look at an expression every time you pause; break on value change = the program pauses when it changes. Debug Console evaluates an expression once, now. Step Over runs the call as one step; Step Into enters your function; Step Out finishes it and returns to the caller. Selecting a stack frame shows that frame's variables and executes nothing. Find the bug by evidence: predict what the variables should be, watch where reality diverges, then state the fix. tasks.json builds with gcc -g (the preLaunchTask ); launch.json runs the program, and the redirected configuration runs it through bash -lc "prog < file" . Common trap: Debugging an old executable because the code changed but the session was not restarted. Common trap: Typing = instead of == in a breakpoint condition. Common trap: Believing selecting a stack frame moves execution. Common trap: Forgetting that the breakpoint line has not run yet. Common trap: Fixing the code without explaining how the debugger showed the cause.

title: Mastery: CL16 · Intro to pointers & program memory
text: Where a program’s data lives (text, data, heap, stack), what a memory address is, and how pointers store addresses: declaring, & (address-of), * (dereference), NULL, aliasing and double pointers, traced with memory diagrams. Parts of program memory (lowest to highest address): text (program instructions), data (global and static variables), heap (dynamically allocated memory, grows as needed), and the stack (function stack frames: parameters, return address, locals). The stack grows toward lower addresses when functions are called and shrinks when they return, automatically. Local variables live only in their function's frame; globals live for the whole run (and are generally discouraged). An address is a byte number. With n address bits you can name 2 n bytes: 8 bytes need 3 bits, 16 bytes need 4, 1 GB (2 30 bytes) needs 30. A 32-bit address space reaches 4 GB; 64-bit addresses are why pointers are 8 bytes (hardware actually uses 48 of the 64 bits: 2 48 = 256 TB). A pointer is a variable that stores a memory address , not a value. int *p; declares p as a pointer to an int; double *d , char *c likewise. Pointer types matter : an int8_t * points only at int8_t s, and so on. Every pointer is 8 bytes whatever it points to. & (address-of) gets a variable's address: int *p = &x; . * (dereference) follows the address: *p reads the value at that address; *p = 10; writes to it, changing x . In a diagram: follow the arrow once , then read or write the location. NULL means “points to nothing valid”. Never dereference NULL (or an uninitialized pointer): the program crashes with a segmentation fault . Aliasing: two pointers holding the same address ( q = p; ) refer to the same variable, so a write through one is visible through the other. Double pointer: int **dp = &p; stores the address of a pointer; *dp is the int * , **dp is the int (follow the arrow twice). Common trap: Thinking a pointer holds the value. It holds where the value lives. Common trap: Writing p = 10; when you meant *p = 10; (the first changes where p points, the second changes the pointed-to variable). Common trap: Writing int *p = x; instead of &x (type mismatch). Common trap: Dereferencing NULL or an uninitialized pointer (segmentation fault / undefined behavior). Common trap: Assuming pointer size depends on the target type: it is always 8 bytes ( sizeof(int8_t *) == sizeof(double *) == 8 ). Common trap: Losing track of aliases: after q = p; , *q = 20; also changes *p and the variable behind them.

title: Mastery: CL17 · Pointers & functions, bytes, arrays & pointer arithmetic
text: Passing pointers to functions so they can modify the caller’s variables (swap, addOne), what a stack frame holds, segmentation faults, how multi-byte values sit in memory (little endian), arrays as contiguous bytes, address calculation and pointer arithmetic. Frame layout. The caller places the parameters , the call places the return address (RA) , then the callee allocates its locals ; with a downward-growing stack this means parameters at higher addresses, then RA, then locals at lower addresses. Pass by value copies; pass by pointer copies the address. A void f(int x) changes only its own copy. A void f(int *x) receives the address of the caller's variable (that address is what is copied), so *x = … changes the caller's variable. The call must pass an address: f(&a) . Correct vs incorrect usage. With void fun(int8_t *a, int8_t *b) called as fun(&a, &b) : *a = 10; *b = 20; changes main's variables; but a = 10; b = 20; only changes the local pointer copies (main's variables are unchanged); and calling fun(a, b) passes values as if they were addresses , so *a = 10 writes to address 5: a segmentation fault . Swap : int16_t temp = *a; *a = *b; *b = temp; called as swap(&x, &y) . addOne : *n = *n + 1; . Bytes and endianness. Memory is an array of bytes; each has an address (written in hex). A multi-byte value occupies consecutive addresses. Little endian (dominant today) puts the least significant byte at the lowest address ; big endian is the reverse. 329421 = 0x000506CD is stored as CD 06 05 00 at addresses 0, 1, 2, 3. Arrays are contiguous. Element i starts at base + sizeof(element) × i . A 10-element int16_t array at 0x34002C has element 9 at 0x34002C + 2×9 = 0x34003E . Arrays as arguments decay to a pointer to the first element: the callee gets the address, so it can change the caller's elements, while scalar parameters (like length ) are copies. Inside the callee sizeof(arr) is the pointer size (8), not the array size. Pointer arithmetic is in elements, not bytes: p + n adds n × sizeof(*p) bytes; arr[i] is *(arr + i) ; p1 − p2 is the number of elements between them (same array only); p++ moves to the next element. Common trap: Passing a instead of &a (the value becomes an address: segfault) or writing a = 10 instead of *a = 10 (changes only the local copy). Common trap: Thinking p + 1 adds 1 byte. It adds sizeof(*p) bytes. Common trap: Reading a multi-byte value in the wrong byte order: in little endian the byte at the lowest address is the least significant. Common trap: Using sizeof(arr) inside a function whose parameter is int arr[] : it is the pointer size. Common trap: Assuming a scalar parameter's changes persist after the call.

title: Mastery: CL15 · Floating point III: IEEE-754, rounding error & FP16/BF16
text: Why denormals use exponent 1 − bias, the IEEE-754 single and double formats, rounding errors (0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3), comparing floats with an epsilon, when adding a small number has no effect, and the 16-bit formats FP16 and BF16 used for LLM weights. Denormal exponent is 1 − bias, not −bias. For the minifloat (bias 3) the smallest normalized exponent field is 001 , giving 1 − 3 = −2 . Denormalized numbers (exponent field all zeros) use that same exponent −2 , but with an implicit 0 instead of an implicit 1: 0.xxxx × 2 −2 vs 1.xxxx × 2 −2 . That is what makes the transition smooth: the largest denormal 15/64 sits exactly 1/64 below the smallest normalized value 16/64. IEEE-754 (1985) is what modern hardware implements: single precision ( float ): 1 sign + 8 exponent bits (bias 127 ) + 23 fraction bits = 32 bits; double precision ( double ): 1 + 11 exponent bits (bias 1023 ) + 52 fraction bits = 64 bits. The same special-case table applies as for the minifloat: exponent all ones with fraction 0 is ±∞, with fraction ≠ 0 is NaN; exponent all zeros is zero or denormalized. Double is more accurate (range and precision) but uses more space and is slower. Floating-point units (FPUs) compute with IEEE rules in hardware, so the same calculation gives the same result on different machines (with the same precision). Use float.exposed to inspect bits: 0x44C00000 = 0 10001001 10000…0 → 1.1 2 × 2 137−127 = 1.5 × 1024 = 1536 . Rounding errors. Most decimals (0.1, 0.2) have no exact binary expansion, so they are stored as the nearest representable value. 0.1 + 0.2 evaluates to 0.30000000000000004…, which is not equal to the stored 0.3. Never compare floats with == . Epsilon comparison: treat two values as equal when fabs(a − b) < epsilon . float.h provides FLT_EPSILON (≈1.19×10 −7 ) and DBL_EPSILON (≈2.22×10 −16 ): the gap between 1.0 and the next representable number. Absorption (precision loss). Adding a tiny delta to a large value can have no effect : both numbers are representable but their exact sum is not, and it rounds back to the large one. For x = 1.0f , delta = 1e-8f does nothing (1e-7 does change it); for double the threshold is around 1e-16, because a double has 52 fraction bits and a float only 23, so doubles near 1.0 are much more closely spaced. FP16 and BF16. LLMs store billions of weights and activations, so bit width matters: 7 billion parameters = 28 GB in FP32, 14 GB in FP16/BF16, 7 GB at 8 bits. FP16 (half): 1 + 5 exponent (bias 15) + 10 fraction, max ≈ 65,504: more precision, less range. BF16 (bfloat16): 1 + 8 exponent (bias 127, same as FP32) + 7 fraction, max ≈ 3.39 × 10 38 : more range, less precision. FP16 overflows more easily; BF16 rounds more. Common trap: Using exponent −bias for denormals. It is 1 − bias , and there is no hidden 1. Common trap: Comparing floating-point values with == . Common trap: Believing a small nonzero delta must change a larger value: both may be representable while their sum is not. Common trap: Mixing up the roles of the two 16-bit formats: FP16 = precision, BF16 = range. Common trap: Forgetting the bias when decoding IEEE-754: exponent field 137 means 2 10 for a float (bias 127). Common trap: Assuming float and double have the same epsilon.

title: Mastery: CL18 · Dynamic memory: malloc, free, lifetimes & realloc
text: Why programs request memory at run time, how the heap differs from the stack, the three lifetimes in C, scope vs lifetime, dangling pointers, malloc and free, memory leaks and use-after-free, and growing an array with realloc. Compile time vs run time. At compile time the compiler translates source to machine code (it checks syntax and types). At run time the program executes; errors like division by zero, invalid memory access or file-not-found happen then. When the amount of memory needed is not known until run time , the program must request it dynamically. Stack vs heap. Stack: automatically managed, holds function frames, freed when the function returns. Heap : manually managed by the programmer, memory stays allocated until you free it. Heap memory is anonymous : it has an address but no variable name, so you reach it only through a pointer. The pointer itself (e.g. int *p; in main) is an ordinary local on the stack . Three lifetimes. Automatic : locals, created at { , destroyed at } . Static : globals and static variables, alive for the whole run. Dynamic : malloc / calloc memory, alive until free . Scope is a compile-time idea (where a name is valid, set by braces); lifetime is a run-time idea (how long the memory exists). A variable can be in lifetime but out of scope (a static local between calls). Dangling pointer : a pointer that outlives the data it points to. Returning &local from a function is the classic bug: the local dies when the function returns, so using the pointer is undefined behavior. Fix: allocate on the heap ( int *x = malloc(sizeof(int)); *x = 42; return x; ) and let the caller free it. void *malloc(size_t size) (needs <stdlib.h> ) reserves size bytes and returns the base address of the block, or NULL on failure (check before using). An array of 20 ints: malloc(sizeof(int) * 20) (never malloc(20) ). The returned memory is uninitialized . p[i] works on it because indexing is *(p + i) . void free(void *ptr) returns a block to the system. It needs no size because the allocator keeps metadata (like the size) in a header before the block. Rules: free each block once ; free only memory from malloc/calloc/realloc; after freeing, the pointer dangles , so set p = NULL (a later bad use crashes early on NULL instead of silently corrupting memory; and free(NULL) is safe). Bugs: memory leak = allocated, never freed, and all references lost (the heap grows and may exhaust memory). Use-after-free = using a pointer after its block was freed. Double free = freeing the same block twice (undefined behavior). The three together explain most heap errors. ptr = realloc(ptr, new_size) resizes a heap block: it preserves existing data (up to the smaller size), may move the block, and returns NULL on failure (the original block is still valid). So assign to a temporary first ( int *tmp = realloc(list, n * sizeof(int)); if (tmp) list = tmp; ) or a failure would leak the old block. This is how a growing list works (like Java's ArrayList). Common trap: Using sizeof(arr) of a malloc'd pointer as the array size (it is the pointer size, 8). Common trap: malloc(20) for 20 ints: that is 20 bytes. Use malloc(20 * sizeof(int)) . Common trap: Not checking malloc for NULL before dereferencing. Common trap: Returning the address of a local variable (dangling pointer). Common trap: Using a pointer after free , or freeing twice, or forgetting to free at all (leak). Common trap: Writing p = realloc(p, n) without a temporary: on failure p becomes NULL and the old block leaks. Common trap: Thinking scope and lifetime are the same: scope is compile-time, lifetime is run-time.
