title: Mastery: CL19 · 2D arrays: row-major order & dynamic grids
text: Array indexing as pointer arithmetic, how a 2D array is laid out in row-major order, the linear-index and address formulas, the two ways to allocate a 2D array on the heap, and how the same bytes can be read through different pointer types. Memory has no types. It is just a sequence of bytes; whether bytes are a char, an int or part of an array comes from the declaration and from how the program accesses them (a starting address plus a size). Reading the same bytes through a different pointer type gives a different answer (little endian: the lowest address holds the least significant byte). Indexing is pointer arithmetic. p[i] is exactly *(p + i) (the element i positions after what p points to); both stack arrays and heap arrays use base + i × sizeof(element) . int *p = arr; is &arr[0] . Static 2D arrays : int matrix[50][100]; (50 rows, 100 columns), matrix[3][7] is row 3, column 7. They are stored in row-major order : all elements of row 0, then row 1, and so on. For R rows and C columns: linear index = i × C + j , and address = base + element size × (i × C + j) . (A 20 × 30 array: [15][20] is index 15 × 30 + 20 = 470.) In a function parameter the column dimension must be given ( int a[][5] ) so the compiler can compute offsets. Method 1 (single malloc). int *grid = malloc(sizeof(int) * R * C); gives one contiguous block of R × C elements; the type is a pointer to the element type. You cannot write grid[i][j] (the compiler does not know C); write grid[i * C + j] via a helper such as idx(i, j, cols) . Everything is contiguous, so one pointer can walk the whole grid. Method 2 (array of rows). int **a = malloc(sizeof(int *) * R); then a[i] = malloc(sizeof(int) * C); for each row: R + 1 allocations. The type is int ** , a[i] is an int * (a row), and a[i][j] works. Only elements within a row are contiguous: rows can sit anywhere in the heap, so a pointer walking row 0 must be reset for each row . Method 1 and 2 have different layouts and types, so one function cannot take both. Freeing and rows. Method 2 needs one free per row, then free the pointer array ( free2d ); Method 1 needs a single free. Swapping two rows in Method 2 just swaps the row pointers ( int *t = a[r1]; a[r1] = a[r2]; a[r2] = t; ). Validate indices before use ( in_bounds : 0 ≤ i < rows and 0 ≤ j < cols ). static inline helpers are small file-local functions the compiler may expand in place. Common trap: Writing grid[i][j] on a Method 1 int * (it does not compile / is wrong); use grid[i * cols + j] . Common trap: Mixing up row and column in the linear index: it is i × C + j (C is the number of columns ). Common trap: Assuming a Method 2 grid is contiguous and walking past the end of a row with pointer arithmetic. Common trap: Forgetting to free each row before freeing the pointer array (leak). Common trap: Omitting the column size in a 2D array parameter. Common trap: Misreading bytes: the lowest address holds the least significant byte (little endian).

title: Mastery: CL20 · Heap manager, realloc & arrays of strings
text: How malloc and free keep track of blocks (free list, first fit, splitting, coalescing), how realloc grows an array, and how to build, grow and free an array of strings (char **) with fgets. The free list. The heap manager keeps a free list : the start address and size of each contiguous unallocated block. Initially the heap is one big free block. After many malloc / free calls the heap becomes fragmented : free space scattered between allocated blocks. First fit. To satisfy malloc(n) the allocator scans the free list from the start and takes the first block large enough . If that block is bigger than needed it is split : the front part is allocated, the remainder stays in the free list. free returns the block to the list, and adjacent free blocks are coalesced (merged) into one larger block. Worked example (1000-byte heap): p1 = malloc(200) takes 0–199; p2 = malloc(300) takes 200–499; free(p1) frees 0–199; p3 = malloc(100) takes 0–99 (first fit), leaving 100–199 free; p4 = malloc(200) does not fit in 100–199, so it takes 500–699; free(p2) frees 200–499, which joins 100–199: free list = 100–499, 700–999 . Resizing. A stack array's size is fixed, but a heap array can be resized with void *realloc(void *ptr, size_t new_size) . Case 1 : there is room right after the block, so it is expanded in place . Case 2 : no room, so realloc allocates a new block, copies the contents, frees the old block, and returns the new address (so the pointer may change). On failure it returns NULL and the old block is still valid, hence the temporary-pointer pattern. Arrays of strings. char **names is an array of char * ; each element points to its own heap string. Four names → the outer array is 4 × 8 = 32 bytes; each string needs strlen + 1 bytes (the NUL): "Eliza" 6, "Aileen" 7, "Akshan" 7, "Avi" 4. Allocate the outer array with malloc(n * sizeof(char *)) and each string with malloc(strlen(s) + 1) (or name_len + 1 ), checking every malloc. fgets and buffers. A buffer is a chunk of memory for data: char name[5]; holds up to 4 characters plus the NUL. fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin) reads one line into the buffer, at most size − 1 characters plus the NUL ; if the line is longer, the rest stays in the input stream. It returns buffer on success and NULL on end-of-file or error. Growing array of strings. Keep words (a char ** ), count and capacity . When count == capacity , double the capacity and realloc through a temporary; for each new word allocate strlen(buffer) + 1 bytes and strcpy it. At the end free every string, then the array of pointers. Common trap: Forgetting the +1 for the NUL when allocating a copy of a string. Common trap: Freeing the outer char ** before the strings it points to (leaks them). Common trap: Treating allocator state as address-independent: first fit depends on the order of the free list. Common trap: Forgetting to coalesce adjacent free blocks after free . Common trap: Assuming realloc never moves memory (keeping an old pointer to the old block). Common trap: Passing sizeof(char *) or sizeof(char) in the wrong place when allocating the two levels.

title: Mastery: CL21 · Garbage collection (Java) & Quiz 2 review
text: How the Java Virtual Machine runs bytecode and reclaims memory automatically, reference counting and why cycles break it, mark-and-sweep, C vs Java memory management, and a Quiz 2 review of pointer, array and heap problems. Toolchains. C: hello.c → gcc (compile + assemble + link) → platform-specific machine code → the shell runs it, the OS loader loads it, the CPU executes it. Java: Hello.java → javac → Hello.class containing bytecode → the Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs the bytecode on the real machine. Machine code built for x86-64 cannot run directly on ARM; the same .class file can run anywhere a compatible JVM exists ( platform-independent ). JVM benefits: portability (no recompiling per OS), memory management (it allocates objects and uses garbage collection), and performance optimization (it can compile frequently run code into optimized machine code). Who manages memory? In C the programmer allocates ( malloc ) and frees ( free ) dynamic memory (locals are automatic). In Java the programmer creates objects ( new ) and the JVM reclaims them when they become unreachable . C gives direct control but makes you responsible for freeing correctly; Java reduces memory errors (leaks, dangling pointers, double free) at the cost of some runtime overhead. Memory is not necessarily reclaimed immediately when an object becomes unreachable. Garbage collector (GC): the runtime component that finds objects no longer reachable and reclaims their memory. After Person p = new Person("Alice"); p = null; the object is eligible for collection. GC can slow a program: stop-the-world pauses (the program is paused while the JVM manages memory) and CPU time spent finding garbage. Reference counting: keep a count of references to each object; at zero it is eligible for collection. Example: a = new Person; b = a; (count 2), a = null (1), b = null (0). Problem: circular references. Two nodes that point at each other keep each other's counts at 1 even when the program can no longer reach either, so a cycle is never reclaimed. This is why Java uses tracing collectors. Mark-and-sweep (tracing): a GC root is a starting point the collector knows is in use (e.g. local variables). Mark : from the roots, follow references and mark every reachable object. Sweep : reclaim every allocated object that was not marked. Cycles that cannot be reached from a root are collected. Common trap: Believing garbage collection makes memory vanish immediately when an object becomes unreachable. Common trap: Thinking reference counting handles cycles: it does not. Common trap: Confusing “platform-independent bytecode” with “no machine code at all”: the JVM still runs native code. Common trap: In Quiz-style pointer problems, losing track of what p points to after p = p - 2 . Common trap: Forgetting that &arr[4] - p is an element count, not bytes.

title: Mastery: Lab 1 · make & Makefiles, Bash scripts
text: Reading a Makefile (default target, which targets rebuild, clean, missing files) and reading, tracing and running Bash scripts (shebang, chmod, conditionals, loops, globs). These were Lab 1 skills and are on Quiz 2. A Makefile is a list of rules : target: dependencies followed by a tab-indented recipe (the commands). make builds a target only if it is missing or older than one of its dependencies (timestamps), so builds are incremental . Variables like CC = gcc and CFLAGS = -Wall -Wextra -g are expanded as $(CC) $(CFLAGS) . Default target: plain make builds the first target in the file, whatever it is called ( all , entry , start , mainline ). A target with only dependencies (like all: stats filter merge ) builds those dependencies in the order listed. Commands you can predict. make : default target. make filter : only filter (and what it depends on). make a b : builds a then b (in the order given). After a successful build, running make again does nothing (“Nothing to be done”). Editing one source file rebuilds only the targets that depend on it (plus any target that depends on those). make clean deletes the built files, so the next make rebuilds everything but make clean then make green builds only green . Errors. If a required dependency ( read.c ) does not exist and there is no rule to create it, make stops with an error ( No rule to make target ). If a file with the target's name already exists and is newer than its dependencies, make considers it up to date and does nothing (even for a target like entry that has no recipe). Shell scripts. A shell script is an executable text file of shell commands run in order; used to automate tasks and group commands, with conditionals and loops. The first line #!/bin/bash (the shebang ) names the interpreter that runs the file. To run ./script.sh it needs the executable permission: view with ls -l , add with chmod u+x script.sh . Conditionals and loops. if [ $x -gt 10 ]; then … else … fi . Integer tests: -eq equal, -gt greater, -lt less, -le / -ge ; string equality [ "$w" = "cat" ] ; file tests -e exists, -f regular file. Arithmetic: count=$((count + n)) , (( count++ )) . for n in 2 4 5 7; do … done runs once per item; for f in data*.txt runs once per glob match ( * any characters, ? exactly one, [0-9] one digit; hidden files starting with a dot are not matched). Common trap: Thinking the default target is the one named all (it is simply the first target). Common trap: Believing make always recompiles: it rebuilds only out-of-date targets. Common trap: Forgetting that make clean followed by make red green builds in the order listed on the command line . Common trap: Letting a glob like log?.txt match log10.txt (? is exactly one character). Common trap: Forgetting that img*.jpg style globs skip hidden files and that [0-9] is one digit. Common trap: Mixing up -gt / -lt or using = for integers (it is for strings). Common trap: Forgetting chmod u+x before running ./script.sh .

text: A script loops over *.c in a directory with a.c b.c c.c and compiles each with gcc -c ; make would rebuild only what changed. After editing only b.c how many object files would make rebuild, and how many would the script rebuild? — make uses timestamps to rebuild only b.o; the loop recompiles every file each time.

title: Mastery: Lab 1 make+Bash
text: A Makefile has the default target all: app tests where app depends on app.c and tests on tests.c , and a clean target. You build everything, edit only tests.c and run make . Explain what is rebuilt and why. Then say what make clean followed by make app does. — make builds the default target all (the first target). It checks app and tests: app is still newer than app.c so it is skipped, but tests.c is now newer than tests so only tests is rebuilt. make clean deletes the built files; make app then builds only app (the named target), not tests.

title: Mastery: Lab 1 make+Bash
text: Describe what this script does when run and give its output: #!/bin/bash , t=0 , for n in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do , if [ $((n % 3)) -eq 0 ]; then t=$((t + n)); fi , done , echo $t . Also explain the first line and how you would make the script runnable. — It loops n over 1..6 and adds n to t only when n is divisible by 3 (3 and 6), so it prints 9. The first line is the shebang naming /bin/bash as the interpreter. To run it as ./script.sh it needs execute permission: chmod u+x script.sh.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 · Practice set (mixed)
text: A mixed practice set in the style of the Quiz 2 practice problems: custom floating-point formats, program memory, byte addresses, low-level memory diagrams, pointer arithmetic, lifetime and memory bugs, code analysis and 2D arrays. (make and Bash practice is in the Lab 1 unit.) What Quiz 2 tests (10/19 at 11 am, covering everything through 10/12: CL13–CL21, RD11–RD19, HW5–HW7, Lab 1, and the Denorm Exponent Guide). Paper, 50 minutes, no calculators, no cheat sheet. The practice problems cover: make and Makefiles, Bash programming, floating point, program memory, byte addresses, low-level memory diagrams, pointer arithmetic, lifetime, and 2D arrays. Floating-point formats are built from the minifloat rules with different widths : normalized (−1) s × 1.f × 2 E − bias ; denormalized (E all zeros, f ≠ 0) (−1) s × 0.f × 2 1 − bias ; E all ones is ∞/NaN. Smallest positive normalized has field 0…01 and fraction 0; largest has field 1…10 and fraction all ones; smallest denormal has fraction 0…01; largest denormal fraction 1…1. Bias = 2 n−1 − 1. Byte addresses : element address = base + size × index; a word at an aligned address reads directly; a byte inside a word uses little endian (lowest address = least significant byte). Low-level memory diagrams : frame starts with the return address; locals are allocated downward in declaration order; each int64 slot is 8 bytes; a pointer stores an address; &arr[j] - &arr[i] is an element count; heap blocks are contiguous from the address malloc returns. Memory bugs and lifetime : automatic (locals), static (globals/statics), dynamic (malloc); leak, double free, dangling pointer, use after free. Pointer arithmetic : p + n moves n elements; p[i] is *(p + i) . Common trap: Using −bias instead of 1 − bias for the denormalized exponent. Common trap: Mixing up the smallest normalized and smallest denormalized values. Common trap: Reading bytes in big-endian order. Common trap: Forgetting that &arr[4] - &arr[0] is 4 (elements), not 32 (bytes). Common trap: Confusing the two stack-error and heap-error lists.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: How do you build a custom floating-point format's rules? — Normalized: 1.f × 2 E−bias . Denormalized (E all 0, f ≠ 0): 0.f × 2 1−bias . E all ones: ∞ (f = 0) or NaN. Bias = 2 n−1 − 1.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Smallest positive normalized value? — Exponent field 0…01, fraction 0: 2 1 − bias .

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Smallest and largest denormal? — Fraction 0…01: 2 −m × 2 1−bias . Fraction 1…1: (1 − 2 −m ) × 2 1−bias .

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Why is the denormal exponent 1 − bias? — It makes the largest denormal one step below the smallest normalized value (no gap).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Lifetime types? — Automatic (locals), static (globals/static), dynamic (malloc until free).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: 2D array formulas? — Linear index i × C + j; address base + size × (i × C + j).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Why is the exponent used for denormalized numbers 1 − bias and not −bias ? (Denorm Exponent Guide) — With −bias there is a gap between 15/128 and 32/128 in the minifloat; with 1 − bias the line is continuous (15/64 then 16/64).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: void doubleValue(int *p) { p = p * 2; } called as doubleValue(&x) . What happens when you compile it? — Dereference to change the value.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: What does this print for float x = 1.0f; ? (1 = the addition had no effect) float x = 1.0f; float delta = 1e-8f; printf("%d", x + delta == x); — A float has only 23 fraction bits, so a tiny delta is absorbed: both numbers are representable but their sum rounds back to 1.0.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: What does this print? double a = 0.1, b = 0.2; printf("%d", a + b == 0.3); — Rounding errors: 0.1 + 0.2 is not the same double as 0.3. Compare with an epsilon instead.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: What does this print? int x = 4; int *p = &x; int **q = &p; *p = *p + **q + 2; printf("%d", x); — *p and **q both read x (4): 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 is written back to x.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: The matrix program fills matrix[i][j] = i * j for 2 rows and 3 columns, prints each row, then frees the rows and the array. What are the two printed rows (digits separated by spaces, rows separated by a slash)? for (int i = 0; i < rows; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < cols; j++) printf("%d ", matrix[i][j]); printf("/"); } — Row 0: 0×j = 0 0 0; row 1: 1×j = 0 1 2.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format A is 9 bits: 1 sign, 3 exponent (bias 3), 5 significand . Special values follow the usual table (exponent all ones: infinity/NaN; exponent all zeros: zero/denormalized). Convert 0b0101001000 … (9 bits) 0b010101000 to decimal (fractions allowed). — Exponent 101 = 5 (normalized): 1.01000 × 2 5−3 = 1.25 × 4 = 5.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format A (1-3-5, bias 3). Convert 0b000000110 to decimal as a fraction. (Exponent all zeros: denormalized, exponent 1 − bias = −2.) — 0.00110 × 2 −2 = 6/32 × 1/4 = 3/64.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format A. Encode each value as a 9-bit pattern. — 3.5 = 1.11 × 2 1 (field 4); 1/32 = 0.00001 is below 1/4, so denormalized: 0.00100 × 2 −2 ; −6.75 = −1.1011 × 2 2 (field 5).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format A. Give the smallest positive normalized , the largest normalized, the smallest positive denormalized and the largest denormalized values (fractions or decimals). — Smallest normalized: field 001 → 1.0 × 2 −2 = 1/4. Largest: field 110, all fraction ones: 1.11111 × 2 3 = 15.75. Denormals use 0.fff × 2 −2 : 1/128 up to 31/128.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format B is 11 bits: 1 sign, 4 exponent (bias 7), 6 significand . Give the denormalized exponent, the bias check (2 n−1 − 1 for n = 4), and the smallest positive normalized value (fraction). — Denormals use 1 − 7 = −6. The smallest normalized field is 0001: 1.000000 × 2 1−7 = 2 −6 = 1/64.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format B (1-4-6, bias 7). Convert 0b11010111000 and 0b00000001010 to decimal (fractions allowed). — First: sign 1, exponent 1010 = 10 → 2 3 , 1.111000 × 8 = 15 → −15 (check: 1.875 × 8). Second: exponent all zeros, fraction .001010 × 2 −6 = 10/64 × 1/64.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Format B. Encode 5.25 and 5/1024 (11-bit patterns). — 5.25 = 1.0101 × 2 2 → exponent field 9. 5/1024 is below the smallest normalized value 1/64, so it is denormalized: 0.101000 × 2 −6 .

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Minifloat design comparison (3 exponent bits, bias 3, 4 fraction bits). For each design give the smallest positive value: Design 1 (no denormals; exponent 000 is normal with exponent −3), Design 2 (denormals with exponent −3), Design 3 (denormals with exponent −2, the real minifloat). — Design 1: 1.0000 × 2 −3 = 1/8. Design 2: 0.0001 × 2 −3 = 1/128. Design 3: 0.0001 × 2 −2 = 1/64.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: For each item answer text , data , heap or stack (where it is stored). — Text: instructions. Data: read-only data, globals and statics. Heap: dynamic memory. Stack: function frames (locals, parameters, return addresses).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Which direction does each region grow? Answer higher or lower (addresses). — The stack grows toward lower addresses as frames are pushed; the heap grows upward as more is allocated.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: A 30-element int array has base address 0xAAAA0000200C (sizeof(int) = 4). Give the address of element 1, 10 and 25 (hex). — base + 4 × index: +4, +40 (0x28), +100 (0x64).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Same array. List the four byte addresses element 6 occupies (hex, comma separated, lowest first). — Element 6 starts at base + 24 and spans four bytes.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Little-endian memory (32-bit words): 0x4000: 0xE842613D , 0x4004: 0xFDA55F61 , 0x4008: 0x5A408FD2 , 0x400C: 0xB08F560E . Give the word at 0x4004 and the byte at each address. Address Data 0x4000 0xE842613D 0x4004 0xFDA55F61 0x4008 0x5A408FD2 0x400C 0xB08F560E — Within a word the lowest address holds the least significant byte: 0x5A408FD2 is D2 8F 40 5A at 0x4008..0x400B; the top byte of the word at 0x400C is at 0x400F.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: The int array {50831, 242803, 384574} sits at base 0xABCD00004000 (4 bytes each, little endian). 50831 = 0x0000C68F , 242803 = 0x0003B473 , 384574 = 0x00055E3E . Give the byte (2 hex digits) at base+0, base+1, base+4, base+5, base+8. — Each int is stored least significant byte first: 8F C6 00 00 | 73 B4 03 00 | 3E 5E 05 00.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Memory diagram. main 's frame starts at 0xFFFFAAAA0040 ; slots are 8 bytes, locals are allocated in declaration order downward after the return address (RA at 0x...0040). Final values after the program: give arr[0] to arr[4] and p as the address (hex). int64_t arr[] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; int64_t *p = arr; p[0] = 100; arr[1] = 200; *(p + 2) = 300; arr[3] = (int64_t)p; // an address! arr[4] = &arr[1] - &arr[0]; — The frame: RA 0x40, arr[4] 0x38, arr[3] 0x30, arr[2] 0x28, arr[1] 0x20, arr[0] 0x18, p 0x10. arr[3] receives the pointer p = &arr[0] = 0xFFFFAAAA0018. &arr[1] − &arr[0] is 1 element.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Heap diagram. main 's frame starts at 0xFFFFAAAA0040 ; malloc returns 0x555555556000 ; the heap array holds int64_t values. Just before main returns, give the heap contents. int64_t *arr = malloc(5 * sizeof(int64_t)); // 0x555555556000 int64_t *p = arr; arr[0] = 100; p[1] = 200; *(arr + 2) = (int64_t)(arr + 1); arr[3] = (int64_t)(p + 2); arr[4] = &arr[2] - &arr[0]; — arr[2] holds the address of arr[1] (0x...6008); arr[3] holds the address of arr[2] (0x...6010) since p + 2 is element 2; arr[4] is the element difference 2.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: For the stack frame rule used above (RA at the frame start 0xFFFFAAAA0040, then locals downward), where do int64_t arr[3] and int64_t *p (declared in that order) live? Give the address of arr[0] , arr[2] and p (hex). int64_t arr[3] = {1, 2, 3}; int64_t *p = arr; — RA 0x40; the 24-byte array occupies 0x38 (arr[2]), 0x30 (arr[1]), 0x28 (arr[0]); p is the next slot, 0x20.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Give the value of each expression. int32_t arr[5] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; int32_t *p = arr; — Each is the element at the given offset; ++p moves to arr[1] first.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: double values[3] = {2.0, 4.0, 6.0}; double *dp = values; and dp holds 0x1000 . Give each address (hex). — A double is 8 bytes: 0x1000 + 8 and + 16.

text: char text[] = "COMP211"; char *cp = text; . Give *(cp + 2) , the byte difference &text[4] - &text[0] (as the pointer difference in elements), and cp[cp[0] - 'A'] . — text = C O M P 2 1 1. cp[0] is 'C'; 'C' − 'A' = 2, so cp[2] = 'M'.

text: Fill in the lifetime table. For each lifetime type give what it applies to using one word: locals , malloc or globals . — Automatic: locals and parameters (block entered → left). Dynamic: malloc memory (allocated → freed). Static: globals and static variables (program start → end).

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: In the pointer-to-pointer version int **ptr , give two ways to write the element at row 1, column 5. — ptr[1] is *(ptr + 1) (the row pointer); adding 5 and dereferencing gives the element.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: A 10-bit format has 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits (bias 7) and 5 fraction bits with the usual special-value rules. Explain how you would find (a) its smallest positive normalized value, (b) its smallest positive denormalized value, and give both values. — (a) Smallest normalized: exponent field 0001, fraction 00000: 1.0 × 2^(1−7) = 2^-6 = 1/64. (b) Denormalized numbers use the exponent 1 − bias = −6 with an implicit leading 0, so the smallest has fraction 00001: 0.00001 × 2^-6 = 2^-5 × 2^-6 = 2^-11 = 1/2048.

title: Mastery: Quiz 2 practice
text: Teach it. Explain how to fill in a low-level memory diagram for a function with an array and a pointer, including where each local goes, what a pointer stores, and what &arr[j] - &arr[i] evaluates to. — Draw the RA, then each local in declaration order growing to lower addresses. Arrays have increasing addresses from arr[0]. Pointers hold addresses; subtracting pointers gives elements.

title: Mastery: Quiz 1 repair · Mistakes that matter for Quiz 2
text: A short repair set built from the Quiz 1 mistakes that Quiz 2 builds on: bit and byte vocabulary, answering in the form asked, two's complement in hex, signed overflow, pointer sizes, PATH commands and glob expansion. Know the sizes cold: byte = 8 bits; nibble = 4 bits; one hex digit (hexit) = 4 bits; a byte is 2 hex digits. n bits give 2 n values. Answer in the form asked. "Interpret 0xE4" asks for decimal values (228 unsigned, −28 signed), not binary. "In hex" means hex digits. Two's complement: negative n in w bits = 2 w − n; or invert all bits then add 1. −4 in 16 bits = 0xFFFC. Sign-extend by copying the top bit. Signed overflow: n-bit signed range is −2 n−1 to 2 n−1 −1. Two positives that give a negative (or two negatives that give a positive) overflowed. Pointers are 8 bytes on a 64-bit machine: an array parameter in a frame is an 8-byte pointer slot with an arrow, not the array size. PATH: export PATH="dir:$PATH" puts dir first and keeps the rest; which cmd shows what will run. Globs expand in the shell before the command runs and match whole names. Common trap: Answering in binary when decimal was asked. Common trap: Writing −4 as 0x8004 (that is sign-magnitude). Common trap: Using : instead of = in a PATH assignment, or leaving out $PATH. Common trap: Drawing a 7-byte slot for an array parameter. Common trap: Forgetting that my_data1.csv does not match data*.csv.

title: Mastery: Quiz 1 repair
text: Interpret 0xE4 as an 8-bit number. Answer in decimal. (E4 = 1110 0100.) — Unsigned: 128+64+32+4 = 228. Signed: the top bit is 1, so subtract 256: 228 − 256 = −28. (Or invert and add 1: 0001 1011 + 1 = 0001 1100 = 28, so −28.)

title: Mastery: Quiz 1 repair
text: Interpret each hex byte as unsigned and as 8-bit two's complement , in decimal. — A leading hex digit of 8 or more means the top bit is set, so the signed value is the unsigned value minus 256.

Give the decimal result and whether overflow occurs for each interpretation. — Unsigned 6 bits reach 63, so 32 fits. Signed 6 bits reach only 31, and 100000 reads as −32: two positives gave a negative, so overflow.

title: Mastery: Quiz 1 repair
text: In a diagram, modify(char arr[], char ch) 's frame holds: the return address (8 bytes), arr , and ch . Give the size of each slot and the total frame size. — 8 + 8 + 1 = 17 (padding is ignored in these diagrams).

Write the command after the shell expands cp data*.csv backup/ (list files in the order the shell sorts them). my_data1.csv data1.csv dataT.csv data33.csv data_info.csv notes.txt backup/ — The glob needs a name that starts with data and ends in .csv , so my_data1.csv is out.
